statement: In healthy, mostly white adults in their twenties, N-acetylcysteine (NAC) capsules, an over-the-counter supplement, taken during a supervised session of beer drinking, compared with identical dummy capsules taken by the same people in another session, did not detectably change next-morning hangover symptoms in a randomized, double-blind crossover trial of 49 completers (median total symptom score 10 against 13 on a 0 to 52 scale, P = 0.45), nor headache, nausea or weakness separately; comparing women with men, women's scores were lower on NAC than on placebo and men's higher (P = 0.04), a subgroup comparison among several uncorrected tests (Coppersmith et al., 2021). Evidence is insufficient to say whether NAC prevents or eases hangover: only medians were reported, without intervals; one low dose range and one timing were tested; drinking after the session was not controlled; and the difference between women and men needs testing in a trial designed for it. Side effects were few and mild with both NAC and placebo. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one trial, capsules of N-acetylcysteine (NAC), sold as a supplement, did not ease next-morning hangover symptoms compared with dummy capsules. Women seemed to do a little better on NAC and men a little worse, but that may be chance. Side effects were few and mild with both.
population: 49 healthy adults (31 men, 18 women; predominantly white, mostly aged 20 to 30) without alcohol use disorder who completed both sessions, at one US hospital
exposure: N-acetylcysteine capsules at low doses, taken during a supervised session of beer drinking (doses and timing are on the study card)
comparator: Identical lactose placebo capsules taken by the same people during another session with the same drinking target
outcome: Next-morning Hangover Symptoms Scale total score; headache, nausea and weakness; side effects
magnitude: Medians, no intervals: total score 10 against 13 (P = 0.45; 19% against 25% of the maximum); headache 1 against 1 (P = 0.93); nausea 0 against 1 (P = 0.11); weakness 1 against 1 (P = 0.72); five-item subset 5 against 5.5 (P = 0.86). Difference scores by sex (NAC minus placebo): women −3.5, men +2 (P = 0.04); nausea P = 0.05, weakness P = 0.03, headache P = 0.32. Side effects after NAC: gastrointestinal 4, headache 2, rash 1, muscle twitches 1, insomnia 1; after placebo: headache 3, gastrointestinal 1.

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Primary outcome: total Hangover Symptoms Scale score did not differ significantly between NAC and placebo (median 10 against 13, P = 0.45; 19% against 25% of the maximum); headache (1 against 1, P = 0.93), nausea (0 against 1, P = 0.11) and weakness (1 against 1, P = 0.72) did not differ significantly either.

evidence.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 1
evidence.extracted: A subset of five valid items gave the same result: median 5 (range 0 to 19) with NAC against 5.5 (0 to 20) with placebo, P = 0.86 (analysed as independent groups with Mann-Whitney tests; 91 observations against 98 expected from 49 completers in two sessions, editors' calculation).

evidence.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 legend; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Difference scores (NAC minus placebo) were −3.5 in women and +2 in men (P = 0.04), with sex differences for nausea (P = 0.05) and weakness (P = 0.03) but not headache (P = 0.32); the Discussion calls the symptom comparisons post hoc.

evidence.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Side effects attributed to the pill: after NAC, gastrointestinal symptoms (4), headache (2), rash (1), muscle twitches (1) and insomnia (1); after placebo, headache (3) and gastrointestinal symptoms (1); no serious adverse events.

evidence.locator: Limitations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: 62 enrolled and 49 completed. The authors name as limitations the low doses, supervised sessions that ended at a breath alcohol target and may have produced milder hangovers than unrestricted drinking, possible drinking after leaving, and unsupervised completion of the scale at home.

risk_of_bias.note: Well blinded and randomized, but 21% of those enrolled were lost and only completers analysed, the interval between sessions is unreported, drinking after the session was uncontrolled, and analyses beyond the primary outcome are inconsistently described.

inconsistency.note: Single study.

indirectness.note: Low doses at one timing during supervised drinking to a fixed target, unlike most real drinking occasions.

imprecision.note: Medians without intervals in 49 people; ranges are wide and a moderate effect cannot be excluded.

grade.reasoning: A randomized, double-blind crossover trial starts high; downgraded for risk of bias, indirectness and twice for imprecision, giving very low. The relation is insufficient evidence because no interval excludes a meaningful effect. The benefit in women is not part of the claim's finding: it is a subgroup difference among several uncorrected tests, with men scoring worse on NAC. The published correction changes only an Introduction passage and does not affect these results. Single study.

statement: In adults with a hangover, whether drinking water prevents or relieves it had not been tested in any experimental study up to July 2024, as described in a narrative review (Mackus et al., 2024). In the review authors' own re-analysis of 176 people with a hangover on a long walk, those who drank more water had worse hangovers, but the amount drunk was not related to how much their hangover or their thirst changed during the day; in student surveys, water was the most used remedy and was rated about 5 to 6 out of 10 for how well it worked. After a night of heavy drinking, thirst was clearly raised only in the morning, while the hangover lasted all day, and small old studies found mild, short-lived changes in fluid balance, which the authors read as dehydration and hangover being separate effects of drinking. Evidence is insufficient to say whether water helps; the figures are second-hand or the authors' own re-analysis. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Nobody had tested whether drinking water stops or cures a hangover; thirst faded by late morning, but the hangover stayed.
population: Adults with a hangover: 176 walkers in Crete (authors' re-analysis), Dutch students (surveys) and small groups of men in old laboratory studies
exposure: Drinking water during a hangover day (amount self-reported) or as a remedy during or after drinking (survey ratings)
comparator: People who drank less water on the same walk (correlation); no untreated comparison in the surveys
outcome: Hangover severity and thirst ratings and their change during the day; perceived efficacy of water; markers of dehydration
magnitude: Water drunk against hangover severity before, during and after the walk: r = 0.176, 0.243 and 0.229 (p from 0.019 to below 0.001); against change in hangover severity r = 0.103 (p = 0.174), 0.017 (p = 0.828) and 0.066 (p = 0.388); against thirst and change in thirst |r| no more than 0.061, none significant. Survey efficacy ratings for water 5.2 to 5.8 out of 10. Thirst above an alcohol-free day only at the 09:30 and 10:30 ratings; hangover above it at every rating to 15:30.

evidence.extracted: The authors state that no experimental study had specifically investigated whether drinking water could counteract dehydration or the alcohol hangover.

indirectness.note: A long walk in the heat, old laboratory studies in a few men, and ratings of perceived efficacy rather than measured effects of water.

imprecision.note: Not applicable: no estimate of the effect of water exists.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence summarized in a narrative review starts low; downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low. The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft (METHODS §6.3). It complements the later small trial of water during drinking, which found no detectable effect (Imai et al., 2026, a separate claim). The authors' conclusion that water is not effective is not adopted: no trial existed, so the finding is that the question is untested.

statement: In college students and young adults, evidence is insufficient to say whether protective behavioural strategies (things people do just before, during or after drinking to limit their drinking or its harms, such as keeping track of drinks, pacing or alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, eating, or using a designated driver) lower drinking or alcohol-related problems. In a meta-analysis of 15 randomized trials published from 2007 to 2023 (Van Nhat et al., 2026; 13 at US universities, nearly all with undergraduates aged 18 to 24), interventions that taught or prompted bundles of these strategies, mostly brief and digital and often combined with other components, compared with assessment only, education or other interventions, did not detectably change how much people said they drank (standardized difference g −0.05, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.02; 9 trials), reduced how often they said they drank by a very small amount (g −0.09, −0.17 to −0.02; 6 trials) and possibly reduced alcohol-related problems by a very small amount (g −0.07, −0.14 to 0.0007; 7 trials; −0.10, −0.19 to −0.01, after removing the largest trial, a step not described as planned); by convention a standardized difference of 0.2 counts as small. No trial tested any single strategy on its own, so the effect of eating, pacing or any other one strategy is not known; the effect on reported strategy use varied widely between trials (I² 98%) and was clear only after one 45-person pilot was removed (g 0.23, 0.07 to 0.40); 14 of the 15 trials had some concerns or a high risk of bias, all outcomes were self-reported and attrition reached 88 to 95 in 100 in one trial; whether strategy use carried the effect was tested in 6 trials, with indirect effects through it in 3 or 4 (the paper's text and tables differ). Larger effects at follow-ups of more than 3 months, and when strategies were one part of a multi-component intervention, were not tested against the other subgroups, and three of the four multi-component trials also gave personalized feedback on how others drink, so those effects cannot be credited to the strategies. Outside trials, as described second-hand in a single-author narrative review of 62 published studies found up to February 2013, which pooled no data (Pearson, 2013), students nearly always reported their strategies, drinking and problems themselves on questionnaires (at least 11 different ones), usually at one sitting and often for no stated period, so most links are associations reported by the same people, not predictions; the author estimates, without showing how, that 80% of the studies gave only cross-sectional data. By the author's account, nearly every study found that students who reported using more strategies also reported drinking less or having fewer problems, mostly as correlations whose sizes the review does not give; with one questionnaire, the link was negative when students rated how often they used strategies when they drank, but positive when they counted how many times they used them, a count that also rises with how often they drink (three studies by the author's team). In three studies, students reporting more strategies showed a weaker link between how much they drank and their problems. Over time the evidence was mixed: in a sample followed for a year after a peer intervention that showed no significant effect, correlations with later drinking were about as strong as those at the same time and changes in some kinds of strategy use went with less drinking or fewer problems, but correlations with later problems were weaker (3 of 9 not significant); in another study, strategy use rose after a brief intervention but the rise did not go with changes in drinking; and in women, strategy use was unrelated to drinking or problems at the same time point but went with fewer problems 4 months later. In two studies of day-by-day reports (a 15-day diary of 40 students, and a 7-day recall at one sitting around the 21st birthday), strategies about the way people drank went with less drinking on the days they were used, but people drank more on days they used limiting or stopping strategies, and drank more and had more problems on days with a designated driver or going home with a friend, which the author suggests reflects these strategies being planned for nights of heavy drinking. Students told to use more strategies reported using more but did not drink less (one experiment, Sugarman and Carey, 2009, which is also one of the meta-analysis's trials). In three trials of brief alcohol interventions, a rise in reported strategy use statistically mediated the interventions' effect on drinking or problems (one of them, Larimer et al., 2007, is also in the meta-analysis); in three others, the interventions did not change strategy use; none mainly targeted strategies. The author calls the trial and follow-up evidence mixed but ends by calling strategy use a promising way to reduce drinking and its harms. Certainty: low. Status: mixed.
plain: In 15 trials, mostly with US college students, teaching bundles of safety habits for drinking made very little difference: students drank very slightly less often, but the amount they drank did not clearly change, and no trial tested any one habit on its own. In surveys, students who said they used more safety habits also said they drank less, but most asked about both at the same time, and day by day students drank more on days they had a designated driver or went home with a friend, which the 2013 review's author thinks happens because these are planned for nights of heavy drinking. So whether the habits themselves lower drinking or harm is not known.
population: College students and young adults: 15 randomized trials (2007 to 2023), 13 at US universities, one at a Swedish university and one Australian pilot, mostly undergraduates aged 18 to 24 (15,714 randomized and 6,587 analysed, editors' calculation); and college students in 62 published quantitative studies found up to February 2013 (some samples appear in more than one study; countries not reported in the review), including incoming students, athletes, women and students sent to alcohol programmes, as summarized by one narrative review
exposure: Protective behavioural strategies taught or prompted in randomized trials, as bundles (limiting or stopping drinking, manner of drinking such as pacing, harm reduction such as a designated driver), alone or within multi-component interventions, mostly brief and digital; and self-reported use of strategies in observational studies, measured with at least 11 questionnaires in many versions (most often the Protective Behavioral Strategies Survey): strategies used just before, during or after drinking, such as setting a limit or leaving at a set time, alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, drinking water, eating, avoiding drinking games or mixing types of alcohol, keeping track of drinks, using a designated driver or going home with a friend; 13 of the 62 studies also counted avoiding drinking altogether
comparator: In trials: assessment only, no intervention, education or other active or attention controls, or the same intervention without a strategies booster; in observational studies: students reporting fewer strategies (between people, mostly cross-sectional), days without a given strategy (within people, two studies), control groups in trials of brief interventions, where strategy use was a measured mediator, not what was randomized, and no instruction to use strategies (one experiment)
outcome: Self-reported alcohol use (quantity, frequency, heavy drinking, estimated blood alcohol), alcohol-related problems and reported strategy use
magnitude: Van Nhat et al. (2026), random effects, Hedges' g at the longest follow-up (3 days to 12 months): quantity −0.05 (95% CI −0.13 to 0.02), 9 trials, I² 22.0%, prediction interval −0.18 to 0.07; frequency −0.09 (−0.17 to −0.02), 6 trials, I² 11.85%, prediction interval −0.19 to 0.001; problems −0.07 (−0.14 to 0.0007), p = 0.052, 7 trials, I² 0%, and −0.10 (−0.19 to −0.01) without Larimer et al. (2007); reported strategy use 0.58 (−0.21 to 1.37), 6 trials, I² 97.8%, prediction interval −1.47 to 2.63, and 0.23 (0.07 to 0.40), I² 49.9%, without O'Donnell et al. (2019). Subgroups, without between-subgroup tests (intervals only in supplements): follow-up over 3 months, quantity −0.12 and frequency −0.13; strategies as an adjunct, quantity −0.10 and frequency −0.13; as a core or primary component, no significant effect on quantity. Risk of bias: 1 trial low, 10 some concerns, 4 high (Fig. 2). Mediation through strategy use in 3 or 4 of 6 trials. Pearson (2013): no pooled estimate; the review gives sizes for almost none of the strategy–outcome links. As described: nearly every study found that students reporting more strategies reported drinking less and/or fewer problems; with one questionnaire, correlations with drinking were negative on a how-often-when-drinking scale and positive on a scale counting the number of times strategies were used, which also counts drinking occasions (3 studies); a weaker drinking–problems link in 3 studies; in one sample followed for 12 months, prospective correlations with drinking similar to same-time ones, change in some kinds of strategy use predicting less drinking or fewer problems, and 3 of 9 prospective correlations with problems not significant; day by day (2 studies, one a 15-day diary of 40 students): less drinking on days with manner-of-drinking strategies, more on days with limiting or stopping strategies, more drinking and more problems on days with serious harm reduction strategies; mediation of intervention effects in 3 trials, no change in strategy use in 3 trials; no fall in drinking after an instruction to use more strategies (1 experiment). Studies with only cross-sectional data: 80% by the author's estimate (not derived; editors' rough count from the review's appendix, about 74% to 77%).

risk_of_bias.note: Trials (card sc_van_nhat_2026): 14 of 15 at some concerns or high risk of bias by the review's RoB 2 figure, mainly from deviations from the intended interventions and missing outcome data; every outcome self-reported; attrition up to 95%; no sensitivity analysis by risk of bias. Observational studies (card sc_pearson_2013): strategies and outcomes self-reported, nearly always at the same sitting, mostly cross-sectional, unappraised, the review's author a co-author of 7 of the 62 studies.

inconsistency.note: The trial estimates for drinking and problems agree (I² 0% to 22%). The observational findings point different ways by strategy and design (less drinking between people, more on days with some strategies), which the status 'mixed' records; the very heterogeneous effect on reported strategy use (I² 98%) is not a drinking outcome. Not rated down, because the graded finding rests on the trials.

indirectness.note: No trial isolated a single strategy: strategies were taught in bundles, often with personalized normative feedback, against a mix of controls, so the effect of the strategies themselves, or of strategies people choose on their own, is not measured; almost all participants were young US university students.

imprecision.note: The intervals for quantity, frequency and problems are narrow and exclude more than a small effect (none goes beyond −0.19); the problems estimate reaches no difference.

publication_bias.note: No funnel asymmetry in any pool, though with 6 to 9 trials the tests have little power; English-language peer-reviewed reports only, without trial registries or grey literature. Not rated down.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; rated down for risk of bias (14 of 15 trials at some concerns or high risk, self-reported outcomes) and indirectness (bundles taught with other components, not single strategies; US students), giving low for what the trials show: teaching bundles of strategies changed reported drinking very little. The relation stays insufficient evidence for the claim's question, whether the strategies themselves lower drinking or harms: no trial tested any single strategy, the bundles' effects are very small and partly attributable to other components, and the observational associations, which by themselves would be very low (narrative review only), point different ways by design. The meta-analysis is AMSTAR 2 low confidence (provisional: its list of excluded studies is in an appendix not read), searched English-language peer-reviewed reports only, and its abstract leads with estimates made after dropping a trial; its PRISMA counts do not add up (564 records by database against 514 printed). Counted once: Larimer et al. (2007) and Sugarman and Carey (2009), described in the 2013 review, are among the meta-analysis's trials. Status mixed: the observational findings differ in direction by strategy and design, with only the review author's untested explanation, while the trials show very small or no effects. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review.

statement: In people diagnosed with eye damage after using poppers (113 people in 32 published reports, 2004 to 2021, pooled in a systematic review), evidence is insufficient to say whether stopping poppers, or taking lutein supplements, compared with continuing or not taking them, helps vision recover: treatment was documented for 45 people, of whom 42 were advised to stop (3 of them also given lutein) and 2 were given lutein alone; whether people really stopped was recorded for 27 (19 had); there was no comparison group, and the review states that the effect of treatment or of stopping on vision could not be analysed. Scans improved in most of those followed up (46 of 75), but this cannot be tied to stopping: of the two people followed longest, one who reportedly kept using had unchanged vision and one whose stopping was not recorded improved, and some earlier series saw no improvement in the first months despite stopping. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Most people with this eye damage were told to stop using poppers, and a few were given lutein, a supplement, but nobody compared them with people who did not stop, so we do not know whether stopping or lutein helps the eyes recover. Many got better over time either way, as far as the reports show.
population: People diagnosed with eye damage after poppers use (113 published cases, 2004 to 2021)
exposure: Stopping poppers use, or oral lutein
comparator: Continuing use, or no lutein (no comparison group in the reports)
outcome: Recovery of vision and of retinal findings
magnitude: No comparative data. Stopping advised for 42 of the 45 with treatment documented; lutein for 5 (3 with stopping, 2 alone); compliance recorded for 27 (19 compliant); OCT improved or resolved in 46 of 75 followed up, without data by stopping.

statement: In people who use benzodiazepines, evidence is insufficient to say whether anything they do themselves before or during use lowers harm: as described second-hand in a 2025 scoping review of 35 sources that did not appraise them (Morrison et al., 2025), no source compared people who used such a practice with people who did not, and none measured harm as an outcome of a practice. Practices appear as people's accounts, researchers' recommendations and reports of behaviour after drug checking: in a study of a Swedish online drug forum about flubromazolam (122 in the review's table), posters described limiting their own access to the drug while intoxicated, staying at home, limiting how often they used, avoiding alcohol at the same time and comparing vendors and batches; in British Columbia during COVID-19, women and gender-diverse people who use drugs (45, in a qualitative study) formed informal peer networks to check on one another because of benzodiazepine contamination and the risk of sexual assault; in an ethnography in Melbourne, one participant described using temazepam at home to avoid losing money or drugs, or being arrested, while sedated; and the authors of a survey of 252 people who inject drugs in Bangkok called for education against injecting alone. Numbers come only from two drug-checking studies, and they describe behaviour, not harm: in a before-and-after pilot without a comparison group, in which 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore received fentanyl test strips, 69% of the 68 followed up a month later reported doing something to lower harm after a result, such as asking someone to check on them, and reported using alone fell from 96% to 68%; and in an observational study of 541 adults who use drugs in several US states, a positive fentanyl test-strip result went, over 28 days, with reports of using smaller amounts, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, most strongly when benzodiazepines were tested (an association in the review's table, which its text words as a result of the strip). The review searched on terms such as harm reduction and did not cover peer-led resources, so practices described elsewhere may be missing; its authors find harm reduction largely absent for people who are not seeking abstinence or treatment. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: People who use benzos describe staying at home, keeping the drug out of reach while high, avoiding alcohol at the same time and having friends check on them. In two studies of fentanyl test strips, people said they took more care after a positive result, such as having someone check on them, but harm was not measured. No study found by a 2025 review compared people who do these things with people who do not, so it is not known whether any of them lowers harm.
population: People who use benzodiazepines, including novel ones, in forum, qualitative, ethnographic, survey, pilot and observational sources gathered by one scoping review: posters on a Swedish drug forum; 45 women and gender-diverse people who use drugs in British Columbia; one participant in Melbourne; 252 people who inject drugs in Bangkok; 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore; 541 adults who use drugs in several US states
exposure: Practices people use themselves before or during use, as described: limiting their own access to the drug while intoxicated, staying at home, limiting how often they use, avoiding alcohol at the same time, comparing vendors and batches, peer check-ins, not using or injecting alone; and reported behaviour after a test-strip result (asking someone to check on them, using smaller amounts, taking turns, keeping naloxone nearby)
comparator: None: no source compared people using a practice with people not using it; the two test-strip studies compared reports before and after receiving strips, or related behaviour to the strip result
outcome: Any harm, such as overdose, assault, injury or arrest (not measured against a comparison in any source); reported behaviour after a test-strip result
magnitude: No source compared people who used a practice with people who did not, and none measured harm. Behaviour after test strips: in a before-and-after pilot (68 of 103 followed up at one month, no control group), reported using alone was 96% before and 68% after, and 69% reported a harm reduction behaviour after a result; in an observational study of 541 adults over 28 days, a positive result went with using smaller amounts, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, most strongly when benzodiazepines were tested (sizes given only in the review's table, second-hand).

statement:
In adults in a pooled analysis of six case-control studies (2,159 people with lung cancer and 2,985 controls; four of the six studies unpublished) and in Swedish male military conscripts (49,321 at the start, 44,257 in the cannabis analysis) followed for 40 years, to about age 60 (the pooled analysis as described by the National Academies committee, a narrative review, and not read here, so its figures are second-hand; the cohort from its own paper, read in full), evidence is insufficient to say whether smoking cannabis, compared with not smoking cannabis, changes the incidence of lung cancer.

In the pooled analysis, habitual cannabis smoking (at least 1 joint-year) against non-habitual (under 1 joint-year, including never) gave an odds ratio of 0.96 (95% CI 0.66–1.38), and 1.03 (0.51–2.08) among people who did not smoke tobacco; for adenocarcinoma alone the odds ratios were 1.73 (0.75–4.00) for more than 1 joint a day and 1.74 (0.85–3.56) for more than 10 joint-years, not significant. The committee says risk rose with duration and intensity without becoming significant. In the Swedish cohort (the paper itself), 'heavy' use meant reporting, once, at conscription at age 18 to 20, more than 50 uses of cannabis in a lifetime (831 men, 1.7%). These men had a hazard ratio of 2.12 (1.08–4.14) for lung cancer against men who reported never using cannabis, adjusted for tobacco smoking (in three bands: none, 1 to 10 and more than 10 cigarettes a day), alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status, each measured only at conscription; unadjusted it was 3.72 (1.96–7.06), and adjusted for tobacco alone 2.24 (1.17–4.29). Ever having used cannabis was not associated with lung cancer once tobacco was counted (1.25, 0.84–1.87, from 1.90 unadjusted), and the lower bands of use showed no rise with more use (fully adjusted, from once to 11 to 50 uses: 1.52, 0.66, 0.68 and 1.68, none significant); the authors report no clear dose–response relationship. Of the men in the heaviest band, 91% also smoked tobacco (62% more than 10 cigarettes a day, against 23% of the men who never used cannabis), and analyses within tobacco groups were unstable or could not be estimated because too few men used cannabis without tobacco: in the paper's Supplemental Table 1, the 678 men who reported using cannabis but no tobacco had one lung cancer between them (in the 216 who had used cannabis once), so no hazard ratio could be estimated for men who had used cannabis more than once without tobacco. Over follow-up from 1970 to 2009 (about 1.9 million person-years), 189 of the 49,321 men had a lung cancer record (about 4 in 1,000; 179 in the analyses); the paper gives no count by cannabis group, so absolute risks by group cannot be given. The committee says studies in an epidemiologic review that are not in the pooled analysis indicate an increased risk.

The committee graded the evidence 'moderate evidence of no statistical association' between cannabis smoking and the incidence of lung cancer (its wording and its judgment; under it sit the pooled case-control analysis and, in its discussion, the cohort and the review). The editors read 'no statistical association' here as not statistically significant in a pooled estimate whose interval does not exclude an odds ratio of 1.38 (a 38% rise) or, among people who did not smoke tobacco, of 2.08, with a cohort pointing up; it is not a finding that smoking cannabis does not raise the risk, and the chapter's highlights go further than its numbered conclusion. A 2018 commentary sets the committee's wording beside a WHO statement (the WHO report was not read) that a cannabis and tobacco mix may increase cancer risk and that the effect of cannabis alone is unknown.

Not measured and limits, as the committee names them: the pooled analysis could not account for differences in smoking technique or in the cannabis smoked, had few people with heavy long-term smoking (imprecise estimates) and relied on self-report without biological confirmation; in the cohort (confirmed in its paper), cannabis and tobacco use after conscription were not recorded, nor how cannabis was smoked, how much or how strong it was; its authors did not know whether participants mixed tobacco into their cannabis, which they say would inflate the cannabis-related risk; and the self-reports were not anonymous, which they say may have led to under-reporting, while some men may have over-reported to be exempted from military training. Follow-up ended when the men were 58 to 60 (editors' calculation from birth years 1949 to 1951), younger than the median age of about 70 at a first lung cancer diagnosis that the authors cite; lung cancers came from hospital inpatient records to 2009 and death records to 2006, not from the cancer register; and the 7.6% of men who did not answer the cannabis questions had a lower risk than men who reported never using it (0.41, 0.17–0.99). The committee adds that cancers have a long incubation period that needs long observation, that cannabis smoke, like tobacco smoke, contains carcinogens, that cannabis use has been associated with cigarette smoking (to which 28.6% of US cancer deaths in 2014 have been attributed, in a study it cites), and that replication is needed because exposures are changing and many associations rest on single studies. No source read compares smoking cannabis with other ways of taking it.

Funding as printed: the committee's report was sponsored by US federal agencies and health foundations, with no cannabis or tobacco industry sponsor listed; the cohort paper was funded by an institutional grant from the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and by the Swedish Council for Working Life and Social Research, which the paper says had no role in the study, and its authors declare no conflicts of interest; the funding of the pooled analysis is not given in the committee's account and is not known here. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: A 2017 report by a National Academies committee graded the evidence on smoking cannabis and lung cancer as 'moderate evidence of no statistical association'. It mostly rested on a combined analysis of six studies that compared people with lung cancer with people without it, which found no clear difference between people who smoked cannabis habitually and people who did not; the results were also compatible with up to about 38% higher odds of lung cancer. A long study of Swedish men found about twice the rate of lung cancer in men who had said, when called up for military service at 18 to 20, that they had used cannabis more than 50 times, compared with men who said they never had, even after taking into account the tobacco they smoked then. But nearly all of those men also smoked tobacco, men who had used cannabis fewer times showed no clear rise, nobody recorded what anyone smoked later in life, and the study ended when the men were about 60, younger than the age at which lung cancer is usually found. So the evidence cannot show either that smoking cannabis raises the risk of lung cancer or that it does not, and none of these studies can show cause. The committee notes that cannabis use has been associated with cigarette smoking, to which more than a quarter of US cancer deaths in 2014 have been attributed in a study it cites.
population: Adults in a pooled analysis of six case-control studies (2,159 people with lung cancer, 2,985 controls; four studies unpublished) and men in a Swedish cohort of military conscripts (49,321 at the start, 44,257 in the cannabis analysis) aged 18 to 20 at the start and followed 40 years, to about age 60 (pooled analysis as described by the National Academies committee; cohort from its own paper)
exposure: Smoking cannabis, self-reported: habitual (at least 1 joint-year) in the pooled analysis; more than 50 lifetime uses reported once, non-anonymously, at conscription at age 18 to 20 in the Swedish cohort (use after conscription, technique, amount, product strength and any tobacco mixed in not recorded)
comparator: Non-habitual cannabis smoking (under 1 joint-year, including never) in the pooled analysis, also within people who did not smoke tobacco; men who reported never using cannabis at conscription in the Swedish cohort (55% of whom smoked tobacco then)
outcome: Incidence of lung cancer (adenocarcinoma analysed separately in the pooled analysis)
magnitude: Pooled analysis of 6 case-control studies (2,159 cases, 2,985 controls; committee's account): habitual against non-habitual cannabis smoking OR 0.96 (95% CI 0.66–1.38); among people who did not smoke tobacco OR 1.03 (0.51–2.08); adenocarcinoma only: more than 1 joint a day OR 1.73 (0.75–4.00), more than 10 joint-years OR 1.74 (0.85–3.56), not significant. Swedish conscript cohort (the paper; 1970 to 2009, about 1.9 million person-years; 179 lung cancers among 44,257 in the frequency analysis): more than 50 lifetime uses at conscription against never, HR 2.12 (1.08–4.14) fully adjusted (tobacco in three bands, alcohol, respiratory conditions, socioeconomic status, all at conscription); tobacco-adjusted 2.24 (1.17–4.29); crude 3.72 (1.96–7.06). Fully adjusted, lower bands: once 1.52 (0.77–3.01); 2 to 4 times 0.66 (0.27–1.62); 5 to 10 times 0.68 (0.21–2.16); 11 to 50 times 1.68 (0.77–3.66). Ever against never: crude 1.90 (1.30–2.75), tobacco-adjusted 1.25 (0.85–1.83), fully adjusted 1.25 (0.84–1.87). Tobacco, more than 10 cigarettes a day against none: 5.03 (3.23–7.81). Absolute: 189 lung cancers among 49,321 men by the end of 2009 (0.38%, about 4 in 1,000; editors' calculation); no counts by cannabis group. Committee's grade (its wording): moderate evidence of no statistical association.

Box B-3 defines moderate as several supportive findings from studies of good to fair quality, with very few or no credible opposing findings, where chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out with reasonable confidence. The Chapter 5 highlight goes further than the numbered conclusion (it says the evidence suggests that smoking cannabis does not increase the risk of lung and head and neck cancer in adults), and the Chapter 5 Summary words the conclusion as no statistically significant association between cannabis use (not specifically smoking) and lung or head and neck cancer. Reader's comment, not the committee's: the grade reads wider than the pooled interval allows, since the interval (0.66 to 1.38) does not exclude a rise, the cohort hazard ratio is 2.12, and the Box B-3 definition asks for very few or no credible opposing findings; the chapter does not explain how these were weighed.

evidence.locator: Appendix B › Literature Search, 1st to 9th paragraphs; Search Strategies (Search 2); Primary Literature: Identification and Quality Review, 3rd paragraph; Data Synthesis and Strength of Evidence Assessment, 1st paragraph; Box B-2; Box B-3; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Method, search: six searches of Medline, Embase and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (PsycINFO for Search 4; the Search 6 listing names only Embase and Medline) covering January 1999 to 2 August 2016; Searches 2 to 6 were combined into a master library of 10,759 unique articles (1,488 first categorised as systematic reviews), first sorted into seven major health endpoint topic areas and later divided into the 11 topic areas of the report's chapters; filtering to the chosen endpoints left 6,540 primary articles and 288 systematic reviews. The Search 2 listing limits to English-language human studies from 1999. Method, appraisal: possible systematic reviews were screened with six questions, then assessed on five attributes adapted from other sources (Higgins et al., 2011) and rated good, fair or poor, each independently by at least two members (disagreements settled by deliberation or a third member); only good or fair reviews informed the report. Primary studies were reviewed guided by the Cochrane tool for randomised trials and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort and case-control studies. The report says the committee was not tasked to conduct a systematic review and that literature may have been missed. Method, wording of conclusions: evidence was privileged in the order randomised trials, non-randomised controlled trials, prospective controlled studies, case-control studies, with case series only when nothing better. The committee says its hierarchy of evidence does not imply how large the observed effect is or how much the health effect matters to individuals or populations, and that its terms reflect the quality, quantity and consistency of the evidence. The weight of evidence was decided in private deliberations of committee subgroups. Box B-3 defines substantial (several supportive findings from good-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings), moderate (several supportive findings from good- to fair-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings; limitations including chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out with reasonable confidence), limited (fair-quality studies or mixed findings with most favouring one conclusion; significant uncertainty) and no or insufficient (mixed findings, a single poor study, or not studied).

evidence.locator: An Urgent Call for Change in Cannabis Research › Complications of cannabis research, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Tobacco and other co-occurring use: about 70% of people who use cannabis also smoke tobacco and cannabis is often combined with tobacco in cannabis cigarettes (reference 33, Subramaniam et al., 2016); statistically controlling for tobacco use can potentially remove valuable variance associated with cannabis use, which raises the question of how to balance specificity with generalisability; the same problem holds for ADHD, depression and anxiety. The authors suggest control groups with specific comorbidities and longitudinal extensions of existing studies.

Respiratory rows: bronchitis and respiratory symptoms (substantial evidence for increased incidence and symptom severity in long-term cannabis users; moderate for improvement after cessation of use), pulmonary function (moderate for acute but not chronic use causing bronchodilatation; moderate for higher lung volume, which the table prints as long volume, but clinical significance is unclear and control for tobacco smoking effects was poor), COPD (limited evidence for increased risk in occasional cannabis smokers, controlled for tobacco smoking; insufficient for COPD severity), asthma (no or insufficient). evidence.locator: Abstract (Methods, Results); Materials and methods › Swedish male conscripts' files; Measurement of cannabis use
evidence.extracted: Cohort and exposure: 49,321 men aged 18 to 20 conscripted for compulsory Swedish military service in 1969–1970 (more than 97% of Swedish men of that age; 2–3% were excused for disqualifying conditions), linked to the Patient Register, the National Cause-of-Death Register and the Total Population Register. Cannabis use was self-reported once, at conscription, in a non-anonymous questionnaire: ever against never, and lifetime frequency (never, once, 2–4, 5–10, 11–50 and more than 50 times); this paper calls more than 50 times heavy use. At baseline 10.5% (5,156) reported lifetime use and 1.7% (831) more than 50 uses.

evidence.locator: Materials and methods › Measurement of tobacco use; Potential confounders; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (never and more-than-50 columns)
evidence.extracted: Tobacco and other covariates: tobacco was measured once, at conscription, as cigarettes smoked a day (none 41.4%, 1–5 a day 11.2%, 6–10 20.7%, 11–20 23.1%, more than 20 3.6%), collapsed into three bands for the models: none, 1–10 and more than 10 a day. Of the 831 men reporting more than 50 cannabis uses, 60 (7.2%) did not smoke tobacco, 242 (29.1%) smoked 1–10 a day, 514 (61.8%) more than 10 and 15 (1.8%) gave no tobacco answer; of the 40,397 men reporting never using cannabis, 18,100 (44.8%) did not smoke tobacco, 12,725 (31.5%) smoked 1–10 a day and 9,364 (23.2%) more than 10. Alcohol above 250 g a week: 23.1% of the more-than-50 group against 2.3% of the never group. Respiratory conditions diagnosed at conscription (chronic bronchitis, emphysema, pneumonia or asthma) about 2% in each group; socioeconomic status from occupation in the 1970 census. The Results say about 91% of the heaviest band reported some tobacco use.

evidence.locator: Materials and methods › Data sources (p. 2: inpatient register; birth years 1949–1951); Study outcome; Validity of lung cancer outcome codes; Statistical analyses; Results, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 1 legend; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Follow-up and outcome: from 1 January 1970 (1 October 1969 for two men) to lung cancer, death from other causes, emigration or 31 December 2009, about 1.9 million person-years in each analysis. Lung cancer (ICD-8/9 162; ICD-10 C33–C34) came from the Patient Register (inpatient care, any diagnostic position) to the end of 2009 and from the Cause-of-Death Register (underlying cause) to the end of 2006; the authors cite 78% to 99% concordance between registers. 189 men had incident lung cancer (95 in both registers, 88 in the Patient Register only, 6 in the death register only), 2,958 (6.0%) died of other causes and 930 (1.9%) emigrated; ten cancers were excluded for missing predictors. Cancers by cannabis group are shown only in Figure 1, a stacked bar chart by year (values not extracted), so no absolute risk by group can be given. The authors note that the only earlier cohort ended at a mean age of 42 and that the median age at a first lung cancer diagnosis is about 70. Editors' calculation: men born in 1949 to 1951 were 58 to 60 at the end of follow-up, and 189 of 49,321 (0.38%, about 4 in 1,000) had a lung cancer record by then.

evidence.locator: Materials and methods › Missing data; Results, 6th paragraph and its continuation after Table 4
evidence.extracted: Missing answers: cannabis answers were missing for 3,768 men (7.64%; ever use) and 3,800 (7.70%; frequency). Against men reporting never using cannabis, these men were not more likely to develop lung cancer: ever-use item crude 0.52 (0.24 to 1.10), tobacco-adjusted 0.47 (0.21 to 1.07), fully adjusted 0.41 (0.17 to 0.99); frequency item 0.51 (0.24 to 1.09), 0.47 (0.21 to 1.06) and 0.40 (0.16 to 0.98). The authors ran these models to check whether the men who did not answer had used cannabis heavily; the paper does not explain their lower risk.

evidence.locator: Results, last paragraph (Supplemental Tables 1–2; pp. 6-7); Discussion, 4th paragraph (drug prevention programmes; p. 7) and 6th paragraph (limitations; p. 8); Conclusions
evidence.extracted: Limits stated by the authors: no detailed information on cannabis or tobacco use before conscription and none after it; residual confounding by tobacco possible, since more than 91% of the heavy group reported some tobacco smoking at conscription; participants may have mixed tobacco into cannabis cigarettes, which would inflate the cannabis-related risk, and whether this was common in Sweden in 1969–1970 is unclear; non-anonymous reports may have led to under-reporting of cannabis use, while anecdotal information suggests some men inflated their use to be exempted from military training. Analyses stratified by tobacco (Supplemental Tables 1 and 2, not available to this reader) gave unstable or inestimable results, because most people who used cannabis, especially frequently, also used tobacco and lung cancer was uncommon. The authors argue that changes in use after conscription would bias the estimates toward the null. Their conclusion calls the finding initial longitudinal evidence, requiring further replication, that cannabis use might raise lung cancer risk, and the Discussion proposes its use in drug-prevention programmes. Editors' note: later tobacco smoking, if more common in the men who used cannabis, would bias the estimate away from the null; the paper names later changes in tobacco use only in its toward-the-null argument, whose examples concern cannabis alone.

evidence.extracted: Supplemental Table 1 (44,257 conscripts with all covariates; 179 lung cancer outcomes), combined cannabis and tobacco exposure: men reporting cannabis use and no tobacco numbered 216 (once; 1 lung cancer; adjusted HR 3.14, 95% CI 0.42–23.10), 214 (2–4 times; 0), 100 (5–10 times; 0), 88 (11–50 times; 0) and 60 (more than 50 times; 0), against 17,700 men who used neither (29 lung cancers; reference). No hazard ratio is given for the groups with no lung cancer.

risk_of_bias.note: Pooled analysis: not appraisable here, seen only through the committee's account (a narrative review; METHODS §6.3), with self-reported exposure without biological confirmation and no account of smoking technique or of the cannabis smoked. Swedish cohort, now read in full (card sc_callaghan_2013): ROBINS-E high, for confounding (tobacco measured once, at age 18 to 20, in three bands, with 91% of the heaviest cannabis band also smoking tobacco; the ever-use association disappeared with this adjustment, so residual confounding by tobacco amount and by later smoking is plausible and would run away from the null) and for exposure measurement (one non-anonymous report of lifetime use 40 years before the outcome; no record of use after conscription, of how cannabis was smoked or of tobacco mixed in).

inconsistency.note: The pooled null result (0.96, 0.66–1.38) and the cohort's hazard ratio of 2.12 point different ways, and the committee does not show how the two were weighed; the sources differ in design, exposure definition and timing, which may explain part of it.

indirectness.note: Second-hand reading of the pooled analysis; exposure definitions differ between the two sources (at least 1 joint-year; more than 50 lifetime uses by age 18 to 20); the cohort is of Swedish men followed only to about age 60, with use as it was in 1969–70; the outcome is incidence of lung cancer with self-reported past use.

imprecision.note: The pooled interval (0.66–1.38) and, among people who did not smoke tobacco, 0.51–2.08 include no difference and a rise; the adenocarcinoma intervals (0.75–4.00; 0.85–3.56) are wide; few people with heavy long-term smoking; in the cohort the heaviest band (831 men) gives 1.08–4.14, and too few men used cannabis without tobacco for any estimate in that group.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: four of the six pooled studies are unpublished, which reduces the risk of missing studies, but the pooled analysis was not read.

dose_response.note: Not counted: in the pooled analysis risk rose with duration and intensity, not significantly; in the cohort the bands below more than 50 uses showed no gradient (fully adjusted 1.52, 0.66, 0.68 and 1.68) and the authors report no clear dose–response relationship.

grade.reasoning: Observational (case-control studies and one cohort), so the claim starts low. It rests on the National Academies committee's account of the pooled case-control analysis (a narrative review; the pooled analysis was not read, so its figures are second-hand and its risk of bias cannot be appraised, METHODS §6.3) and on the Swedish cohort's own paper, read in full (ROBINS-E high). Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 pass the floor, so the certainty is very low; any two would give the same. The relation is insufficient evidence (METHODS §6.1): neither an effect nor its absence can be shown with precision, because the pooled interval does not exclude a rise of 38% (and, among people who did not smoke tobacco, an odds ratio of 2.08), while the cohort's raised estimate is confined to its heaviest band, with no gradient below it, no association for ever use once tobacco was counted, tobacco smoked by 91% of that band and no estimate possible for men who did not smoke tobacco. The committee's grade, moderate evidence of no statistical association, is its own judgment and concerns statistical significance; the editors do not adopt it as a finding of no effect (METHODS §6.3: no detectable effect needs precision). Not rated as 'causes': every source is observational and none can show cause. The status is mixed (a pooled null and a cohort that points up in one band, not reconciled by the committee; the cohort paper does not resolve it). With the cohort paper read, the claim no longer rests only on narrative reviews; it stays a draft as a section 7 claim held for the senior author.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only, no advice. Rests on the National Academies report (Chapter 5 lung cancer section, Chapter 5 gaps and summary, Appendix B; read in full text on NCBI Bookshelf), the Cousijn commentary and, from batch 10, the Swedish conscript cohort's own paper (Callaghan et al., 2013), read in full by AI reader 91 (first reader) from the online-first PDF, which has no printed page numbers, so its anchors cite the PDF's pages 1 to 10 (the electronic supplement with the tobacco-stratified tables was not available). The cohort's exposure definition, adjustment, crude and tobacco-adjusted estimates, the null ever-use result, the absence of a gradient, tobacco co-use, follow-up to about age 60, outcome sources and funding now come from the paper; the eight new anchors need a second reader. The committee anchor that describes the cohort (evidence 1) still says the cohort paper was not read, which is now out of date. Not read and without a reference record: Zhang et al. 2015, the pooled analysis (DOI 10.1002/ijc.29036) and Huang et al. 2015, the epidemiologic review (DOI 10.1158/1055-9965.EPI-14-1026). The relation insufficient-evidence and the certainty very low are the editors' reading under METHODS §6.1 and §6.3, not the committee's: its grade concerns statistical significance over a pooled interval that does not exclude a rise, with a cohort pointing up in its heaviest band, and its chapter highlight is stronger than its numbered conclusion. The cohort's full text does not settle the question, so mixed is kept; the senior author may still prefer contested, with a debate box. Cousijn's table drops the word statistical from the committee's cancer conclusion, and its criticism of a 500-participant cut-off was not found in the chapters read, so the commentary is used only for the tobacco co-use point and the WHO contrast (the WHO report was not read). Head and neck cancer (Conclusion 5-2) was read and is on the study card, not in this claim. No industry sponsor of the report is listed; the cohort was funded by an Ontario ministry grant to CAMH and a Swedish research council, with no conflicts declared; the funding of the pooled analysis is not known here. The simple line gives no amounts.

statement: In one laboratory trial of 17 healthy adults who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days (398 days on average), each of whom completed six 8.5-hour sessions at least a week apart, cannabis flower inhaled from a desktop vaporizer, compared with the same flower smoked in a small handheld pipe (10 mg or 25 mg of THC loaded, from 13.4% THC flower, taken over 10 minutes; study conditions only), was associated with higher average peak ratings of drug effect on a 0 to 100 scale at the lower amount (69.5 against 45.7; editors' calculation of the difference, 23.8 points, 95% CI 5.4 to 42.2) but with no flagged difference at the higher amount (77.5 against 66.4), and with a larger rise in heart rate at the lower amount (23.3 against 11.3 beats a minute) but not at the higher. Average peak whole-blood THC was also higher after vaporizing (7.5 against 3.8 ng/mL, and 14.4 against 10.2), but the paper reports no test of that difference and the editors' intervals for it include zero. On attention and psychomotor tasks, three contrasts between the methods were flagged, all showing worse performance after vaporizing; at the higher amount both methods raised ratings of unpleasant effects, anxiety, memory impairment and throat irritation or coughing over placebo, with no flagged difference between them. Three adverse events were reported, all at the higher amount (vomiting once after each method, hallucinations once after vaporizing), too few to compare. Effects outlasted blood THC, which was back to zero within 4 hours while drug-effect ratings were still above baseline at 6 hours. Only some contrasts between the methods were flagged, and none was corrected for the 32 outcomes. The authors say that earlier comparisons (not read here) found similar profiles for the two methods, and suggest that those let people adjust their own dose. This trial gave a fixed amount of one flower to people who rarely use cannabis, with one pipe and one vaporizer, in a laboratory, and followed people only through each session. The authors note that the largest amount given was smaller and weaker than prerolls sold in dispensaries (from a survey they cite, not read here). It did not test joints, bongs, portable vaporizers, oil cartridges, concentrates, tobacco mixed in, self-paced or repeated use, or effects on the lungs, and it did not measure how much THC left each device. Funding as printed: a US federal health agency (SAMHSA), which also provided technical assistance on design, analysis, interpretation and manuscript approval; one author reports consulting fees or honoraria from Zynerba Pharmaceuticals, Insys Therapeutics, Battelle Memorial Institute and Canopy Health Innovations; no industry funding is printed.
plain: In one small laboratory study, 17 healthy adults who rarely use cannabis took the same cannabis flower two ways on different days, smoked in a small pipe and breathed in from a vaporizer, and also had a dummy version of each. At the lower of two amounts, vaporizing gave higher scores for how strong the effect felt, and a bigger rise in heart rate, than smoking; at the higher amount the two ways did not clearly differ. Average blood THC was higher after vaporizing, but the study did not test whether that was more than chance. Both ways made some tasks harder, and three bad reactions were reported (vomiting twice, hallucinations once), too few to compare the two ways. This was one small study in a laboratory with fixed amounts, one pipe and one vaporizer. It did not test joints, vape pens, oil cartridges or concentrates, and says nothing about the lungs or regular use.
population: 17 healthy adults (9 men, 8 women; mean age 27) who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days (mean 398 days since last use, median 365 days)
exposure: Cannabis flower (13.4% THC) vaporized in a desktop vaporizer and inhaled from a balloon, with 10 mg or 25 mg of THC in the material loaded, over 10 minutes (study conditions only)
comparator: The same flower with the same THC loaded, smoked in a small handheld pipe in the same people; each method also had a placebo session (flower under 0.01% THC) as its reference
outcome: Peak ratings of drug effect and other effects, heart rate and blood pressure, whole-blood THC, performance on attention and psychomotor tasks, and adverse events, within 8.5-hour sessions
magnitude: Drug-effect rating (0 to 100), mean (SD) peak: smoked 45.7 (26.4) at 10 mg and 66.4 (28.6) at 25 mg; vaporized 69.5 (26.4) and 77.5 (23.4); placebo 11.2 and 2.1. Vaporized minus smoked, editors' calculation (unpaired, conservative): 23.8 points (95% CI 5.4 to 42.2) at 10 mg; 11.1 (-7.2 to 29.4) at 25 mg. Heart rate rise, beats per minute, mean (SD): smoked 11.3 (10.4) and 19.1 (17.1); vaporized 23.3 (11.8) and 26.8 (16.6); only the 10 mg difference between methods flagged; editors' unpaired differences 12.0 (4.2 to 19.8) and 7.7 (-4.1 to 19.5). Peak whole-blood THC, ng/mL, mean (SD): smoked 3.8 (5.9) and 10.2 (12.4); vaporized 7.5 (5.5) and 14.4 (9.4); no test reported; editors' unpaired differences 3.7 (-0.3 to 7.7) and 4.2 (-3.5 to 11.9). Differences between methods flagged: 4 of 20 rating items at 10 mg and 2 at 25 mg; 3 task contrasts (Divided Attention distance at 10 mg; Digit Symbol Substitution attempted and correct at 25 mg); none corrected across 32 outcomes. Adverse events: 3 reported among 17 people, all in 25 mg sessions. Blood THC back to zero within 4 hours; drug-effect ratings above baseline at 6 hours after both 25 mg conditions.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Methods › Study Design and Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: 17 healthy adults (9 men, 8 women; mean age 27.3) who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days (mean 398 days, median 365, range 30 to 1,825 since last use) each completed six 8.5-hour sessions at least a week apart: flower with 0, 10 or 25 mg THC loaded, smoked in a small handheld pipe or vaporized in a Volcano Medic vaporizer and inhaled from a balloon, over 10 minutes. Method order was counterbalanced across people and dose order randomized within each method.

evidence.locator: Methods › Study Drug
evidence.extracted: Flower from the US National Institute on Drug Abuse supply with 13.4% delta-9-THC (placebo batch under 0.01%); the same weight of plant material (186.6 mg) in every session, with placebo material mixed in to reach 10 mg. The 'dose' is the THC in the material loaded; the paper does not report how much THC left each device.

evidence.locator: Table (Drug effect row); Results › Subjective Drug Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Abstract
evidence.extracted: Drug-effect rating (0 to 100), mean (SD) peak change: smoked 45.7 (26.4) at 10 mg and 66.4 (28.6) at 25 mg; vaporized 69.5 (26.4) and 77.5 (23.4); placebo (0 mg) sessions 11.2 (15.9) smoked and 2.1 (5.2) vaporized. Vaporized exceeded smoked at 10 mg (flagged P below .05) and no difference was flagged at 25 mg. Editors' calculation (unpaired, conservative): vaporized minus smoked 23.8 points (95% CI 5.4 to 42.2) at 10 mg and 11.1 (-7.2 to 29.4) at 25 mg.

evidence.extracted: Peak whole-blood THC, mean (SD) ng/mL: vaporized 7.5 (5.5) at 10 mg and 14.4 (9.4) at 25 mg; smoked 3.8 (5.9) and 10.2 (12.4). Peak at the first sample (10 minutes), back to zero within 4 hours in every condition. The paper reports no test or interval for the difference between methods. Editors' calculation (unpaired): vaporized minus smoked 3.7 ng/mL (-0.3 to 7.7) at 10 mg and 4.2 (-3.5 to 11.9) at 25 mg.

evidence.locator: Table (Physiological measures); Results › Physiological Measures, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Heart rate, mean (SD) peak rise in beats per minute: smoked 11.3 (10.4) at 10 mg and 19.1 (17.1) at 25 mg; vaporized 23.3 (11.8) and 26.8 (16.6); placebo (0 mg) sessions -3.7 smoked and -4.3 vaporized. Only the 10 mg difference between methods was flagged (P below .05); editors' calculation (unpaired), vaporized minus smoked: 12.0 beats per minute (4.2 to 19.8) at 10 mg and 7.7 (-4.1 to 19.5) at 25 mg. evidence.locator: Table (Cognitive measures); Results › Cognitive and Psychomotor Measures, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Task performance, peak change from baseline. Digit Symbol Substitution (number correct): vaporized -8.3 at 10 mg and -13.8 at 25 mg, both below the vaporized placebo session; smoked +3.4 and -7.0, neither different from its placebo session. Differences between methods at the 10 and 25 mg doses were flagged for three contrasts only: Divided Attention distance at 10 mg, and Digit Symbol Substitution attempted and correct at 25 mg (the Table also carries the between-method flag on two 0 mg vaporized cells, Divided Attention distance and Divided Attention total correct). Deficits typically peaked 30 to 60 minutes after dosing and in some instances had not returned to baseline at 6 to 8 hours.

evidence.locator: Results › Subjective Drug Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table
evidence.extracted: At 25 mg both methods raised ratings of unpleasant effects (smoked 32.9, vaporized 24.4), anxious or nervous (21.4; 25.5), memory impairment (14.2; 16.2), throat irritation or coughing (27.8; 22.18) and difficulty performing routine tasks (30.6; 34.2) over placebo, with no difference between methods flagged for the unpleasant, anxious, memory or throat items. Paranoid ratings rose over placebo only after vaporized 25 mg; sick only after smoked 25 mg. Between-method differences were flagged for 4 of 20 rating items at 10 mg and 2 at 25 mg.

evidence.locator: Results › Adverse Events
evidence.extracted: Adverse events as reported: two people vomited (one after 25 mg vaporized, one after 25 mg smoked) and one had hallucinations after 25 mg vaporized. No counts are given for placebo or 10 mg sessions and no other events are listed; the paper gives no incidence figures behind the abstract's statement of increased incidence of adverse effects at 25 mg, and these three are the only events it lists.

evidence.locator: Results › Subjective Drug Effects, 2nd paragraph; Results › Correlations Between Whole-Blood THC Concentrations and Pharmacodynamic Profiles; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: After both 25 mg conditions mean drug-effect ratings were still above baseline at 6 hours (smoked 12.2, vaporized 10.8) although blood THC was back to zero within 4 hours. Blood THC correlated with drug-effect ratings (r above 0.37) and heart rate (r above 0.24) but, for performance, only with Digit Symbol Substitution correct at 25 mg vaporized (r = -0.32); the authors conclude that blood THC is not a valid indicator of intoxication or impairment.

evidence.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors state that earlier controlled comparisons (not read here) found similar profiles for smoked and vaporized cannabis, and suggest that the different result here may be because those studies let people adjust their dose while this one gave a fixed amount, and that vaporizing delivers THC more efficiently because smoking loses THC to combustion and side-stream smoke (not tested).

evidence.locator: Limitations, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Limits stated by the authors: a limited range of doses, one type of cannabis (raw plant material, high THC, low cannabidiol), one vaporizer at a fixed temperature, enrolment limited to people who rarely use cannabis, and a sample too small to study individual characteristics. They note that the largest amount given (0.19 g of 13.4% THC flower) is smaller and weaker than prerolls sold in dispensaries (about 1 g, often over 18% THC, citing a 2018 paper that was not read here).

evidence.locator: Study Registration Dates; Study Overview; Primary and Secondary Outcome Measures; Design Details
evidence.extracted: Registry record NCT03676166: study start 16 June 2016, completion 17 January 2017, first submitted 16 September 2018 (after the study ended); actual enrolment 18 against 17 analysed in the paper; registered primary outcome quantity of THC in blood at 8 hours; secondary outcomes drug-effect rating, Digit Symbol Substitution, Paced Auditory Serial Addition and Divided Attention.

evidence.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis; Methods › Study Design and Procedure, 1st paragraph; Table (all rows)
evidence.extracted: The Table reports 32 outcomes (editors' count). Contrasts against placebo within each method used a threshold of P below .025 (Bonferroni for two comparisons); the contrasts between methods at each amount were treated as orthogonal and tested at P below .05 with no correction; nothing was corrected across the 32 outcomes (up to 192 planned contrasts, editors' count), and no interval or exact P value is given for any contrast. No double-dummy procedure was used to hide the inhalation method from participants and staff. The sample size of 17 was justified by a meta-analysis of six acute drug administration studies (reference 24), not by a cannabis route comparison.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 'some concerns' overall: sequence generation not described; the person inhaling knows the method and the main ratings are self-reported; registered after the study ended, with 32 outcomes and no correction for multiple comparisons; one implausible blood-pressure value and some text-versus-table mismatches.

inconsistency.note: One trial. Earlier smaller comparisons the authors cite reportedly found similar profiles for the two methods; they were not read.

indirectness.note: Worded for this trial's people and conditions. Read as a claim about vaping against smoking as people do them (joints, bongs, portable pens, cartridges, regular use, self-paced), it would be indirect.

imprecision.note: 17 people; wide interval for the lower-amount difference in drug-effect ratings; higher-amount difference includes zero; blood THC difference untested; between-method differences flagged for only a few items.

grade.reasoning: A placebo-controlled within-person laboratory trial with counterbalanced method order and randomized dose order starts high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias -1: RoB 2 'some concerns' in four of six domains (sequence generation not described; method cannot be hidden and the main ratings are self-reported; late registration with 32 uncorrected outcomes). Imprecision -1: 17 people; the lower-amount difference in drug-effect ratings has a wide interval (5.4 to 42.2), the higher-amount difference includes zero, the blood THC difference was not tested, and between-method differences were flagged for only 4 of 20 rating items at the lower amount, 2 at the higher and 3 task contrasts. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is worded for this trial's people and conditions; strict reading: as a claim about vaping against smoking in everyday use it would be indirect and the certainty would be very low. Not downgraded for inconsistency or publication bias on one trial; the earlier comparisons the authors cite, which they say found similar profiles, were not read and would matter if they had been. Worded as an association rather than 'increases' because only some contrasts were flagged, none was corrected for the number of outcomes, and the trial is small.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only, no advice. Rests on one 17-person crossover trial (Spindle 2018). The earlier smoked-against-vaporized comparisons the authors cite were not read, so the claim is shown as a single study although its authors say earlier studies found similar profiles; those would be the independent work to pair with it. Trial amounts appear only as study conditions. No industry funding is printed; one author's consulting ties are reported as printed. No awaited PDF is needed for this claim.

statement: In one survey of 2,553 young adults in a Southern California school-based cohort (mean age 19; asked once, between June 2018 and October 2019; 75% took part), people who reported vaping THC or hash oil, or dabs, were more likely to report bronchitic symptoms in the past 12 months (daily cough for 3 months in a row, congestion or phlegm, or bronchitis) than people who reported never doing so, after adjustment for age, sex, race and ethnicity, financial status, body mass index, nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis: adjusted odds ratios 1.73 (95% CI 1.01 to 2.96) for those whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months earlier, 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56) for 6 months to 30 days earlier, 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47) for 1 or 2 days in the past 30 and 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06) for 3 or more days. Wheeze was raised only in the top band (2.27, 1.17 to 4.37), and shortness of breath was not reliably raised after full adjustment. Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30 was associated with all three symptoms when only age, sex, race, finances and body mass index were adjusted (odds ratios 1.41 to 1.78) and with none after also adjusting for cannabis vaping and smoking (0.85 to 0.96). Overall 17.5% reported bronchitic symptoms (384 of 2,194), 13.0% wheeze and 20.4% shortness of breath; the paper gives no rates by vaping group (editors' rough calculation from its counts: about 12% to 14% of people who never vaped cannabis against about 23% to 31% of those who vaped it on days in the past 30, depending on how people with missing symptom data are counted). The survey was a single snapshot, so which came first is unknown, and symptoms were self-reported with no lung-function test. It did not record the product, device, source or amount vaped, or tobacco mixed into smoked cannabis, and it ran until October 2019, when the national outbreak of vaping-related lung injury (EVALI) was under way, so it cannot show whether the symptoms were linked to the products involved in it. Odds were raised even in people whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months earlier (1.73, against 2.19 to 2.79 for vaping in the past 30 days), which argues for caution about reading the link as an effect of recent vaping and points to residual confounding as a possible explanation. A 2024 systematic review of heart and breathing effects by route (42 sources; nothing pooled; no risk-of-bias assessment of the included studies reported; AMSTAR 2 critically low here; this survey is not among its sources) found no study comparing people who vape cannabis with people who do not use it, and none following people who vape over time. Its vaping evidence, second-hand, compares vaping with smoking: in a laboratory crossover (11 adults who smoked cannabis often and 9 occasionally; dried cannabis in a vaporizer), vaporised cannabis raised exhaled carbon monoxide less than smoked cannabis and breathing rate did not change with either; Canadian medical cannabis patients (a survey of 364) rated vaporizing as less harmful to breathing than smoking; and in a one-month study without a control group, 22 people who used cannabis often and had breathing symptoms switched to a vaporizer, and the 12 who did not develop a respiratory illness reported fewer symptoms and had a higher FVC, with FEV1 not significantly changed. None of these studied THC oil cartridges or dabs, and the survey's authors say longitudinal research is lacking. Funded by the US National Cancer Institute; no conflicts reported.
plain: In one survey of 2,553 young adults in Southern California, those who said they had vaped cannabis (THC or hash oil, or dabs) were more likely to report long-lasting cough, phlegm or bronchitis than those who had never vaped it, even after allowing for nicotine vaping and for smoking cigarettes or cannabis. Wheezing was more common only in people who vaped cannabis on 3 or more days in the last month, and shortness of breath was not clearly more common. Nicotine vaping went with these symptoms until cannabis vaping and smoking were taken into account, and not after that. This was one survey at one point in time, based on what people said, with no breathing test. It did not record what was vaped, how much, or whether tobacco was mixed into joints, and it ran until a national outbreak of vaping-related lung injury in 2019, so it cannot show that vaping caused the symptoms. Even people who had last vaped cannabis more than six months earlier reported more symptoms. A 2024 review of studies by way of use found none that compared people who vape cannabis with people who do not use it, or that followed people who vape over time; small studies that compared vaping with smoking found less carbon monoxide in the breath after vaping and fewer breathing complaints after people switched, but one had no comparison group and none tested oil vapes.
population: 2,553 young adults (mean age 19.3; 58% women; 47% Hispanic) in a Southern California school-based cohort, surveyed once a year after high-school graduation (outcome data for 2,194 to 2,396)
exposure: Self-reported vaping of THC or hash oil in an electronic device, or dabs, by recency and days of use (lifetime but not past 6 months; past 6 months but not past 30 days; 1 or 2 days in the past 30; 3 or more days in the past 30)
comparator: Young adults in the same survey who reported never vaping cannabis (for the nicotine comparison, never vaping nicotine); the full model also adjusts for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis
outcome: Self-reported bronchitic symptoms (daily cough for 3 months in a row, congestion or phlegm, or bronchitis) and wheeze in the previous 12 months, and shortness of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill
magnitude: Bronchitic symptoms, cannabis vaping, full-model adjusted odds ratios against never (95% CI): lifetime but not past 6 months 1.73 (1.01 to 2.96); past 6 months but not past 30 days 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56); 1 or 2 days in the past 30 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47); 3 or more days 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06). Wheeze: 1.12 (0.61 to 2.03), 1.47 (0.92 to 2.35), 1.84 (0.88 to 3.86), 2.27 (1.17 to 4.37). Shortness of breath: 0.90 (0.57 to 1.40), 1.25 (0.86 to 1.84), 1.55 (0.81 to 2.96), 1.41 (0.80 to 2.48). Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30, bronchitic symptoms, wheeze, shortness of breath: sociodemographic model 1.78 (1.32 to 2.41), 1.41 (1.01 to 1.96), 1.45 (1.08 to 1.96); full model 0.96 (0.63 to 1.46), 0.85 (0.54 to 1.35), 0.96 (0.64 to 1.42). Absolute: 17.5% (384 of 2,194) bronchitic symptoms, 13.0% (312 of 2,396) wheeze, 20.4% (488 of 2,389) shortness of breath overall; editors' rough calculation for bronchitic symptoms from Table 2 counts: about 12% to 14% in people who never vaped cannabis, about 27% to 31% (1 or 2 days) and 23% to 27% (3 or more days) in those vaping in the past 30 days, depending on how missing symptom data are counted. Editors' note: odds ratios overstate rate ratios when the outcome is this common. 2024 review by route (second-hand; vaping against smoking, not against no use): less exhaled carbon monoxide after vaporised than smoked cannabis from 0.25 to 6 hours and no route effect on breathing rate (laboratory crossover, 11 and 9 adults); lower perceived respiratory harm (survey of 364 medical cannabis patients); fewer symptoms (t(11) = 6.22) and higher FVC (t(11) = 2.90) after a one-month switch in the 12 of 22 who did not develop a respiratory illness, FEV1 not significant (no control group).

Outcome data were available for 2,194 (bronchitic symptoms), 2,396 (wheeze) and 2,389 (shortness of breath). Bronchitic symptoms were daily cough for 3 months in a row, congestion or phlegm other than with a cold, and/or bronchitis in the previous 12 months; wheeze in the previous 12 months; shortness of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill.
