evidence.extracted: Shortness of breath and cannabis vaping: sociodemographic model raised at 3 or more days (1.67, 1.09 to 2.53) and for past 6 months but not past 30 days (1.35, 1.04 to 1.75); in the full model no level was reliably raised (0.90, 0.57 to 1.40; 1.25, 0.86 to 1.84; 1.55, 0.81 to 2.96; 3 or more days 1.41, 0.80 to 2.48).

evidence.locator: Table 3 (frequency of vaping nicotine rows); Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30, sociodemographic model: bronchitic symptoms 1.78 (1.32 to 2.41), wheeze 1.41 (1.01 to 1.96), shortness of breath 1.45 (1.08 to 1.96); full model 0.96 (0.63 to 1.46), 0.85 (0.54 to 1.35), 0.96 (0.64 to 1.42), with no nicotine vaping level reliably associated with any outcome. The authors say residual confounding by cannabis vaping and by smoking cigarettes or cannabis could partly explain the earlier associations.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Limitations, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Limits and explanations given by the authors: cross-sectional design, so temporality is unknown; a school-based Southern California sample with 75% participation, not nationally representative; the cannabis vaping measure includes dabs; longitudinal research on cannabis vaping and symptoms is lacking; possible reasons for a difference from nicotine vaping (chemicals in THC e-liquids, device and heating differences, tampering with products, deeper or longer puffs) were not measured.

evidence.locator: Table 3 (cannabis vaping rows, bronchitic symptoms, full adjustment); Methods › Measures
evidence.extracted: Editors' reading of Table 3: odds of bronchitic symptoms were raised even in people whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months before the survey (1.73, 1.01 to 2.96), against 2.19 to 2.79 for vaping on days in the past 30, so the data show no clear gradient with recency; this argues for caution about an effect of recent vaping and for residual confounding. The Methods describe no product, device, source, additive or amount of cannabis vaping, and no record of tobacco in joints or blunts (the questionnaire is in the eAppendix, which was not read).

evidence.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 title
evidence.extracted: Weekly hospital admissions for the national vaping lung injury outbreak (EVALI) peaked at 215 in the week of 15 September 2019, within the period (June 2018 to October 2019) in which this survey was taken; the survey asked about nicotine and about THC or hash oil/dabs vaping but not about specific products or additives, and its Methods describe no question on whether anyone had that injury.

evidence.locator: Article notes (Conflict of Interest Disclosures; Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor)
evidence.extracted: Funding as printed: National Cancer Institute grants U54CA180905, R01CA229617-01 and K24DA048160; the funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit; no conflicts reported.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Methods › Search strategy; Table 1 and its note; Study selection, abstraction, and analysis; Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1; Table 4 (Cavazos-Rehg 2016 row, for 'of tweets')
evidence.extracted: The 2024 review by route: a systematic review without meta-analysis, guided by PRISMA, with no protocol or registration stated. Search of Web of Science, ProQuest, PsycINFO, Embase and Medline (the Abstract also names Scopus) in November–December 2019, updated August–December 2023, plus reference lists; peer-reviewed English-language articles from January 2009 to December 2023 reporting the route of administration, with cannabis confirmed by drug screening; studies including other illicit drugs, or people with pre-existing heart or lung conditions, excluded. In Table 1 the cannabis terms are combined with AND NOT Tobacco. 1,873 records, 110 full texts, 42 included: 6 case reports or series, 21 literature reviews and 15 empirical studies (2 randomised trials, 5 retrospective analyses, 1 content analysis of tweets, 3 longitudinal studies, 3 cross-sectional surveys, 1 pre/post study). Abstract selection was independent (kappa 0.89). The Methods say the strength of evidence was graded for each outcome, but no grades and no appraisal of individual studies are reported, and nothing was pooled.

evidence.locator: Results › Empirical studies › Cardiovascular effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Respiratory effects, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 4 (Cooper and Haney 2009, Newmeyer 2017 rows); Discussion, paragraph beginning Second
evidence.extracted: Routes compared in laboratory studies (second-hand): Newmeyer 2017 (double-blind, placebo-controlled, double-dummy crossover; 11 adults who smoked cannabis frequently and 9 occasionally; smoked, vaporised and oral cannabis in separate sessions): smoking produced significantly greater increases in expired carbon monoxide than vaporisation from 0.25 to 6 h after dosing; route had no significant effect on breathing rate or blood pressure; heart rate rose above placebo by 12.2 (smoked) and 10.7 (vaporised) beats a minute at 0.5 h and by 13.0 and 10.2 at 1.5 and 3 h after oral cannabis, increases that did not differ significantly between routes. Cooper and Haney 2009 (24 healthy volunteers; blunts against joints of the same cannabis at three strengths including inactive): more expired carbon monoxide after blunts at every strength (p ≤ 0.01); joints gave greater increases in plasma THC; heart-rate increases were equivalent. The review's Discussion gives the Newmeyer sample as n = 11, against 11 and 9 in its Table 4.

evidence.locator: Results › Literature reviews, 2nd paragraph; Table 3 (Russell 2017 row); Results › Empirical studies, 1st paragraph; Respiratory effects, 2nd paragraph; Table 4 (Kaczor 2021, Newmeyer 2017, Pepin 2023, Shiplo 2016, Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 rows); Discussion, paragraph beginning One study in this review
evidence.extracted: Vaping in the review (second-hand): three empirical studies have a vaping arm, and all compare vaping with smoking (Newmeyer 2017 also with placebo). Newmeyer 2017 (the laboratory crossover; dried cannabis in a vaporizer). Shiplo 2016 (online survey of 364 adults approved to use medical cannabis in Canada, April to June 2015): a vaporizer and eating in food were rated lower in perceived harm (cough, phlegm, chest tightness) than smoking, and the number of side effects lower for the vaporizer than for smoking or eating. Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 (pre/post design, no control group): 22 people who used cannabis frequently, were not interested in treatment and reported at least two respiratory symptoms used a vaporizer for 1 month; the 12 who did not develop a respiratory illness during the trial had fewer symptoms (t(11) = 6.22) and higher FVC (t(11) = 2.90, p = 0.007 as printed), while FEV1 did not change significantly (p = 0.053 as printed); the amount used a day fell slightly and not significantly (p = 0.10 as printed), though the text says vaping reduced it. The scoping review of Russell 2017 is reported as finding that vaping reduced respiratory symptoms. The text's list of vaping studies also names Kaczor 2021 and Pepin 2023, which Table 4 gives as edible studies in children. No included study examined THC oil cartridges, followed people who vape for longer than a month, or compared them with people who do not use cannabis; the authors call for research on long-term outcomes of vaping and on vaping-associated lung injury with THC-containing e-liquids. Editors' calculation: two-tailed p values for t(11) = 2.90 and 1.77 and t(18) = 1.34 are about 0.014, 0.10 and 0.20, so the printed values match one-tailed tests, and the printed d values equal 2t divided by the square root of the degrees of freedom, a formula for two independent groups.

evidence.locator: Abstract (Conclusion); Discussion, 1st paragraph; Discussion, paragraphs beginning Nevertheless, Evidence on the cardiovascular (its First point), Second, Third and In addition; Strength and limitations; Conclusion; Disclosure statement; Funding
evidence.extracted: The review's conclusions and limits: the authors conclude that cannabis use does cause cardiovascular and respiratory effects but that conclusions by route remain tentative because of the studies' methodological limitations. They state that most studies were cross-sectional or retrospective, from which temporality cannot be determined; that the three longitudinal studies all concerned smoking and breathing; that the two randomised trials were small (n = 24 and, as they give it, n = 11); that only five of the 15 empirical studies reported cardiovascular effects; and that only three sources specified the type of smoking (joints against blunts); only English articles from 2009 to 2023 were included. In the Discussion they write that each route was associated with effects of some kind, suggesting a need to avoid cannabis altogether, followed by harm-reduction recommendations (the authors' advice, not derived from a synthesis and not adopted here). No funding; no conflicts of interest declared. Editors' reading: the causal wording is not supported by the designs the authors describe, nothing was pooled and no appraisal is reported (AMSTAR 2 critically low on the card), and several studies within the review's window and topic that this library has read are not among its sources (Monte 2019 on emergency visits after eating against inhaling cannabis, Braymiller 2020 on vaping and bronchitic symptoms, Spindle 2018 on smoked against vaporised cannabis, Ghasemiesfe 2018, a systematic review of respiratory outcomes).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high: confounding high (one time point; coarse five-level bands for the other exposures; tobacco in joints and blunts not recorded); self-reported symptoms from people who also reported the exposure; outcome data missing for 14% (bronchitic symptoms), related to vaping and smoking; the stated multiple-testing correction is not shown.

inconsistency.note: One survey.

indirectness.note: Worded for self-reported symptoms in this cohort. Read as a claim about lung disease or lung function, or about other ages and regions, it would be indirect.

imprecision.note: Lower bounds of 1.01 to 1.04 for three of four full-model estimates for bronchitic symptoms; the 1 or 2 day and 3 or more day bands hold 90 and 155 people; most wheeze and breathlessness intervals include 1.

grade.reasoning: Observational and cross-sectional, so it starts low. Risk of bias -1: confounding is high, because one time point and coarse adjustment cannot separate cannabis vaping from other exposures (tobacco in joints and blunts, secondhand smoke, asthma) or from reverse causation, and odds were raised as much in people who last vaped cannabis long before the survey as in people who vaped recently. Imprecision -1: several full-model lower bounds sit at 1.01 to 1.04 and the top bands are small. Not upgraded for a large effect (some odds ratios above 2): the most adjusted model still leaves residual confounding that runs away from the null, there is no clear gradient with recency or frequency, and the lower bounds are close to 1. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is worded for self-reported symptoms in this cohort. Rating: very low. Worded as an association, never as an effect of vaping; no longitudinal study of cannabis vaping was read; the 2024 review by route adds only comparisons of vaping with smoking (a laboratory crossover, a perceived-harm survey and an uncontrolled one-month switch with spirometry), second-hand through a review of critically low confidence, which do not change the rating.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only. Rests on one cross-sectional survey (Braymiller 2020) for the comparison with people who never vaped cannabis; the authors say longitudinal research is lacking and none was read. Batch 10 (AI reader 91, first reader): the 2024 review by route (Muheriwa-Matemba 2024, PDF; card sc_muheriwa_matemba_2024, AMSTAR 2 critically low) was read; its vaping evidence (a laboratory crossover, a perceived-harm survey and an uncontrolled one-month vaporizer switch with spirometry) compares vaping with smoking, is second-hand, does not include this survey, and its text wrongly lists two studies of children who ate cannabis as vaping studies; the four new anchors need a second reader. The abstract's adjusted odds ratios for bronchitic symptoms differ from Table 3 (Table 3 used). The rough absolute rates are an editors' calculation from Table 2 counts and need the second reader's recomputation. The comparison with smoked cannabis and the lungs belongs to the smoked-lungs claim of reader 73. The paper's supplement (eTable 1, on who lacked respiratory data) was not read. No awaited PDF is needed for this claim.

statement: EVALI (e-cigarette, or vaping, product use-associated lung injury) was a surveillance case definition: vaping or dabbing in the previous 90 days, a lung infiltrate on imaging, no other plausible diagnosis, and negative infection testing (confirmed cases) or an infection judged not the sole cause (probable cases). The CDC authors say its high sensitivity likely lowered specificity, so some patients may not have had EVALI. By 14 January 2020 the CDC had been told of 2,668 hospitalized patients (1,401 confirmed, 1,267 probable): median age 24, 66% male; weekly admissions peaked in the week of 15 September 2019 and fell afterwards. Of the 2,022 patients (76%) with information on what they had vaped or dabbed in the previous 3 months, 82% reported a THC-containing product, 57% a nicotine-containing product, 41% both and 14% nicotine only; products were unknown for 24% and were not checked against what was in the devices (in the lung-fluid study, THC or its breakdown products were found in 9 of 11 patients who said they had not used THC products in the 90 days before illness). The CDC authors give three possible reasons for the nicotine-only reports: patients not reporting or not knowing what they vaped, some patients not having EVALI, or accurate reports. Deaths and intensive care are second-hand: CDC figures quoted in the laboratory papers give 52 deaths among about 2,400 reported cases by 12 December 2019 and 47% needing intensive care; the update read gives neither, nor outcomes after discharge. Vitamin E acetate, a form of vitamin E sold online as a diluent or thickener for cannabis oil, was found in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients in 16 states (94%; editors' exact 95% interval 84% to 99%), including all 25 confirmed cases (editors' deduction), and from none of 99 healthy volunteers, none of whom vaped THC (0% to 4%); other additives tested were found in at most one patient. FDA testing, quoted second-hand, found it in 49% of case-associated THC product samples and none of 197 case-associated nicotine products. In 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids from cartridges recovered from 10 New York patients, 23 (64%) held vitamin E acetate (16% to 57% by mass) and 13 held none above 1%; 31 of the 36 held at least one pesticide (editors' count), a pattern the authors judge intermittent and not due to a single pesticide. These findings come from different laboratories, patients and sample types and point the same way, but they do not show cause: the comparison lungs came from people who did not vape THC, so the contrast cannot separate vitamin E acetate from other features of vaping THC products in 2019; no fluid from people who vaped the same products without injury was tested; none of these studies tested whether inhaling it injures the lung (the authors say laboratory studies are needed); the CDC authors state that "evidence is not sufficient to rule out the contribution of other chemicals of concern" in some cases; and a screen of 38 cartridges listed many other chemicals by library match, without counts per cartridge. The cartridge papers call the products illicit or counterfeit; neither describes how this was established. The sources implicate certain vaping products, mostly THC-containing cartridges, and an additive in them. None tested whether THC or cannabis itself injures the lung, or looked at cannabis smoked or eaten or flower vaporized in dry-herb devices; the one screen with medical-grade cartridges (number not stated) found retinol acetate rather than vitamin E acetate in them, and fewer listed contaminants, though some harmful chemicals were identified. So the sources neither show that other forms of cannabis carry this injury nor show that they are free of it. Funding as printed: CDC authors for the surveillance report; National Cancer Institute, FDA Center for Tobacco Products and Ohio State University for the lung-fluid study; none external for the two cartridge studies; no industry funding is printed.
plain: EVALI was an outbreak of lung injury in people who vaped, mostly in 2019. By January 2020, 2,668 people in hospital had been reported to the US CDC; most were young (median age 24) and two thirds were male. Of those who said what they had vaped, most had used products with THC, and some had used only nicotine products. Vitamin E acetate, an oil sold for thickening cannabis oil, was found in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients and from none of 99 healthy volunteers, who did not vape THC. It was also found in the liquid of about two thirds of 36 cartridge samples from 10 patients in New York. This does not prove that it caused the injury: these studies did not test that, the volunteers were not people who vaped THC and stayed well, and the CDC says other chemicals are not ruled out. These studies point to certain vaping products (mostly THC cartridges, which the authors call illicit or counterfeit) and an additive in them. They did not test cannabis smoked, eaten or vaporized as plant material. One small screen of medical-grade cartridges did not find the additive in them. So the studies cannot say whether other forms of cannabis carry the same risk.
population: People hospitalized with EVALI in the US (2,668 reported to CDC by 14 January 2020); 51 of them with lung fluid tested in 16 states; 10 New York patients whose cartridges were tested (38 samples)
exposure: Vitamin E acetate found in patients' lung fluid and in vaping cartridge fluid (cartridges that held THC or other cannabinoids)
comparator: Lung fluid from 99 healthy volunteers in an unrelated study, none of whom vaped THC; no comparison cartridges within the cartridge studies
outcome: EVALI (hospitalization with vaping-associated lung injury)
magnitude: Surveillance (CDC, 14 January 2020): 2,668 hospitalized (1,401 confirmed, 1,267 probable); median age 24 (13 to 85); 66% male; among 2,022 with product information: any THC 82% (1,650), any nicotine 57% (1,162), both 41% (834), THC only 33% (669), nicotine only 14% (274), neither 2% (44); peak 215 admissions in the week of 15 September 2019. Second-hand: 52 deaths among 2,409 reported cases by 12 December 2019 (about 2%, editors' calculation); 47% needed intensive care in an earlier CDC report. Lung fluid (Blount et al.): vitamin E acetate in 48 of 51 patients (94%; editors' exact 95% CI 83.8% to 98.8%) against 0 of 99 healthy volunteers (0% to 3.7%); 25 of 25 confirmed cases (editors' deduction; 86.3% to 100%) and 23 of 26 probable cases; THC or metabolites 40 of 47 (85%), including 9 of 11 who reported no THC product use; nicotine or metabolites 30 of 47 (64%); coconut oil 1 of 48, limonene 1 of 39, all other priority substances 0 of 12 to 49. Cartridges (Duffy et al.): vitamin E acetate in 23 of 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids (64%; exact 95% CI 46% to 79%, treating fluids as independent) at 16 to 57% by mass, from 10 patients; 13 without it, 12 of which held medium-chain triglyceride oil; 31 of 36 with at least one pesticide (editors' count); update to 12 December 2019 without methods: 101 of 147 THC-containing fluids (69%) from 61 cases; 3 of 6 commercial diluents and thickeners essentially pure vitamin E acetate. Screening (Muthumalage et al.): over 500 chemicals in cartridge liquids; no counts per compound.

evidence.locator: Methods › Case Definitions; Table 1 (Case Definitions for Patients with EVALI)
evidence.extracted: CDC case definitions as printed in the paper: confirmed and probable cases both need vaping or dabbing in the 90 days before symptom onset, a lung infiltrate on chest imaging and no evidence in the medical record of an alternative plausible diagnosis; confirmed cases also need a negative respiratory viral panel, a negative influenza test (if local epidemiology supports influenza testing) and negative results for all other clinically indicated infection tests; probable cases may have an infection identified, or incomplete testing, when the clinical team judges the infection is not the sole cause of the lung injury. State and local health departments assigned case status.

evidence.locator: Abstract; main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Case status row)
evidence.extracted: As of 14 January 2020, all 50 states, the District of Columbia, the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico had reported 2,668 hospitalized EVALI patients to CDC: 1,401 (53%) confirmed and 1,267 (47%) probable cases.

evidence.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Sex, Median age, Age group, Race/Ethnicity rows)
evidence.extracted: Median age 24 years (range 13 to 85); 404 (15%) aged 13 to 17, 979 (37%) 18 to 24, 631 (24%) 25 to 34, 335 (13%) 35 to 44, 223 (9%) 45 to 64, 47 (2%) 65 and over, of 2,619 with age; 1,731 of 2,606 (66%) male; of 1,856 with race and ethnicity, 73% non-Hispanic white and 15% Hispanic.

evidence.locator: Abstract; main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Substances used rows and footnotes)
evidence.extracted: Among 2,022 patients with information on substances used (76% of 2,668), who had vaped or dabbed at least one substance in the 3 months before symptom onset: any THC-containing product 1,650 (82%); any nicotine-containing product 1,162 (57%); both 834 (41%); THC only 669 (33%); nicotine only 274 (14%); neither 44 (2%). Product information was missing for 24% of patients. The four exclusive categories add to 1,821, not 2,022.

evidence.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 title
evidence.extracted: Weekly hospital admissions for EVALI reported to CDC (Figure 1: 2,398 patients by week of admission, February 2019 to 14 January 2020) peaked at 215 in the week of 15 September 2019 and declined steadily after that to the end of the data.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 4th and 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Limits given by the authors: product-use data missing for 24% of patients and many not interviewed; the emergency visit query may have been affected by awareness of the outbreak; coverage of the surveillance system uneven and changing over time. The case counts are of hospitalized patients (the Methods say states report hospitalized or deceased patients); the report does not report deaths or what happened to patients after discharge (it says long-term consequences need long-term follow-up).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors state that vitamin E acetate is strongly linked to THC-containing products used by EVALI patients (citing the lung-fluid study), that a minority of patients consistently report only nicotine-containing products (possible reasons: patients may not report or know the content of what they vaped; the high sensitivity of the case definition likely lowered specificity, so some patients may not have EVALI; or the reports may be accurate), and that evidence is not sufficient to rule out other chemicals of concern, in THC- or non-THC-containing products, in some cases. It is not known whether additives other than vitamin E acetate could cause similar injury.
evidence.quote: evidence is not sufficient to rule out the contribution of other chemicals of concern

evidence.locator: Abstract; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Lung-lavage (BAL) fluid from 51 patients with EVALI in 16 states (collected August to December 2019 during routine clinical care; 25 confirmed, 26 probable; median age 23, 69% male) and from 99 healthy participants of an unrelated Ohio State University tobacco-product study (52 who neither vaped nor smoked, 18 who vaped nicotine only, 29 who smoked cigarettes only; sampled 2016 to 2019, 90 before 2019). The authors call the cases a convenience sample; collection was not standardized. New York is not among the 16 states.

evidence.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 3 (vitamin E acetate row)
evidence.extracted: Vitamin E acetate was found in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients (94%) and from none of the 99 healthy participants (0 of 52, 0 of 18, 0 of 29). Editors' calculation, exact binomial 95% intervals: patients 83.8% to 98.8%; comparators 0% to 3.7%.

evidence.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 3; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Other priority substances in patients' lung fluid: coconut oil 1 of 48, limonene 1 of 39 (the limonene patient had no vitamin E acetate or THC and reported daily flavoured nicotine products); medium-chain triglyceride oil 0 of 49, plant oil 0 of 49, squalane 0 of 38, squalene 0 of 38, pinenes and 3-carene 0 of 39, petroleum distillates 0 of 12. None of these was found in any comparator.

evidence.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 4; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The three patients without detectable vitamin E acetate were all probable cases, with other plausible diagnoses recorded in Table 4, so all 25 confirmed cases were positive (editors' deduction; exact binomial 95% interval for 25 of 25, 86.3% to 100%, editors' calculation).

evidence.locator: Abstract; Results, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2
evidence.extracted: THC or its metabolites were found in lung fluid from 40 of 47 patients (85%); 9 of 11 patients who reported no THC product use in the 90 days before illness had THC or metabolites in lung fluid; nicotine or metabolites in 30 of 47 (64%). Self-reported (43 patients): nicotine products only 7 (16%), THC products only 11 (26%), both 22 (51%).

evidence.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Healthy comparators: none reported vaping THC products; urine THC biomarkers positive in 21 of 82 (26%); nicotine or metabolites in 52% of lung fluids; all negative for every priority substance.

evidence.locator: Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Second-hand context quoted by the authors from CDC and FDA web pages and earlier CDC reports (none read here): more than 2,400 hospitalized patients and 52 deaths as of 12 December 2019 (CDC web page); 78% under 35; nearly half (47%) needed intensive care for respiratory failure (earlier CDC report). FDA testing (FDA web page) found vitamin E acetate in 49% of case-associated THC product samples and none of 197 case-associated nicotine products; in Minnesota (earlier MMWR report) 0 of 10 products seized in 2018 contained it against 20 of 20 THC products seized in September 2019.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 8th and 9th paragraphs; Discussion, 7th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Limits stated by the authors: vitamin E acetate may be a marker of another toxicant; products formed when it is heated were not examined; sample collection was not standardized; timing and burden of exposure could not be assessed; case and comparator samples come from independent studies at single time points, so unknown confounding remains. Animal studies are needed to show whether vitamin E acetate alone causes the injury.

evidence.locator: Acknowledgments; Footnotes
evidence.extracted: Funding as printed: National Cancer Institute grant P50CA180908; FDA Center for Tobacco Products grant P30CA016058; Ohio State University Pelotonia Intramural Research. Authors are mostly CDC staff, with Ohio State University and FDA authors; the publisher's disclosure forms were not read.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Introduction, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1
evidence.extracted: Thirty-eight samples of fluid from vaporizer cartridges recovered from the first 10 New York State patients with EVALI for whom cartridges were obtained; two held nicotine and no cannabinoids and 36 held cannabinoids. The laboratory began receiving cartridges in August 2019.

evidence.locator: Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1 (VEA column); Discussion 4.1, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Vitamin E acetate was found in 23 of the 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids (64%), at 16 to 57% by mass (Table 1 maximum 57.6%; 58% in the Discussion); 13 held none above 1% by mass. Editors' calculation: exact 95% interval 46% to 79%, treating the 36 fluids as independent, which they are not.

evidence.locator: Results 3.2, 4th paragraph; Table 1 (MCT column)
evidence.extracted: Medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil, another diluent, was estimated at 3 to 24% by mass in the 15 fluids the text says held it (Table 1 marks 14, by the editors' count); 12 of the 13 fluids without vitamin E acetate held MCT oil and 2 held both. MCT was estimated roughly because standards for its components are not available.

evidence.locator: Results 3.1, 4th paragraph; Results 3.3; Table 2; Discussion 4.1, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Pesticides: myclobutanil was quantified in 22 fluids (up to 28.3 micrograms per gram), the pesticide synergist piperonyl butoxide in 18 (up to 24.1), and several other fungicides, insecticides and acaricides above 1 microgram per gram in 25; 31 of the 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids held at least one (editors' count). The authors judge the pattern intermittent and random, and say it would suggest that EVALI is not due to exposure to a single pesticide. No mycotoxins (below 4.8 ng/g) and no synthetic cannabinoids or opioids (below 0.05% by mass) in any fluid.

evidence.locator: Results 3.4; Table 3; Discussion 4.2, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Of six commercial products bought online as cannabis-oil diluents or thickeners, two diluents and one thickener were essentially pure vitamin E acetate; the others were squalane-based or alpha-bisabolol-based. The sellers did not list ingredients on label or website.

evidence.locator: Conclusions
evidence.extracted: Update to 12 December 2019, given in the Conclusions without methods or a table: 206 fluids from 61 New York cases, 147 with THC and 59 with nicotine; 101 of the 147 THC-containing fluids (69%) held vitamin E acetate. Editors' calculation: exact 95% interval 61% to 76%, treating fluids as independent. Whether the first 38 fluids are included is not stated. The authors also cite CDC counts of 2,409 hospitalized cases and 52 deaths as of 12 December 2019, and 205 New York cases including 2 deaths as of 10 December.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.1; Discussion 4.1, 2nd paragraph; Discussion 4.3, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Conclusions
evidence.extracted: Limits and inferences stated by the authors: the cause or causes of EVALI are unknown; extensive in vitro and in vivo studies are required to establish a causative role of vitamin E acetate or other agents. The paper has no cartridges from people who vaped without injury, gives no per-patient results, and does not say how the cartridges were judged illicit; its contrast with the laboratory's medical-program products is stated without data.

evidence.locator: Funding; Conflicts of Interest; author affiliations
evidence.extracted: Funding as printed: none external. Declared conflicts: none. Authors work at the New York State Department of Health (Wadsworth Center; Center for Environmental Health), the University at Albany and Albany Medical Center.

evidence.locator: Methods 2.3, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results 3.1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 1
evidence.extracted: A library-matched GC-MS screen of liquid from 38 counterfeit or patient-provided THC cartridges, 4 CBD cartridges and medical-grade cartridges found more than 500 chemicals. Chemicals described as specific to the counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges include silicon compounds (siloxanes, tetramethyl silicate), esters, benzophenone, glycerol tricaprylate, terpenes and vitamin E acetate; Table 1 lists 47 entries for these cartridges against 13 for CBD and 15 for medical-grade (editors' count). No count of cartridges containing any compound is given.

evidence.locator: Methods 2.4 and 2.5; Results 3.2 and 3.3; Table 2

risk_of_bias.note: All four study cards are rated high overall: the surveillance report has missing and self-reported product data and a sensitive case definition; the lung-fluid comparison used healthy volunteers from another study, sampled mostly before 2019, none of whom vaped THC; the cartridge studies had no comparison cartridges and gave no per-patient results; the screening paper's identifications are library matches without counts.

inconsistency.note: The studies agree in direction. The share holding vitamin E acetate differs (94% of patients' lung fluid; 64% of 36 cartridge fluids, 69% of 147 in a later update; 49% of case-associated THC product samples in FDA testing as quoted second-hand), which different sample types and sources can explain.

indirectness.note: Worded for the people and products sampled.

imprecision.note: 48 of 51 and 0 of 99 are precise as counts.

grade.reasoning: Observational: a surveillance case series, a case-comparator lung-fluid study and laboratory analyses of cartridges, so it starts low. Risk of bias -1 (all four study cards rated high overall); the rating cannot fall below very low. Not upgraded for a large effect: the 94% against 0% contrast has no adjusted model, and the comparison lungs came from people who did not vape THC and were sampled mostly before 2019, so the contrast probably overstates what separates vitamin E acetate from other features of THC cartridge use in 2019. Not downgraded for inconsistency (the studies agree in direction; the proportions differ for reasons of sample type and source), imprecision (the counts are precise) or indirectness (the claim is worded for the people and products sampled). Strict reading: the presence of vitamin E acetate in nearly all lung fluid tested and in most THC-containing cartridge fluids sampled is consistent across two laboratories, but the rating applies to the association and to the description as worded; that it is the cause or the only cause is a separate claim that none of these studies tests, and is lower still. Status replicated: two independent laboratories (CDC with state laboratories; New York State Department of Health), different patients (New York is not among the 16 states of the lung-fluid study) and different sample types, same direction; a third laboratory (University of Rochester) found it in many but not all cartridge liquids, without counts. The earlier CDC report of 29 patients (whether its patients are among the 51 is not stated) and the New York update of 206 fluids (which presumably includes the 38) are not counted as further replications.

statement: At one Colorado university hospital's emergency department, 2012 to 2016, clinicians judged 2,567 visits (visits, not people) to be at least partly due to cannabis; 238 (9.3%) were recorded as edible and 2,329 as inhaled (135 of these had no route written down and were counted as inhaled). Compared with inhaled visits, edible visits more often involved intoxication (48.3% against 27.8%; difference 20.5 percentage points, 95% CI 13.9 to 27.1), acute psychiatric symptoms (18.0% against 10.9%; 7.1, 2.1 to 12.1) and cardiovascular symptoms (8.0% against 3.1%; 4.9, 1.4 to 8.4), and less often gastrointestinal symptoms (15.1% against 32.3%; cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4% against 18.0%) or admission to hospital (18.9% against 32.9%); psychiatric symptoms of any kind were similar (26.1% against 24.5%). Severe heart events (heart attack, dangerous heart rhythm) occurred in both groups, with no counts given. Because edibles were under a tenth of the visits, most visits for each of these reasons were inhaled (647 of 762 intoxication visits, 254 of 297 acute psychiatric visits, 73 of 92 cardiovascular visits; editors' arithmetic from the table counts), and the authors write that, given how often inhaled visits occurred and led to admission, education about inhaled cannabis may have the greatest public-health effect. The two groups also differed in who they were (women 51.3% against 33.1%; living outside Colorado 40.8% against 6.6%); a 2016 letter from the same hospital group, cited second-hand in the overview described below and not read, reported that edible-related visits by out-of-state patients rose from 85 to 168 per 10,000 visits between 2013 and 2014, with no significant change for Colorado residents. Against Colorado sales in 2014 to 2016, edibles were 10.7% of this hospital's attributable visits but 0.32% of THC sold by weight, under assumed product contents; the authors call this about 33 times the share expected if the routes were equally likely to lead to a visit, and list its limits (assumed contents, one hospital set against statewide sales, home-grown and illicit supply not counted). A 2016 narrative overview (no stated search or appraisal of studies; its figures are second-hand) quotes another measure, edible units at about 45 percent of Colorado cannabis sales in 2014, without saying how sales were counted, so any such ratio depends on the denominator chosen. No source read here timed effects in patients. The hospital paper and the overview both describe, citing pharmacology work that was not read here, a later and longer effect after eating THC than after inhaling it (the overview: a start within minutes of inhaling against 30 to 90 minutes after eating; the hospital paper: clearance within about 4 hours against about 12). The overview adds that more of the active product 11-OH-THC reaches the blood after eating, which it says may account for stronger, longer-lasting effects; that blood THC after eating is lower than after smoking and tracks intoxication differently from person to person; and that this variation and the delay may lead people to take more than intended before the effect starts, which its abstract says often results in profoundly adverse effects (no count given). The hospital paper cites a consumer survey and an analysis of Twitter posts (neither read) in which people report longer-lasting effects with edibles than with smoking or vaping, and more intense effects and unpleasant psychiatric symptoms. The overview relays anecdotal reports from patients, including patients who took cannabis daily, of eating a whole product after feeling no effect from a first serving, and describes one death in Colorado in 2014 (a 19-year-old man; the autopsy named cannabis intoxication a chief contributing factor) after he ate the whole cookie within two hours of a first serving, having not felt intoxicated within an hour (a public-health case report, as cited). The hospital paper cites three deaths linked to edibles from news reports; none of its 2,567 visits ended in death. No source read here counts how often people eat more after a slow start. What these sources cannot show: how many people took each form (shares of visits are not the chance that a form leads to a visit); who took which form (no adjustment); how much was eaten (a dose was charted for 130 of the 2,567 visits, 80 of them edible; the authors could not verify doses, say eaten doses may have been larger than inhaled ones, and were surprised that the charted edible doses were low); what the products contained (not tested in the hospital study; a separate laboratory test of other products found most of them more than 10% away from their labels; see the claim on edible labels); and what happened to people who took cannabis without harm or did not attend hospital (the authors note that most people who take cannabis may have no adverse effect). Route came from chart notes and patients' own accounts, and the authors say counting undocumented routes as inhaled could bias toward more illness in the inhaled group. Inhaled visits were not split by product (flower, vaped oil, concentrates) or checked for tobacco mixed in, and no comparison was made with people who do not use cannabis. The overview states that edible products account for most health-care visits for cannabis intoxication, citing a 2015 viewpoint not read here; the hospital count has edibles at 115 of 762 intoxication visits (15.1%). The overview also infers that eating cannabis does not seem to affect lung function or cancer risk, citing no study of people who eat cannabis. A 2024 systematic review of heart and breathing effects by route (42 sources; nothing pooled or appraised; AMSTAR 2 critically low here; this hospital study is not among its sources) also found no study of the lungs of adults who eat cannabis. Its oral-route evidence, second-hand, is a laboratory crossover in which heart rate rose about as much after eating cannabis as after smoking or vaporising it (about 10 to 13 beats a minute above placebo) and breathing rate did not change with route; a survey in which Canadian medical cannabis patients rated eating as less harmful to breathing than smoking; and records of children who ate cannabis products (calls to US poison centres and two hospital chart reviews), in which a fast heart rate was common, some children needed help with breathing, and severe heart and breathing effects were seen at higher doses for their body weight. Its abstract nonetheless says edibles were associated with minimal respiratory effects. Follow-up was the visit itself: the hospital data do not follow anyone afterwards, and the overview has no data of its own.   Funding as printed: the hospital paper, the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (competitive grant; the paper says the funder had no part in design, analysis, interpretation or dissemination), with the first author's NIH support and membership of the Colorado Retail Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee; the overview, RTI International internal funds and a US National Institute on Drug Abuse grant, with no conflict statement printed; No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding is printed for the hospital paper or the overview.
plain: At one big Colorado hospital, 2,567 emergency visits over five years were judged to be at least partly due to cannabis. Only 238 of them, about 1 in 11, were linked to eating or drinking cannabis; the rest were linked to smoking or vaping it. Compared with the smoking and vaping visits, the edible visits more often involved being very intoxicated, sudden mental-health symptoms such as acute anxiety or psychosis, or heart symptoms, and less often involved vomiting or being admitted to hospital. But because far more visits involved smoking or vaping, most visits for each of those problems still involved smoking or vaping. Two papers describe a slower start and a longer-lasting effect from eating cannabis than from inhaling it, and some case reports describe people eating more after feeling nothing at first, but no study here timed effects in patients or counted how often people eat more. The hospital study and the overview could not count how many people took each form, how much they took, what was in the product, or who never went to hospital, so they cannot say how likely any form is to lead to a hospital visit, and they did not compare either form with people who do not use cannabis.
population: 2,567 emergency visits (median age 30; 65.2% male; 9.8% from outside Colorado) to one Colorado university hospital, 2012 to 2016, that clinicians judged at least partly due to cannabis: 238 recorded as edible and 2,329 as inhaled. Visits, not people (for example, 301 people accounted for 440 of the visits for cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome). Timing and case-report material comes from a 2016 narrative overview citing laboratory studies and case reports (not read).
exposure: Cannabis recorded in the chart as eaten or drunk (edible; 238 visits), from the nursing questionnaire and providers' notes, self-reported and unverified; a dose was charted for 80 of the 238 (study measure only); product contents not tested in the hospital study.
comparator: Visits recorded as inhaled (2,194 documented as smoked or otherwise inhaled, plus 135 with no route written down, counted as inhaled) at the same hospital in the same years. No comparison group of people who took each form and did not attend hospital, and no comparison with people who do not use cannabis; for the sales comparison, flower and edible units sold in Colorado in 2014 to 2016 under assumed THC contents.
outcome: Reasons for the visit coded from the chart (intoxication; acute, acute-on-chronic and chronic psychiatric symptoms; gastrointestinal symptoms including cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome; cardiovascular symptoms), admission and length of stay; the later and longer effect after eating as described from cited pharmacology and case reports, not measured in patients.
magnitude: Hospital chart review (Monte 2019), share of each group's visits, edible-attributed (n = 238) against inhaled-attributed (n = 2,329), % (difference in percentage points, 95% CI): intoxication 48.3 vs 27.8 (20.5; 13.9 to 27.1); acute psychiatric symptoms 18.0 vs 10.9 (7.1; 2.1 to 12.1); cardiovascular symptoms 8.0 vs 3.1 (4.9; 1.4 to 8.4); any psychiatric symptom 26.1 vs 24.5 (1.6; -4.2 to 7.4); gastrointestinal symptoms 15.1 vs 32.3 (-17.2; -22.1 to -12.2), of which cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4 vs 18.0 (-9.6; -13.5 to -5.7); admitted 18.9 vs 32.9; women 51.3 vs 33.1; living outside Colorado 40.8 vs 6.6 (each P < 0.001); median length of stay 2 hours (range 1 to 54) vs 3 hours (0 to 121). Severe heart events (myocardial infarction, ventricular dysrhythmia) in both groups, no counts. Edible-attributed visits as a share of all visits for each reason, editors' arithmetic from Table 2 counts: intoxication 115 of 762 (15.1%), acute psychiatric 43 of 297 (14.5%), cardiovascular 19 of 92 (20.7%); edible 238 of 2,567 visits (9.3%). Route recorded in 2,432 of 2,567 visits (94.7%); dose charted in 130 (5.1%), 80 of them edible, 19 of those at 50 mg of THC or more (as charted, unverified; study measure only). Eight symptom groups compared, no correction for multiple comparisons. Colorado sales 2014 to 2016: 219 edible and 1,819 inhaled attributable visits (edible 10.7%); edible 0.32% of THC sold by weight (flower 327,990 kg at an assumed 20% THC; 21.2 million edible units at an assumed 10 mg each); flower-to-edible THC ratio 309 (range 279 to 325); visit share about 33 times the share expected if both routes were equally likely to lead to a visit (authors). Overview (Barrus 2016, narrative, second-hand figures): Colorado 2014 edible units 1.96 million medicinal and 2.85 million retail, said to be about 45 percent of total cannabis sales (measure not stated); timing as cited, inhaled start within minutes and effects tapering within 2 to 3 hours, eaten start 30 to 90 minutes and peak 2 to 4 hours after eating (hospital paper, from the same pharmacology review: clearance about 4 hours after inhaling, about 12 hours after eating); oral bioavailability 6 to 10 percent of the amount in the product (as cited); 83 percent of tested medicinal edibles more than 10 percent from their labelled THC (second-hand; the paper itself, now read, gives 62 of 75, 82.7%, editors' arithmetic); out-of-state patients' edible-related visits 85 to 168 per 10,000 visits, 2013 to 2014 (second-hand, not read).

evidence.locator: Abstract; Results, 1st (unlabelled) paragraph; Methods › Study Participants and Coding, paragraph; Methods › Measurements, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Chart review of all emergency visits to one Colorado university hospital, 1 January 2012 to 31 December 2016: 449,031 eligible visits, 9,973 with a cannabis-related diagnosis code (the participants were adults with such a code), 2,567 (25.7% of the 9,973) judged at least partly attributable to cannabis. Route was recorded in 2,432 of the 2,567 (94.7%): 238 edible (9.3% of the 2,567; 9.8% of the 2,432) and 2,194 inhaled; the 135 visits with insufficient documentation were counted as inhaled, giving 2,329. A dose was recorded in 130 (5.1%). Cannabis use is assessed in the nursing assessment questionnaire and the providers' notes; the route was captured from the medical record, and inhalation was presumed when it was not documented. Visits attributable to inhaled and to edible cannabis both rose each year (Figure 2, an image, not read).

evidence.locator: Table 2; Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 2nd paragraph; Abstract
evidence.extracted: Table 2, edible-attributed (n = 238) against inhaled-attributed (n = 2,329) visits, % (difference in percentage points, 95% CI): intoxication 48.3 vs 27.8 (20.5; 13.9 to 27.1); acute psychiatric symptoms 18.0 vs 10.9 (7.1; 2.1 to 12.1); cardiovascular symptoms 8.0 vs 3.1 (4.9; 1.4 to 8.4); any psychiatric symptom 26.1 vs 24.5 (1.6; -4.2 to 7.4); gastrointestinal symptoms 15.1 vs 32.3 (-17.2; -22.1 to -12.2); cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4 vs 18.0 (-9.6; -13.5 to -5.7). The text adds that severe adverse cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction and ventricular dysrhythmia, occurred in both groups; no counts are given. Only two route groups appear in the tables and text, edible and inhaled; the inhaled group is not broken down by product, and tobacco mixed into joints is not recorded.

evidence.locator: Table 2, counts; Results › Reasons for Cannabis-Attributable ED Visits, paragraph
evidence.extracted: Table 2 counts, edible and inhaled: intoxication 115 and 647 (762 in all); acute psychiatric symptoms 43 and 254 (297); cardiovascular symptoms 19 and 73 (92); gastrointestinal symptoms 36 and 752; cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 20 and 420. Editors' arithmetic: edible-attributed visits were 15.1%, 14.5% and 20.7% of the intoxication, acute psychiatric and cardiovascular visits, so most visits for those reasons were inhaled-attributed. Across the 2,567 visits (reasons not mutually exclusive): gastrointestinal symptoms including cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 788 (30.7%), of which cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 440 visits (17.1%) by 301 people; intoxication 762 (29.7%), psychiatric symptoms 633 (24.7%), cardiovascular symptoms 92 (3.6%).

evidence.locator: Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Discussion, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Edible-attributed against inhaled-attributed visits: women 51.3% vs 33.1%; living outside Colorado 40.8% vs 6.6%; admitted 18.9% vs 32.9% (each P < 0.001); median length of stay 2 hours (range 1 to 54) vs 3 hours (0 to 121); age similar, no figures. Table 1, all 2,567 attributable visits: median age 30; 65.2% male; 9.8% from outside Colorado; 31.6% admitted, 62.5% discharged, 2.1% transferred to a psychiatric facility, no deaths. The Discussion says the higher admission rate in the inhaled group seemed driven by admission of patients with cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome; this is not analysed.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors write that, although less frequent overall, edible products lead to more acute psychiatric events and cardiovascular symptoms than inhaled exposure, and that the high frequency of visits and the greater likelihood of admission with inhalable products suggest that education about the adverse health effects of inhalable cannabis may have the greatest effect on public health.

evidence.locator: Results › Colorado Sales Data by Route of Exposure; Table 3; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Colorado sales, 2014 to 2016 (Table 3): 219 edible-attributed and 1,819 inhaled-attributed visits, so edibles were 10.7% of attributable visits, against 0.32% of THC sold by weight (flower 327,990 kg at an assumed 20% THC; 21.2 million edible units at an assumed 10 mg each; ratio of flower to edible THC 309, range 279 to 325). The authors call the observed share about 33 times higher than expected if both routes were equally toxic and say careful interpretation is required: THC content was assumed, one hospital was compared with state-level sales, home-grown and black-market cannabis were not counted, and sales are not geocoded.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph; Abstract (Limitation)
evidence.extracted: Limits stated by the authors: retrospective design with exposure captured largely through self-report; no comparative community-based exposure cohort; patients presenting to the emergency department differ from the overall population of people who use cannabis, most of whom may have no adverse effects, so a prospective cohort of people who use cannabis and people who do not is needed; doses could not be verified and ingested doses may have been larger than inhaled doses. A dose was documented in 80 edible-attributed visits and in 19 it was 50 mg or higher; the authors were surprised by the low edible doses reported, given the THC content of a typical Colorado joint. Route was presumed inhaled when not documented, which they say could have biased the analyses toward greater toxicity in the inhaled group. The hospital has the second most visits per year in the state and is in an area of high cannabis availability.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Timing as described by the authors, citing a pharmacology review (Grotenhermen 2003, not read): inhaled cannabis gives clinical effects within 10 minutes, a peak blood concentration within 30 to 90 minutes and complete clearance within 4 hours; oral THC does not reach a significant blood concentration until at least 30 minutes, peaks at about 3 hours and clears about 12 hours after ingestion. People report longer-lasting effects with edibles than with smoking or vaping (reference 8, Giombi 2018, on consumers' perceptions of edibles; its design is not stated on the page) and more intense effects and unpleasant psychiatric symptoms (reference 9, an analysis of Twitter posts); neither was read. Death has been associated with edible products in three cases taken from news reports (references 10 to 12). No timing was measured in this study's patients.

evidence.locator: Methods › Role of the Funding Source, paragraph; Grant Support, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Funded by a competitive grant from the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment for a project on the adverse health effects of edible cannabis products; the paper states that the department was not involved in study design, analysis, data interpretation or dissemination. The first author received support from NIH K23 GM110516, NIH CTSI UL1 TR001082 and CDPHE 17 FHHA 96950 (Grant Support). Disclosures: the first author reports grants from the department during the study and sits on the Colorado Retail Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee, a group of clinicians and scientists reviewing the literature on the public health effects of cannabis; another author reports department grants; authors not named disclosed no conflicts. No cannabis-industry, tobacco-industry or advocacy funding is printed.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Introduction, paragraph
evidence.extracted: A narrative overview published by RTI Press (PMC lists it as Methods Rep RTI Press), written for the educated layperson and policy makers. The Abstract says little research has evaluated how ingestion differs from other methods of cannabis use in therapeutic efficacy, subjective effects and safety; that the most prominent difference between ingestion and inhalation of cannabis extracts is the delayed onset of drug effect with ingestion; and that consumers who do not understand this may consume more than intended before the effect starts, often resulting in profoundly adverse effects (no count is given). The Introduction says the authors describe promises and challenges and critically examine extant research; no search method, selection criteria or appraisal of studies is described.

evidence.locator: Overview of Edibles, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: In Colorado in 2014, 1.96 million units of edible medicinal cannabis-infused products and 2.85 million units of edible retail products were sold, which the authors say accounted for about 45 percent of the total cannabis sales in the state (a state report, as cited); the measure of sales is not stated. Homemade edibles are not tracked, and the data show sales and not the proportion of people who consume edibles.

evidence.locator: Challenges of Edibles, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: After eating, liver first-pass metabolism forms 11-OH-THC, a potent psychoactive metabolite that appears in blood in higher quantities after ingestion than after inhalation (as cited); the authors write that it may be responsible for the stronger and longer-lasting effect of edibles compared with comparable doses of smoked cannabis. Inhaled THC takes initial effect within minutes and shows peak effect in about 20 to 30 minutes, with psychoactive effects tapering off within 2 to 3 hours; the initial psychoactive effect of edibles takes 30 to 90 minutes to be felt and the high is longer-lasting, with a peak 2 to 4 hours after ingestion (Grotenhermen 2003 and others, as cited, not read). Weight, metabolism, gender and eating habits are said to affect how soon and how long.

evidence.locator: Challenges of Edibles, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: After oral doses, plasma THC is lower than after smoking or infusion, and its correlation with degree of intoxication varies considerably across individuals (Hollister 1981, as cited); oral bioavailability is 6 to 10 percent of the amount in the product (Schwilke 2009, as cited). The authors say the lack of consistency and the delayed intoxication may lead both new and experienced people to take more than intended, and write that edible products are responsible for the majority of health care visits due to cannabis intoxication, which they say is likely due to people's failure to appreciate the delayed effects (a 2015 JAMA article by Monte, Zane and Heard, as cited, not read).
evidence.quote: responsible for the majority of health care visits due to cannabis intoxication

evidence.locator: Challenges of Edibles, 7th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Dosage estimation for retail products may be inexact (Vandrey 2015, as cited). Anecdotal reports from medicinal cannabis patients are said to confirm that even people who take cannabis daily may consume more than expected (Hudak 2015, a letter in the American Journal of Psychiatry, as cited): having eaten the suggested serving first, patients ate the entire product after not feeling any effects, and found it practical to eat the entire product in one sitting.

evidence.locator: Challenges of Edibles, 14th paragraph
evidence.extracted: One death after an edible is described: in March 2014 a 19-year-old man died of injuries from jumping from a fourth-floor balcony in Colorado after eating a cannabis-infused cookie (a public-health case report, as cited). The text says he was told to eat one serving, and that having not felt intoxicated within 60 minutes he ate the whole cookie within 2 hours of that serving; the autopsy identified cannabis intoxication as a chief contributing factor.

evidence.locator: Promises of Edibles, 10th and 11th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: On smoke: cannabis and tobacco smoke are said to be similar in kind in toxicity; cannabis smoke is linked to lung inflammation and bronchitis; the link to chronic lung disease is unclear; epidemiological research links habitual cannabis smoking to several cancers but is complicated by small samples and co-occurring tobacco smoking. The authors then write that eating edibles does not seem to affect lung function or raise cancer risk, calling this a solid rationale for choosing this route as opposed to smoking cannabis, particularly for medical conditions such as cancer. No study of people who eat cannabis is cited for the last point.

evidence.locator: Acknowledgments; author-information panel
evidence.extracted: Preparation of the manuscript was supported by RTI International internal funds and National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DA-03672. All eight authors are at RTI International. No conflict-of-interest statement is printed in the manuscript, and no cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are declared.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Methods › Search strategy; Table 1 and its note; Study selection, abstraction, and analysis; Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1; Table 4 (Cavazos-Rehg 2016 row, for 'of tweets')
evidence.extracted: The 2024 review by route: a systematic review without meta-analysis, guided by PRISMA, with no protocol or registration stated. Search of Web of Science, ProQuest, PsycINFO, Embase and Medline (the Abstract also names Scopus) in November–December 2019, updated August–December 2023, plus reference lists; peer-reviewed English-language articles from January 2009 to December 2023 reporting the route of administration, with cannabis confirmed by drug screening; studies including other illicit drugs, or people with pre-existing heart or lung conditions, excluded. In Table 1 the cannabis terms are combined with AND NOT Tobacco. 1,873 records, 110 full texts, 42 included: 6 case reports or series, 21 literature reviews and 15 empirical studies (2 randomised trials, 5 retrospective analyses, 1 content analysis of tweets, 3 longitudinal studies, 3 cross-sectional surveys, 1 pre/post study). Abstract selection was independent (kappa 0.89). The Methods say the strength of evidence was graded for each outcome, but no grades and no appraisal of individual studies are reported, and nothing was pooled.

evidence.locator: Abstract (Results); Results › Empirical studies, 1st paragraph; Cardiovascular effects, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 4 (Cao 2016, Kaczor 2021, Newmeyer 2017, Pepin 2023, Shiplo 2016 rows); Discussion, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Oral route in the review (second-hand): five empirical studies have an oral arm. In adults, the Newmeyer 2017 laboratory crossover found heart rate 13.0 and 10.2 beats a minute above placebo at 1.5 and 3 h after oral cannabis, not significantly different from smoked or vaporised cannabis, and no effect of route on blood pressure or breathing rate; in the Shiplo 2016 survey of 364 Canadian medical cannabis patients, eating was rated lower in perceived respiratory harm than smoking. The other three are records of exposures, two of them in children only: Cao 2016 (430 exposures to cannabis food products reported to US poison centres, 2013 to 2015): tachycardia in 84 (printed as 31%, which 430 cannot give), hypertension, chest pain or hypotension in a few, and respiratory depression in 3, reported only in children aged 5 or younger; Kaczor 2021 (chart review of 32 children): 5 (16%) needed respiratory support; Pepin 2023 (records of 80 children younger than 6 with a known THC dose): tachycardia and hypotension most common, with severe cardiovascular toxicity and severe respiratory symptoms (hypoxia, then apnea and bradypnea) at recorded doses above 2 mg/kg of body weight. The Abstract nonetheless says cannabis edibles were associated with minimal respiratory effects, and the Discussion that severe cardiovascular effects were associated with higher THC doses in all routes. No included study measured lung function or breathing symptoms in adults who eat cannabis against adults who do not use it.

evidence.locator: Abstract (Conclusion); Discussion, 1st paragraph; Discussion, paragraphs beginning Nevertheless, Evidence on the cardiovascular (its First point), Second, Third and In addition; Strength and limitations; Conclusion; Disclosure statement; Funding
evidence.extracted: The review's conclusions and limits: the authors conclude that cannabis use does cause cardiovascular and respiratory effects but that conclusions by route remain tentative because of the studies' methodological limitations. They state that most studies were cross-sectional or retrospective, from which temporality cannot be determined; that the three longitudinal studies all concerned smoking and breathing; that the two randomised trials were small (n = 24 and, as they give it, n = 11); that only five of the 15 empirical studies reported cardiovascular effects; and that only three sources specified the type of smoking (joints against blunts); only English articles from 2009 to 2023 were included. In the Discussion they write that each route was associated with effects of some kind, suggesting a need to avoid cannabis altogether, followed by harm-reduction recommendations (the authors' advice, not derived from a synthesis and not adopted here). No funding; no conflicts of interest declared. Editors' reading: the causal wording is not supported by the designs the authors describe, nothing was pooled and no appraisal is reported (AMSTAR 2 critically low on the card), and several studies within the review's window and topic that this library has read are not among its sources (Monte 2019 on emergency visits after eating against inhaling cannabis, Braymiller 2020 on vaping and bronchitic symptoms, Spindle 2018 on smoked against vaporised cannabis, Ghasemiesfe 2018, a systematic review of respiratory outcomes).

risk_of_bias.note: Chart review (Monte 2019): ROBINS-E overall high, with confounding, exposure measurement and selection each high (no adjustment for who took each form; route self-reported and presumed inhaled when not written down; everyone in the data attended an emergency department). Overview (Barrus 2016): a narrative review with no stated search or appraisal and second-hand figures, judged high overall.

inconsistency.note: One data set (route at hospital visits), so consistency cannot be judged. The overview's statement that edibles account for most intoxication visits conflicts with the hospital count (115 of 762, 15.1%) but rests on a 2015 viewpoint that was not read, so it is shown as a contradicting anchor, not as a second data set.

indirectness.note: Worded for one Colorado hospital, 2012 to 2016, in an area of high cannabis availability. Route is edible against inhaled only (inhaled not split into flower, vaped oil or concentrates). The later and longer effect is cited from pharmacology work that was not read and was not measured in patients; the sales ratio uses assumed product contents.

imprecision.note: 238 edible visits; the intervals for the cardiovascular (1.4 to 8.4 points) and acute psychiatric (2.1 to 12.1) differences are wide for their size; eight symptom groups compared without correction; a dose charted in only 5.1% of visits.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with one data set.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low (METHODS §6.3). The route comparison rests on one chart review at one hospital and a narrative overview with no data of its own. Risk of bias -1: ROBINS-E overall high for the chart review (no adjustment; route self-reported and presumed inhaled when undocumented; every person in the data attended an emergency department); the overview has no stated search or appraisal and its figures are second-hand. Indirectness -1: one hospital in an area of high availability; edible against inhaled only; timing and the 11-OH-THC explanation come from pharmacology work that was not read and were not measured in patients; the sales ratio rests on assumed contents. Imprecision -1: 238 edible visits, wide intervals for two of the three findings that favour more events with edibles, no correction across eight symptom groups, a dose charted for 5.1% of visits. These downgrades together pass the floor, so the certainty is very low. Not downgraded for inconsistency or publication bias: one data set per question; the overview's statement that edibles account for most intoxication visits conflicts with the hospital count (15.1%) but rests on a viewpoint that was not read, so it is shown as a contradicting anchor and flagged. Worded as 'describes' rather than 'increases' or 'is associated with' because the data are shares of visits, not risks, with no count of people taking each form, and the claim combines counts, the authors' interpretation and second-hand pharmacology. The Discussion's causal wording and the 33-fold ratio are the authors' own reading and are reported as such, not adopted.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only, no advice. Rests on one chart review at one hospital (Monte 2019, the only primary study of route read for this claim) and a narrative overview (Barrus 2016: no stated search or appraisal; its timing, label-testing, child-poisoning and out-of-state figures are second-hand). Label accuracy (Vandrey 2015) and children's poison-centre calls (Tweet 2023) are now claims of their own (cl_can_edibles_labels, cl_can_edibles_children), split by the editor on 2026-10-23. The overview's statement that edibles account for most intoxication visits conflicts with the hospital count (115 of 762, 15.1%); its source, a 2015 viewpoint by the hospital group (Monte, Zane, Heard), was not read, and the conflict is shown as a contradicting anchor, not resolved. The editors' arithmetic (edible shares of visits by reason) needs recomputation by a second reader. Papers cited by the sources (Kim 2016, Hall 2018, Wang 2014, Cao 2016, Grotenhermen 2003) were not read; the hospital group's papers are not independent of each other. Amounts, strengths and timings appear only as study conditions, as measured product content, or as the sources describe them. Funding as printed: Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (Monte); RTI International internal funds and a NIDA grant (Barrus). No cannabis-industry funding is printed for Monte or Barrus. The Discussion's causal wording ('lead to') and the 33-fold ratio are the authors' reading; the claim does not adopt them.
