statement: A laboratory test of products, read with its July 2015 correction (whose wording is followed where the saved letter differs), measured 75 labelled edible products of 47 brands (baked goods, drinks, candy or chocolate) bought in August to October 2014 at nine medical-cannabis dispensaries in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle, in markets the authors call unregulated. Against the THC printed on the package, 13 (17%) were within 10%, 17 (23%) held more than the label said (on average 28% more, at most 55% more) and 45 (60%) held less (on average about half the labelled amount: 47% less in the table's overall row, about 53% less from its city rows, editors' arithmetic; at most 99% less, some with almost none). Products holding more than their label were commonest in Los Angeles (9 of 20) and products holding less in Seattle (18 of 23, where 1 product was within 10%); San Francisco had 8 of 32 within 10% (χ² = 12.94, P = .01). Only 13 products printed a CBD content, and none held it within 10% (4 more, 9 less; editors' arithmetic), although 44 of the 75 contained some CBD. Whole packages were mixed before testing, so the test cannot say how evenly THC was spread between pieces or servings (two samples of the same mixed package differed by more than 10% in 37 products, which were then analysed whole), and it measured no effects in people: the authors' statements that products with less THC may not give the intended medical benefit and that products with more put patients at risk of adverse effects are their inference. The sample was not random and may not generalize, as the authors say, and the cost of the testing was covered by Werc Shop Laboratories, with which four of the six authors are affiliated (see funding). Funding as printed: the label test, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, except the cost of the laboratory testing, which Werc Shop Laboratories covered (four of the six authors are affiliated with Werc Shop Laboratory; the paper says neither funder had any role in the design, conduct, analysis or reporting, while its list of contributions credits two of those four with the concept, design and supervision of the study; one author reported personal fees and nonfinancial support from Tilray (Division of Privateer Holdings) and travel reimbursement from Americans for Safe Access; the paper does not say what these organisations do).
plain: A laboratory test of 75 edibles bought in three US cities in 2014 found that only about 1 in 6 held the amount of THC printed on the label: about 1 in 4 held more, and about 3 in 5 held less, some almost none.
population: 75 labelled edible products (products, not people) bought at nine medical-cannabis dispensaries in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle, August to October 2014.
exposure: the THC and CBD measured in each whole package by laboratory chromatography.
comparator: the THC or CBD content printed on the package, within 10% counted as accurate.
outcome: measured content within 10% of the label, more than 10% above it, or more than 10% below it.
magnitude: Label test (Vandrey 2015, as corrected in JAMA 2015;314(2):188; products, not people): 75 labelled edibles of 47 brands (22 baked goods, 13 beverages, 40 candy or chocolate; editors' sums), nine medical-cannabis dispensaries in three cities, August to October 2014; measured THC against the label: within 10%, 13 (17%; Wilson 95% CI 10.4 to 27.4, editors' calculation); more than 10% above, 17 (23%; 14.7 to 33.3); more than 10% below, 45 (60%; 48.7 to 70.3); outside 10%, 62 (82.7%; 72.6 to 89.6). Mean deviation (SD): within, -3% (4); above, +28% (13), largest +55%; below, -47% (29) in the overall row, against -52.5% from the city rows (-44%, -55% and -61% for 20, 7 and 18 products; editors' arithmetic), largest -99%. By city, within / above / below: San Francisco 8 / 4 / 20 of 32; Los Angeles 4 / 9 / 7 of 20; Seattle 1 / 4 / 18 of 23 (χ² = 12.94, P = .01; degrees of freedom not printed; 3 of 9 expected counts below 5, editors' calculation). By type, within / above / below: baked goods 2 / 7 / 13; beverages 3 / 2 / 8; candy or chocolate 8 / 8 / 24. CBD detected in 44 (59%); printed on 13, of which 4 above and 9 below the label (none within 10%, editors' arithmetic); median THC:CBD 36:1. Measured THC per package (measured product content): median 54 mg, range under 1 to 1,236 mg; labelled 2 to 1,000 mg. Duplicate samples differed by more than 10% in 37 of 75.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' checklist for a laboratory analysis of products: some concerns overall (non-random sample of products; laboratory method not validated in the letter; two sentences with labels reversed, corrected in July 2015). Not serious enough to downgrade on its own for a measurement of product content.

inconsistency.note: One data set; the 2016 overview's second-hand figure (83% more than 10% from the label) and a newspaper investigation it cites point the same way, but neither is an independent measurement read here.

indirectness.note: 75 products from nine medical dispensaries in three US cities in 2014, in markets the authors call unregulated; it does not describe products sold elsewhere or later, under other rules, or what people actually took.

imprecision.note: 75 products (17% within 10%; 95% CI 10.4 to 27.4, editors' calculation), 20 to 32 per city.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with one data set.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low (METHODS §6.3). One laboratory test of 75 products: indirectness -1 (three US cities, medical dispensaries, 2014, unregulated markets) and imprecision -1 (75 products, wide interval), so the certainty is very low. Worded as 'describes' because it measures product content, not effects in people; the authors' statements about benefit and risk are their inference.

evidence.locator: Challenges of Edibles, 19th paragraph
evidence.extracted: A 2014 newspaper investigation found the actual THC content of retail edibles often differed significantly from labels; from mid-2014 Colorado required THC in recreational edibles to be tested and labelled but tested only against a threshold, which does not check label accuracy. One study of medicinal edibles sold in California and Washington is reported to have found that the total THC content of 83 percent of edibles tested differed from the labelled amounts by over 10 percent, with more than half containing significantly less than claimed and nearly a quarter significantly more (Vandrey 2015, as cited; not read).

evidence.locator: Methods, 1st, 2nd, 4th and 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Products, not people: dispensaries in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle were picked at random from an Internet directory until three per city were found that sold at least one edible in each of three categories (baked goods, beverages, candy or chocolate) with a specific delta-9-THC content on the label. Between August and October 2014, purchasers with a physician's letter and no history of buying edibles bought as wide a variety as possible within $400 per city; purchasers, but not dispensary staff, knew the products would be tested. Whole packages were homogenized and two samples tested by high-performance liquid chromatography, averaged and scaled to the product's weight; where the two differed by more than 10% (37 products) the whole product was analysed. Within 10% of the label counted as accurate, more than 10% above as underlabelled and more than 10% below as overlabelled.

evidence.locator: Results, 1st paragraph, 1st sentence (p. 2491); Table 1, Overall (3 Cities) rows (p. 2492)
evidence.extracted: Of 75 products (47 brands), THC was within 10% of the label in 13 (17%), more than 10% above it in 17 (23%) and more than 10% below it in 45 (60%). Mean deviation (SD): within, -3% (4), largest 9%; above, +28% (13), largest +55% (measured 34 to 1,236 mg against labelled 20 to 1,000 mg); below, -47% (29), largest -99% (measured under 1 to 267 mg against labelled 2 to 325 mg). By type (within / above / below): baked goods 2 / 7 / 13; beverages 3 / 2 / 8; candy or chocolate 8 / 8 / 24. Editors' calculation: 62 of 75 (82.7%) outside 10%; Wilson 95% intervals 10.4% to 27.4% (within), 14.7% to 33.3% (above) and 48.7% to 70.3% (below); the city rows (-44%, -55% and -61% for 20, 7 and 18 products) give an n-weighted mean shortfall of -52.5%, not the overall row's -47%.

evidence.locator: Table 1, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle rows
evidence.extracted: Within 10% / more than 10% above / more than 10% below the THC label: San Francisco 8 (25%) / 4 (13%) / 20 (62%) of 32 products; Los Angeles 4 (20%) / 9 (45%) / 7 (35%) of 20; Seattle 1 (4%) / 4 (17%) / 18 (78%) of 23. Mean shortfall of the products below their label: San Francisco -44%, Los Angeles -55%, Seattle -61%; largest -93%, -99% and -99%.

evidence.locator: JAMA 2015;314(2):188, Correction, 'Incorrect Labels in Text and in Table 1 Column Headings', right column
evidence.extracted: The correction gives the Results as: 17% accurately labelled, 23% underlabelled and 60% overlabelled for THC; underlabelled products (more THC than the label) likeliest in Los Angeles and overlabelled products (less THC) in Seattle (chi-squared 12.94, P = .01); for CBD, 4 products underlabelled and 9 overlabelled; the third column of Table 1 headed Underlabelled and the fourth Overlabelled. The saved PDF of the letter (p. 2491) prints the city sentence (against its own Table 1) and the CBD sentence the other way round; the correction is followed.

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph, 3rd sentence as corrected in JAMA 2015;314(2):188 (p. 2491); Table 2 (p. 2493)
evidence.extracted: 44 of 75 products (59%) had detectable CBD; only 13 printed a CBD content, of which, as corrected, 4 held more than 10% more and 9 more than 10% less than labelled. Median THC:CBD ratio of products with detectable CBD 36:1; 7 had ratios below 10:1 and 1 a 1:1 ratio. Measured content per product (measured product content), mg, median (interquartile range as printed) and range: THC 54 (99), under 1 to 1,236; THCA 2 (15), under 1 to 173; CBD 2 (3), under 1 to 51. So none of the 13 CBD labels was within 10% (editors' arithmetic).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors write that the products, though unregulated, failed basic label-accuracy standards for pharmaceuticals; that more than half held significantly less cannabinoid than labelled (meaning beyond the 10% limit; no statistical test per product), some with negligible THC, and may not give the desired medical benefit; and that others held significantly more THC than labelled, which they say puts patients at risk of adverse effects, citing two sources (no effects were measured). They state that few cities, dispensaries and products were included and that, because no source lists all dispensaries and many products have no cannabinoid label, a true random sample was not possible and the results may not generalize.

evidence.locator: Author Affiliations (p. 2491); Author Contributions, Conflict of Interest Disclosures, Funding/Support, Role of the Funder/Sponsor (p. 2493)
evidence.extracted: Funded by Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine except the cost of analytical testing, which Werc Shop Laboratories covered; neither, the paper says, had a role in the design, conduct, data, manuscript or decision to submit. Four of the six authors are affiliated with Werc Shop Laboratory (Pasadena, California; Bellevue, Washington); concept and design are credited to Vandrey, J. Raber, Douglass and Bonn-Miller, and supervision to Vandrey, J. Raber and Douglass. Bonn-Miller reported personal fees and nonfinancial support from Tilray (Division of Privateer Holdings) and travel reimbursement from Americans for Safe Access; no other disclosures. The paper does not describe these organisations.

statement: In one Colorado field study of 121 adults who already used cannabis at least four times a month (55 using flower, 66 using concentrates; each person chose the form, and a labelled strength was assigned at random within each form), blood THC measured about 13 minutes after they used their own product in their own way at home was higher in the concentrate group than in the flower group (mean 0.32 against 0.14 µg/mL), and so was the active by-product 11-OH-THC, at every time point including before use. Even so, self-rated intoxication (form effect P = .11) and the marijuana effects scale (P = .18) did not differ by form, tension and vigor ratings were lower in the concentrate group, and inhibitory control scores were higher in the flower group at every time, including before use. Delayed verbal recall worsened after use in both groups (form effect P = .65), and eyes-closed balance worsened and was back at its pre-use level by one hour in both (form effect P = .85); the main text reports no effects of labelled strength within a form at its set threshold (P < .01), with the strength tests in a supplement that was not read. The authors offer three untested explanations for similar intoxication despite higher blood THC (greater tolerance in the concentrate group, receptor saturation, individual differences) and read the lack of a blood-level difference by strength within a form as suggesting that people adjust how much they take. The groups were not alike before the session: the concentrate group had used concentrates on 16.5 of the past 30 days against 3.5, had begun regular use at 17.7 years against 20.0 and had about twice the baseline THC metabolite, and it used about half as much product by weight at the session. There was no placebo or no-use session, so changes after use cannot be told apart from repeating the tests; follow-up was one hour; form was not randomised, so earlier differences between the groups may account for some findings; 12 of the 133 people assessed were left out because blood THC after use was very low (9 of 64 on flower, 3 of 69 on concentrates; editors' arithmetic from the group sizes); and people had to have used the strongest product they could be assigned before without a bad reaction and to use no other drugs or daily tobacco, so the findings do not reach people who use cannabis rarely, are new to it, or do not use it. Tobacco mixed into joints was not recorded and cannabinoids other than THC were not reported. The authors' Conclusions voice concern about long-term effects, which were not measured, and the Abstract and Results print the spread of blood THC as standard errors although the Discussion gives standard deviations. A scoping review done for the State of Colorado searched seven databases to mid-2022 and mapped 452 human studies that report a THC concentration or a high-concentration product (225 observational studies, 142 randomised trials, 51 case reports and 34 case series; earliest 1971, 60% published 2017 to 2022). Only 54 (12%) examined concentrates and a health outcome directly and 189 (42%) examined THC concentration directly; 63% studied generic cannabis types, and products typically high in concentration (oils, concentrates, hash, extracts, resins) were examined in about 2% to 10% of studies. The median strength studied was 12% THC where given as a percentage (15 mg where given in milligrams), well below the Colorado market strengths the authors cite from other sources for 2020 (flower averaging 19%, concentrates 68%), which they think likely reflects the restriction of research cannabis to a federal supply without concentrates. Only 47% of studies had a control group and 41% reported effect estimates, and most did not capture the elements of use needed to estimate exposure. The review extracted no study results and did not assess bias, so it shows what has been studied and not what was found; its Conclusions say the literature has serious limits in generalisability to the current market and that high-quality evidence bearing on whether to regulate THC concentration is scarce. Searches were English-only, designed to be sensitive rather than specific, and screened with AI assistance, so studies may be missing; the evidence map and the appendix were not read. Of the 452 studies, 25 (6%) were funded by the cannabis industry and 58 (13%) had an author with a disclosed industry tie, while 24% reported no funding source and 32% no conflict statement. A systematic review of observational studies searched to January 2021 (Petrilli et al., 2022; 20 articles from 16 studies by the editors' count, none rated good quality, no meta-analysis because every study relied on what people said they used and definitions of strength differed) found stronger cannabis (skunk-type, or types of 10% THC or more) associated with psychosis in two case-control studies and one cohort, all rated fair: against never-use, first-episode psychosis was more likely with skunk-type use in a UK study (adjusted odds ratio 2.91, 95% CI 1.52 to 3.60) and with types of 10% THC or more across six countries (1.6, 1.2 to 2.2; 4.8 with daily use), but not with hash-type or lower-strength use (0.83; 1.1), and relapse after a first episode was more likely with continued daily use of stronger cannabis (3.28, 1.22 to 9.18, against former use); none of these three studies looked at concentrates as a separate form. Findings for anxiety and depression varied. The studies of concentrates themselves were all cross-sectional and rated poor: in a 20-country online survey of 181,870 people, those who used butane hash oil more often reported a past diagnosis of anxiety (odds ratio 1.80, 1.60 to 2.01) or depression (1.34, 1.21 to 1.48) than those who used lower-strength herbal cannabis, but not of psychosis (1.11, 0.85 to 1.46); a US sample of 156 found no clear association of concentrate use with psychosis, anxiety or depression symptoms, and another of 191 no difference in anxiety or depression between people who frequently used concentrates and people who frequently used herbal cannabis; in a within-person survey of 574 people, mostly using infrequently, psychosis-like experiences were slightly less frequent with concentrates than with herbal cannabis (Cohen's d 0.12); and among 71 Japanese patients, liquid or resin forms went with less residual or late-onset psychosis than dry herbal cannabis (odds ratio 0.21, 0.06 to 0.74). The review's findings on strength and cannabis use disorder are set out in a separate claim. Its authors argue that people taking less of stronger products would weaken rather than inflate these associations, and that people with poorer mental health may choose stronger products. No study read here follows people who use concentrates beyond one hour, compares them with people who do not use cannabis, or reports lung or other long-term physical outcomes for concentrates. Funding as printed: the field study, the US National Institutes of Health and the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, with the paper stating that the funders had no role in the study; participants bought their products at one local dispensary that set aside allotments for the study, with no payment declared; the review, the State of Colorado under House Bill 21-1317 (funder not involved), with authors' interests as printed (a paid consultancy for Health Canada on conflict of interest, a paid UpToDate chapter, research funding from the Institute of Cannabis Research and a seat on the state health department's marijuana advisory committee); the systematic review, an Economic and Social Research Council doctoral studentship, Cancer Research UK fellowship and project awards and a Wellcome Trust grant (funder without a role), with one author reporting previous funding from Pfizer (GRANT scheme) and a scientific consulting company doing unrelated work, and its senior author an author of several of the studies it reviews, including the butane hash oil survey. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are printed for any of the three papers.
plain: In one Colorado study, 121 adults who already used cannabis regularly used their own flower or their own concentrate (a strong extract of cannabis, such as wax or shatter) at home while researchers took blood and ran memory and balance tests. People who used concentrates had more THC in their blood than people who used flower, but they did not rate themselves as more intoxicated, and the memory and balance tests changed in similar ways in both groups. The two groups were not alike to begin with (the concentrate group already used concentrates much more often), nobody had a dummy dose, and people were followed for only an hour, so the study cannot show that concentrates are more or less impairing than flower, or what happens with longer use, and it did not include people who do not use cannabis. A separate review for the state of Colorado found 452 studies that report THC strength, but only 54 looked at concentrates and a health outcome directly; its authors say the strengths studied are well below those now sold, and the review did not check how good the studies were or report what they found. A third paper, a review of studies that asked people which cannabis they used, found that stronger cannabis, such as skunk, was linked to psychosis in studies that compared people with and without psychosis. The studies of concentrates themselves asked people only once, were rated poor, and did not agree: in one large online survey, people who used butane hash oil more often said they had been diagnosed with anxiety or depression than people who used lower-strength herbal cannabis, while two small US studies found no clear link with mental-health symptoms.
population: 121 adults in Colorado (mean age about 28; 42% to 48% women) who used cannabis at least four times a month, had used the strongest product they could be assigned before without a bad reaction, and used no other non-prescription drugs or daily tobacco (Bidwell 2020); and 452 human studies that report a THC concentration or a high-concentration product, 1971 to 2022 (Bero 2023, scoping review); and 16 observational studies in 20 articles of people who use cannabis, people with psychosis and population controls, and people using medical cannabis, in Europe, the Americas and Japan and in online surveys across 20 and 175 countries (Petrilli 2022, systematic review).
exposure: Concentrates (laboratory-tested, labelled 70% or 90% THC, assigned at random within the form; the form itself self-chosen), used in the person's usual way at home (glass rig or tube 92%, hash pen 8%) in one session after 5 days of free use (study conditions only); in the review, studies of concentrates or other high-concentration products and of THC concentration; in the systematic review, self-reported use of concentrates (butane hash oil, concentrates, or liquid or resin forms) or of stronger herbal cannabis (skunk-type, or types of 10% THC or more), as each study defined them.
comparator: Flower (labelled 16% or 24% THC; pipe 51%, bong 31%, vaporizer 11%, joint 7%) in a separate group of regular consumers who chose flower; no placebo or no-use session, and no people who do not use cannabis. In the review, no comparison of outcomes (an inventory of studies). In the systematic review, lower-strength herbal cannabis, hash-type cannabis or never-use, as each study defined them; the concentrate studies compared people who use cannabis in different forms, never with people who do not use cannabis.
outcome: Blood THC and 11-OH-THC, self-rated intoxication and marijuana-effects scale, mood (tension, vigor), delayed verbal recall, inhibitory control and working memory, and balance, before use, about 13 minutes after use and 1 hour after use. In the review, counts of studies by exposure, outcome, design and reporting. In the systematic review, psychosis (first episode, relapse, symptoms, self-reported diagnosis), psychosis-like experiences, and anxiety and depression (diagnosis or symptoms); its cannabis use disorder findings are in a separate claim.
magnitude: Field study (Bidwell 2020), concentrate group (n = 66) against flower group (n = 55), means before use, about 13 minutes after use (mean 13.3, range 3 to 47) and 1 hour after use. Blood THC, µg/mL: concentrate 0.01, 0.32, 0.03; flower 0.004, 0.14, 0.02; form effect F(1,228) = 11.00, P < .01. 11-OH-THC, µg/mL: concentrate 0.004, 0.011, 0.008; flower 0.001, 0.005, 0.004; form effect P < .001. Self-rated intoxication (scale range inconsistently described in the paper): concentrate 0.14, 2.35, 1.63; flower 0.08, 2.40, 1.93; form effect P = .11. Marijuana effects scale: form effect P = .18. Tension and vigor lower in the concentrate group (P < .01 and P < .001). Delayed verbal recall errors: concentrate 0.90, 1.50, 2.33; flower 0.65, 2.21, 1.88; change after use P < .001; form effect P = .65; form by quadratic time P = .02 (above the set threshold). Eyes-closed sway: concentrate 0.64, 0.69, 0.64; flower 0.63, 0.73, 0.63; quadratic time P < .001; form effect P = .85. Inhibitory control higher in the flower group at every time (P < .001). Thirteen outcomes tested at a fixed threshold of P < .01; no placebo. Baseline, concentrate against flower group: concentrate use on 16.5 vs 3.5 of the past 30 days; regular use begun at 17.7 vs 20.0 years; THC-COOH 0.087 vs 0.044 µg/mL; product used at the session 0.11 g vs 0.22 g (study measure only). Labelled strengths assigned at random within form: flower 16% or 24%, concentrate 70% or 90% THC; groups of 26 to 33 people. 133 assessed (64 flower, 69 concentrate); 12 left out for post-use blood THC below 0.02 µg/mL (9 flower, 3 concentrate). Scoping review (Bero 2023): 49,729 unique records, 5,828 full texts, 452 studies (225 observational, 142 randomised trials, 51 case reports, 34 case series); 54 (12%) concentrates and an outcome directly, 189 (42%) THC concentration and an outcome directly, 114 (25%) and 62 (14%) indirectly; control group in 212 (47%); effect estimates in 184 (41%); generic cannabis types in 284 (63%); products typically high in concentration in about 2% to 10%; THC given as a percentage in 172 studies, median 12% (mean 17.4%, range 0% to 100%, interquartile range 3.6% to 24%), and in milligrams in 113, median 15 mg (mean 37.4, range 0.3 to 500, interquartile range 7.5 to 26); market strengths cited by the authors from other sources for Colorado: flower averaging 14% (2014) to 19% (2020), concentrates 46% to 68%. Funding of the included studies: 25 (6%) cannabis industry, 58 (13%) author with an industry tie, 109 (24%) no funding source reported, 143 (32%) no conflict statement. Outcome domains most studied: mental health 40%, neurologic 30%, pain 29%, cardiometabolic 24%, gastrointestinal 22%, psychosocial 22%, sleep 21%. Systematic review (Petrilli 2022; 16 studies in 20 articles, none rated good): psychosis, adjusted odds ratios against never-use, skunk-type 2.91 (95% CI 1.52 to 3.60) and hash-type 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77) in the UK GAP study; types of 10% THC or more 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2) and under 10% 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5) in the six-country EU-GEI study, daily use 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3) and 2.2 (1.4 to 3.6); relapse with continued daily use of stronger cannabis 3.28 (1.22 to 9.18) against former use (58% against 24% relapsed). Concentrate studies (cross-sectional, rated poor): butane hash oil against lower-potency herbal cannabis in a 20-country survey of 181,870, self-reported diagnosis of anxiety 1.80 (1.60 to 2.01), depression 1.34 (1.21 to 1.48), psychosis 1.11 (0.85 to 1.46); concentrate use in 156 US adults, psychosis symptoms r 0.11 (-0.20 to 0.40), anxiety 0.21 (-0.10 to 0.49), depression 0.17 (-0.15 to 0.45); frequent concentrate against frequent herbal use in 191 US adults, anxiety means 1.1 and 0.66, depression 0.72 and 0.76, not significantly different; psychosis-like experiences in 574 people, means 1.1 with concentrates and 1.2 with herbal cannabis (0 to 10 scale; Cohen's d 0.12); 71 Japanese patients, liquid or resin against dry herbal cannabis, residual or late-onset psychotic disorder 0.212 (0.061 to 0.735). Anxiety and depression with higher- against lower-potency herbal cannabis: generalised anxiety disorder 1.92 (1.11 to 3.32) in a UK sample of 1,087; 1.05 (0.98 to 1.12) for anxiety and 1.18 (1.11 to 1.25) for depression in the 20-country survey; major depression 1.28 (0.68 to 2.32) in the UK sample.

evidence.locator: Methods › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Baseline Appointment, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Experimental Appointment, paragraph
evidence.extracted: Adults aged 21 to 70 who had used cannabis at least four times in the past month and had used, at least once, the strongest product that could be assigned (24% THC flower or 90% THC concentrate) with no adverse reaction; no other non-prescription drug in the past 60 days, no daily tobacco, light alcohol use. Within each form, participants were randomly assigned by random-number table to a labelled strength (flower 16% or 24%; concentrate 70% or 90%), bought it at a local dispensary that set allotments aside for the study, used it freely for 5 days, and on the fifth day the mobile laboratory came to their home: they gave the first measures there, used the product in their preferred way at home, and returned to the laboratory for the short-term post-use measures (mean 13.3 minutes away from it, range 3 to 47) and the 1-hour post-use measures. The form itself was each person's own choice.

evidence.locator: Results › Descriptive Information, paragraph; Abstract; Table 1
evidence.extracted: 133 people were assessed (64 in the flower group, 69 in the concentrate group). Twelve were excluded because blood THC after use was below 0.02 µg/mL (study mean 0.24), taken to mean they had not used the product at home as instructed, leaving 121 (55 flower, 66 concentrate, so 9 and 3 were left out from the two groups; editors' arithmetic); mean age 28.8 and 28.3 years; 42% and 48% women in Table 1 (the Abstract gives 46% and 45%). Table 1: concentrate group glass rig or tube 92% and hash pen 8%; flower group pipe 51%, bong 31%, vaporizer 11%, joint 7%.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Results › Cannabinoids, paragraph; Table 2; Figure 1; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: THC and 11-OH-THC peaked at the short-term post-use assessment and then fell. Mean blood THC after use was 0.32 µg/mL in the concentrate group and 0.14 µg/mL in the flower group (printed as SE 0.43 and 0.16 in the Abstract and Results; the Discussion gives them as standard deviations). THC and 11-OH-THC were consistently higher in the concentrate group across assessments, including before use (Table 2, THC 0.01, 0.32, 0.03 against 0.004, 0.14, 0.02; 11-OH-THC 0.004, 0.011, 0.008 against 0.001, 0.005, 0.004 µg/mL); form effect for THC F(1,228) = 11.00, P < .01. The text reports no effects of labelled strength within a form on blood levels.

evidence.locator: Results › Subjective Drug Effects, paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Self-rated intoxication, the marijuana effects scale, tension and vigor peaked at the short-term assessment and decreased by 1 hour. Intoxication did not differ by form (form effect P = .11; means 0.08, 2.40, 1.93 in the flower group and 0.14, 2.35, 1.63 in the concentrate group); the marijuana effects scale did not differ by form (P = .18); tension (P < .01) and vigor (P < .001) were lower in the concentrate group across assessments. No associations with labelled strength are reported in the main text.

evidence.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis, paragraph; Results › Neurobehavioral Performance › Cognition, paragraph; Table 2; Figure 3
evidence.extracted: Delayed verbal recall errors rose after use in both groups (linear effect P < .001; flower 0.65, 2.21, 1.88; concentrate 0.90, 1.50, 2.33 before, short-term and 1 hour after); form effect P = .65, form by quadratic time P = .02 (above the set threshold). Inhibitory control and working memory scores rose over the session, which the authors suggest may reflect practice; inhibitory control was higher in the flower group across all assessments, with no short-term change and no association with labelled strength.

evidence.locator: Results › Neurobehavioral Performance › Balance, paragraph; Table 2; Discussion, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Eyes-closed sway rose after use and returned to its pre-use level by 1 hour in both groups (quadratic time P < .001; form effect P = .85). Eyes-open balance showed a trend (P = .05) that did not meet the a priori threshold; the eyes-closed head-back condition showed no change from before to after use. The authors describe about an 11% increase in sway with eyes closed, which they say is consistent with effects of moderate alcohol (as cited).

evidence.locator: Table 1; Results › Descriptive Information, paragraph; Methods › Baseline Appointment, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: At baseline, concentrate group against flower group: concentrate use on 16.5 against 3.5 of the past 30 days; flower use on 15.4 against 20.6 days; regular use begun at 17.7 against 20.0 years; baseline THC-COOH 0.087 against 0.044 µg/mL; product used at the session 0.11 g against 0.22 g. Between the two strength groups within each form there were no differences except in race among the concentrate groups (P < .01), and none in the amount used.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors write that there was no within-form association of labelled strength with blood levels, suggesting that people may titrate toward similar THC exposure as strength rises. For similar intoxication despite higher blood THC they offer greater tolerance in the concentrate group, receptor saturation, and individual differences in metabolism or sensitivity, and say future research must test them.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Limitations, paragraph
evidence.extracted: Ethical limits precluded random assignment to concentrate or flower, so pre-existing differences between the groups may partially account for the findings; there was no placebo control because such products do not exist on the legal market; federal rules restricted control over dosing and masking to product strength; interactions of cannabinoid strength and ratio, mode of use, expectancies and technique were not tested.

evidence.locator: Conclusions, paragraph; Key Points › Meaning
evidence.extracted: Delayed recall and balance impairment were associated with short-term use even in regular consumers; people who used concentrates showed similar or lower subjective intoxication and short-term impairment than people who used lower-potency flower forms of cannabis; THC exposure was much higher in the concentrate group, prompting concern about long-term clinical and neurobehavioral implications. The Key Points say concentrates were associated with higher THC exposure and potentially greater risk. Long-term and clinical outcomes were not measured.

evidence.locator: Author-information panel (Conflict of Interest Disclosures; Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor); Methods › Baseline Appointment, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Funding: NIH grant DA039707 (Hutchison) and Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment grant 96947 (Bidwell); the funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, manuscript preparation or the decision to submit. Disclosures: Bidwell reports grants from NIH/NIDA and the State of Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment; Ellingson NIH; Klawitter the department and NIH; Sempio the department and NIH; Bryan NIH and the State of Colorado; no other disclosures. Participants bought their assigned products at one local dispensary that set allotments aside for the study; no payment from the dispensary is declared.

evidence.locator: Results, 1st (unlabelled) paragraph; Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Study Selection Criteria, 1st paragraph; Methods › Study Selection Criteria › THC concentration of products, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Methods › Data Sources and Searches
evidence.extracted: Seven databases were searched (October 2021, updated July 2022; English language and human studies only) for human studies of any design that reported a THC concentration in any unit or a product from which a high concentration could be inferred. Searches identified 49,729 unique records, 5,828 full-text reports and 452 included studies: 225 observational studies, 142 randomized trials, 51 case reports and 34 case series. The earliest was published in 1971 and 60% (269) in 2017 to 2022.

evidence.locator: Results › Potential for Evidence Synthesis, paragraph
evidence.extracted: Of 452 studies, 54 (12%) examined a direct association between concentrates and a health outcome and 189 (42%) a direct association between THC concentration and an outcome; 114 (25%) examined an indirect association between THC concentration and outcomes and 62 (14%) an indirect association between concentrates and outcomes; 212 (47%) had a control group; effect estimates were reported in 184 (41%), measures of precision in 274 (61%), significance tests in 335 (74%) and raw data in 232 (51%).

evidence.locator: Results › Exposures, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Most studies concerned generic cannabis types (284, 63%); products typically high in concentration (oils, concentrates, hash, extracts, skunk, resins) were examined in approximately 2% to 10% of all studies. When THC was given as a percentage (172 studies, 349 exposures) the median was 12% (mean 17.4%, range 0% to 100%, interquartile range 3.6% to 24%); when given in milligrams (113 studies, 143 exposures) the median was 15 mg (mean 37.4, range 0.3 to 500, interquartile range 7.5 to 26). Units and indices varied.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Concentrations Studied, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Market strengths the authors cite from other sources: a 2018 survey of products sold in 7 US states found most products between 15% and 30% THC; in Colorado the average THC of flower assayed rose from 14% to 19% between 2014 and 2020 and that of concentrates from 46% to 68%. They describe the median of 12% studied as well below what is currently on the market and say the low strengths studied are likely due to the restriction of research cannabis in the United States to a federal supply that lacks concentrates.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Exposure Assessment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Study Selection Criteria › THC concentration of products, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors write that most studies failed to capture all the elements of cannabis use needed to estimate exposure dose, and recommend that studies at least report THC concentration, product used, frequency of use and route, in THC units that can be standardised. They state that THC concentration is not the same as dose.

evidence.locator: Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Funding and interests in the included studies: 24% (109) did not report a funding source and 32% (143) did not report whether authors had conflicts of interest; 25 studies (6%) were funded by the cannabis industry and 58 (13%) had an author who disclosed a financial tie with the industry.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Conclusions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion › Limitations, paragraph; Abstract
evidence.extracted: Conclusions: the review supports strong conclusions about the usefulness of the literature for characterising risks and benefits of the current marketplace; there are serious limitations in the generalisability of the studies to the current marketplace or to the people who buy its products; high-quality evidence on whether THC concentration should be regulated is scarce. Limits: searches were sensitive rather than specific; relevant studies may have been missed despite AI-assisted screening; heterogeneity of designs did not allow risk-of-bias assessment of individual studies; incomplete and inconsistent reporting left gaps in the extracted data.

evidence.locator: Acknowledgments, 1st paragraph; Conflicts of Interest, paragraph; Introduction, 2nd paragraph (PMC shows it under the Plain-Language Summary heading as its 3rd paragraph)
evidence.extracted: Funded by the State of Colorado under House Bill 21-1317, which asked the Colorado School of Public Health for a review of the physical and mental health effects of high-potency THC marijuana and concentrates; the funder was not involved in the design, conduct or publication of the paper. As printed: one author is a paid consultant as conflict-of-interest advisor for Health Canada, including its cannabis committees; one is a paid author for UpToDate for a chapter on cannabis intoxication; one has research funding from the Institute of Cannabis Research (Colorado State University) and serves on the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment's Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are printed.

evidence.locator: Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (pp. 736-737); Figure (p. 737); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 737); Discussion, 5th and 7th paragraphs (p. 748); Tables 1 to 4, risk-of-bias column
evidence.extracted: Systematic review of observational studies: MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO from inception to 14 January 2021 with English search terms, plus reference lists; human observational studies comparing higher- with lower-potency cannabis as each study defined it, for depression, anxiety, psychosis or cannabis use disorder; experimental studies, conference abstracts, editorials and correspondence excluded; PROSPERO CRD42021226447. 4,171 titles screened, 89 full texts assessed, 20 articles included, printed as 20 studies with 119,581 participants (8 on psychosis, 8 anxiety, 7 depression, 6 cannabis use disorder); by the editors' count the tables hold 16 distinct studies (the GAP study in four articles, EU-GEI in two), and the printed participant total is smaller than one included survey (181,870). None was rated good on a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (editors' count: 5 fair, 11 poor). No meta-analysis was possible because exposure was self-reported, no precise measure of THC exposure was available and definitions of higher and lower potency differed.

evidence.locator: Results, 3rd, 4th, 7th and 8th paragraphs (pp. 740-742); Table 1 (pp. 738-739)
evidence.extracted: Two case-control studies and one cohort, all rated fair. UK GAP study (410 patients with first-episode psychosis, 370 controls from the same area): against never-use, skunk-type use adjusted odds ratio 2.91 (95% CI 1.52 to 3.60), hash-type 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77), daily skunk-type use 5.40 (2.80 to 11.30); onset about 4 years earlier with higher- than with lower-potency use (hazard ratio 1.68, 1.08 to 2.63; adjusted for gender and frequency of use). EU-GEI study (901 patients and 1,237 population controls in England, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain and Brazil): types of 10% THC or more against never-use 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2), under 10% 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5); daily use 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3) and 2.2 (1.4 to 3.6). Both adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, education, employment, tobacco, alcohol and other drugs. UK cohort of 256 patients after a first episode: 58% of those who continued daily use of higher-potency cannabis relapsed within 2 years against 24% of those who had used cannabis in the past (adjusted odds ratio 3.28, 1.22 to 9.18); lower-potency or infrequent higher-potency use 1.82 (0.36 to 8.75); adjusted for alcohol, other illicit drugs, cigarettes, care intensity at onset and medication adherence. None of these three studies looked at concentrates as a separate form.

evidence.locator: Results, 5th, 6th, 9th, 15th and 21st paragraphs (pp. 740-747); Tables 1, 3 and 4 (pp. 739-746)
evidence.extracted: Studies of concentrates and one of liquid or resin cannabis, all cross-sectional and rated poor. 20-country online survey of 181,870 (self-report with pictorial aids; adjusted for age, gender, sexual orientation, education and other substance use), butane hash oil against lower-potency herbal cannabis: self-reported lifetime psychosis diagnosis 1.11 (0.85 to 1.46), anxiety diagnosis 1.80 (1.60 to 2.01; 1.72, 1.55 to 1.91, against higher-potency herbal), depression diagnosis 1.34 (1.21 to 1.48; 1.15, 1.03 to 1.25, against higher-potency herbal). US sample of 156: higher-potency concentrate use and psychosis symptoms r 0.11 (-0.20 to 0.40), anxiety 0.21 (-0.10 to 0.49), depression 0.17 (-0.15 to 0.45). US sample of 191, frequent concentrate against frequent herbal use: anxiety means 1.1 and 0.66, depression 0.72 and 0.76, no significant difference. Within-person survey of 574 people who used cannabis in the past year, mostly infrequently: psychosis-like experiences mean 1.1 with concentrates and 1.2 with herbal cannabis (0 to 10 scale; Cohen's d 0.12). 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders, liquid or resin against dry or herbal cannabis: residual or late-onset psychotic disorder odds ratio 0.212 (0.061 to 0.735), which Table 1 labels no association.

evidence.locator: Results, 14th, 15th, 20th and 21st paragraphs (pp. 746-747); Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 747-748); Tables 3 and 4 (pp. 743-746)
evidence.extracted: Anxiety, four cross-sectional studies (one fair): generalised anxiety disorder more likely with higher- than with lower-potency use in a UK sample of 1,087 aged about 24 (odds ratio 1.92, 1.11 to 3.32; adjusted for sex, childhood socio-economic position, depression score at 13 and frequency; rated fair); no difference between higher- and lower-potency herbal cannabis in the 20-country survey (1.05, 0.98 to 1.12). Depression, four cross-sectional studies (one fair): a slight increase in the 20-country survey (higher- against lower-potency herbal 1.18, 1.11 to 1.25) and little evidence in the UK sample (higher- against lower-potency 1.28, 0.68 to 2.32). Studies of people using medical cannabis (four for anxiety: one cross-sectional, rated fair, and three repeated-measures, rated poor; three repeated-measures studies for depression, all poor) gave varied results that the authors call hard to interpret. The authors conclude there is some evidence for anxiety and little for depression.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th, 6th, 8th and 9th paragraphs (pp. 748-749)
evidence.extracted: Most studies took potency from self-reported product type, an approximate proxy for THC content, and none accounted for THC intake as opposed to content; the authors argue that titration, which evidence suggests is partial, would be expected to weaken rather than inflate associations. Some studies compared higher with lower potency directly and others each with no use, so the contrast can be read only within each study. Cross-sectional designs cannot establish direction: people with poorer mental health might choose higher-potency cannabis as self-medication. There is no agreement on confounders; amount used was adjusted for in only one study; frequency was a covariate in some studies and part of a combined potency-and-frequency variable in others, and may be a confounder or a mediator.

evidence.locator: Contributors; Declaration of interests; Acknowledgments (p. 749); references 14, 15, 22, 27 and 30 (pp. 749-750)
evidence.extracted: Funding: Economic and Social Research Council South West Doctoral Training Partnership studentship (KP); Cancer Research UK Population Researcher Postdoctoral Fellowship C56067/A21330 and project award PPRCPJT\100023 (GT); Wellcome Trust 209158/Z/17/Z (LH); the funder had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing. Interests: GT reports previous funding from Pfizer (GRANT scheme) and owns a scientific consulting company doing work unrelated to the project; the other authors declare none. The reference list shows the senior author (T P Freeman) as an author of included studies, among them the 2017 butane hash oil survey and the 2019 EU-GEI paper, and L Hines as first author of the 2020 UK sample; no procedure for appraising the authors' own studies is described.

risk_of_bias.note: Field study (Bidwell 2020): ROBINS-E overall high; confounding and selection each high (self-chosen form, groups differing in concentrate days, years of regular use and baseline THC metabolite; volunteers who had used the strongest product before; 12 people left out by their post-use blood THC), no placebo, thirteen outcomes tested at a fixed threshold, near-threshold results described inconsistently. Scoping review (Bero 2023): AMSTAR 2 critically low (provisional), mainly because it does not assess bias in the studies it maps; it extracts no results. Systematic review (Petrilli 2022): AMSTAR 2 low confidence (provisional; the list of excluded studies is in an appendix not read); none of its 16 studies was rated good, and its concentrate studies are cross-sectional and rated poor.

inconsistency.note: One field study for the acute comparison; the scoping review reports no results to compare with it. For mental-health outcomes, the concentrate studies in the systematic review disagree with one another (more self-reported anxiety and depression diagnoses with butane hash oil in one survey, no clear association in two small US samples, slightly fewer psychosis-like experiences in a within-person survey, less chronic psychosis in a small clinical sample); they qualify the claim and do not change the rating of its acute finding.

indirectness.note: Regular consumers who had used the strongest assigned product before without a bad reaction, one dispensary in one state, one session of free use, blood measured about 13 minutes and 1 hour after use; impairment inferred from change in the same people without a placebo; the review's counts concern studies, not health effects.

imprecision.note: 121 people, 26 to 33 in each strength group; the reported null form effects (intoxication, recall, balance) come from a study not designed to show equivalence and give no confidence intervals; results at P = .02 and P = .05 are unresolved.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with one field study.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low (METHODS §6.3). The field study randomised labelled strength within each form but not the form, so the concentrate-against-flower comparison that this claim reports is observational. Risk of bias -1: ROBINS-E overall high (self-chosen form with baseline differences in concentrate use, years of regular use and THC metabolite; selected volunteers; no placebo or no-use session; exclusion of 12 people by an outcome; thirteen outcomes at a fixed threshold). The scoping review adds counts of what has been studied and no results, and is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (provisional: the appendix was not read) chiefly because it does not appraise the studies it maps. Indirectness -1: regular consumers, one dispensary, one session, blood at about 13 minutes and 1 hour, impairment inferred without a placebo. Imprecision -1: 121 people, 26 to 33 per strength group, no confidence intervals, null form effects from a study not built to show equivalence, results at P = .02 and P = .05 unresolved. These downgrades together pass the floor, so the certainty is very low. Not downgraded for inconsistency or publication bias: one field study. Worded as 'is associated with' because each person chose the form and the groups differed at baseline; the statement of what the scoping review found is a statement about the literature, not about health effects. The systematic review added in version 0.3.0 (Petrilli 2022; AMSTAR 2 low confidence, provisional) qualifies the claim without changing its rating: the psychosis associations it reports for stronger cannabis come from case-control and cohort studies that did not look at concentrates as a separate form, and its studies of concentrates and mental health are cross-sectional, rated poor and inconsistent with one another.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only, no advice. Rests on one field study of 121 regular consumers (Bidwell 2020: one group of researchers, one state, one session, follow-up one hour; registered as NCT03522103, protocol and supplement not read, so strength results are as the main text reports them), one scoping review that maps studies and extracts no results (Bero 2023: AMSTAR 2 provisional; appendix, evidence map and OSF protocol not read), and, from version 0.3.0, one systematic review of observational studies on potency and mental ill health and addiction (Petrilli 2022: read in full from the PDF by AI reader 93, first reader, 2026-10-23; AMSTAR 2 low confidence, provisional, appendix not read; its six anchors here are ai-located and need a second reader). Petrilli 2022's psychosis, anxiety and depression findings are added here as qualifying anchors; its cannabis use disorder findings, with Inman 2026 (narrative review of flower, concentrates and edibles and cannabis use disorder) and Leung 2020 (meta-analysis of how many people who use cannabis have a cannabis use disorder, as the base rate), are drafted as a separate section 7 claim, cl_can_potency_dependence (staged in data/claims/_incoming/can7_reader93.json), because dependence by strength and form is a different outcome and body of evidence from the acute comparison this claim reports. Petrilli's senior author is an author of the butane hash oil survey that gives the only positive concentrate findings here: a reason to read closely, not to discount. No cannabis-industry funding is printed for any of the three papers, so there is no industry-funded finding to pair; the review counts that 6% of the studies it maps were industry-funded and 13% had an author with an industry tie. The field study and the scoping review draw on money or advice from the Colorado state health department (Bidwell: its grant; Bero: state funding under House Bill 21-1317 and an author on the department's advisory committee): a reason to read closely, not to discount. Strengths, amounts and times appear only as study conditions or measured content (labelled strength, grams used, minutes after use); none appears in the plain wording. The 'strong conclusions' wording in Bero's Abstract refers to the usefulness of the literature, not to health effects.
