evidence.locator: Chapter 11: Cardiovascular diseases › Main findings › Heart rate; Blood pressure; Peripheral resistance and arterial stiffness; Comparisons with other reports, 1st paragraph; Conclusion, 1st paragraph; Implications, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review concludes that the extent to which vaping presents a risk for cardiovascular health remains uncertain, but that based on the toxicant profile in vaping products and aerosols the risk is expected to be much less than that of cigarette smoking (an expectation, not a measured rate). It states that, as in 2018, there is still no available evidence on whether vaping is associated with clinical cardiovascular outcomes (coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease) or subclinical atherosclerosis; that 27 of the 41 included studies were cross-over or acute exposure studies, which cannot answer questions about the cardiovascular health outcomes most relevant to public health; and that studies comparing rates of cardiovascular diseases between non-users, users of tobacco and users of nicotine vaping products are needed. Measured: immediately after use vaping increased heart rate less than smoking; in pooled cross-sectional studies of longer vaping (at least 3 months or one year) people who vaped had lower blood pressure than people who smoked and no difference from people who neither vaped nor smoked; the longest follow-up of arterial stiffness after switching was 4 months.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Summary page › Chapter 16 › introductory paragraphs, 2nd paragraph; Evidence statements, 1st paragraph; Chapter 1 › Objective of the report, 1st paragraph; Issues addressed, 3rd paragraph and its list; Authors and citation. Main findings page › 1. The review, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review's closing chapter states that, despite the increase in research on vaping since 2015, weaknesses in the choice of assessments and biomarkers, populations, groups studied and exposure, and study designs all limit the conclusions that can be drawn. Its 61 evidence statements broadly follow the National Academies' definitions of level of evidence, and the authors write that, as the National Academies noted, the framework is a guide and a great deal of expert judgement, here by the report's co-authors, is involved. The scope left out two questions: vaping and later smoking (a Cochrane review of people under 30 was examining it) and the effectiveness of vaping for stopping smoking (covered in the series' previous report and by a Cochrane living review). The report is the eighth in a series described as independent and commissioned by Public Health England and then the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities; it was led by academics at King's College London with international collaborators (eight authors are named); the pages read carry no competing-interest statement.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › Evidence Review: Methods, 1st paragraph; Evidence Review: Results › Comparison of Toxic Levels in E-Cigarettes and Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes, 3rd to 6th paragraphs and Synthesis
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, four studies compared emissions from e-cigarettes and combustible cigarettes (three laboratory studies and one comparison based on published literature). Using published data and assuming 15 puffs equal one cigarette, selected toxic compounds in smoke were 9- to 450-fold higher than in aerosol (Goniewicz et al., 2014). Of 150 chemicals examined, about 100 were detected in smoke and 16 were generated by one e-cigarette, and toxicants were 82% to more than 99% lower per puff in the aerosol depending on the list and puffing method (Margham et al., 2016). Smoke held about 1,500 times more harmful and potentially harmful constituents than aerosol or room air (Tayyarah and Long, 2014). Of 11 metals with smoke data, the aerosol of one cartomizer was higher for four (aluminium, iron, nickel, sodium), within the smoke range for five and lower for two (Williams et al., 2013). The committee's synthesis: aerosol is substantially less complex than smoke and, except for nicotine, exposure to potentially toxic substances under typical conditions of use is significantly lower (substantial evidence, Conclusion 5-3). The studies are laboratory measurements, not measurements in people.

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Switched from Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes to E-Cigarettes › Comparison of Nicotine and Toxicant Exposure, 2nd to 11th paragraphs (Cravo; 5-day study; Goniewicz; McRobbie; Shahab); Synthesis; Conclusion 18-1
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, studies that followed people who switched from cigarettes to e-cigarettes lasted from 5 days to 8 months; examples: a 12-week trial of 420 people (urinary biomarkers of benzene, acrolein and a nitrosamine fell); a 5-day trial of 105 people (urinary biomarkers 29% to 95% lower in those who switched partly or completely; exhaled carbon monoxide down 88% to 89% in the groups that switched completely or stopped all nicotine); 20 people over 2 weeks (a nitrosamine breakdown product, NNAL, down 57% after 1 week and 64% after 2 weeks); and 40 people over 4 weeks (carbon monoxide down 80% in those who only vaped and 52% in those who also smoked). One cross-sectional study compared 181 people who had used these products for a long time, in five groups: nitrosamine and volatile organic compound breakdown products were lower in people who only vaped, or only used nicotine replacement, than in people who smoked, and similar in people who smoked only, vaped and smoked, or used nicotine replacement and smoked (Shahab et al., 2017). Synthesis: all studies showed significantly reduced biomarkers of exposure to potentially toxic chemicals in people who switched, and nicotine intake in people who had stopped smoking and were experienced at vaping was comparable to that from cigarettes. Conclusion 18-1: conclusive evidence that completely substituting e-cigarettes for cigarettes reduces exposure to numerous toxicants and carcinogens (the committee's judgment).

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › Evidence Review: Methods, 2nd paragraph; Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Switched… › Health Risk Profile (Carnevale; Cibella; Flouris; Wadia), Comparison of Nicotine and Toxicant Exposure (Martin), Toxicity in In Vitro and Animal Studies, 1st paragraph; Synthesis (after the animal studies); Conclusion 18-2
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, the committee found 15 longitudinal observational and cross-over studies of health outcomes in people who switched from cigarettes to e-cigarettes (follow-up from single sessions to about two years; several retrospective record reviews). Examples: a one-year randomised trial of 300 people found no significant differences in lung-function indexes between groups defined by what people did after the trial began, except one flow measure (forced expiratory flow 25-75%) that rose in those who quit smoking, with cough, phlegm and breathlessness falling over follow-up (Cibella et al., 2016); in 15 people white blood cell counts rose after cigarettes but not after e-cigarettes in 30-minute sessions (Flouris et al., 2012); in a cross-over study of 20 adults who smoked and 20 who did not, acute use of either product changed markers of oxidative stress and blood-vessel function, with flow-mediated dilation and vitamin E effects not statistically different between the products and the e-cigarette showing a lesser effect on three other markers (Carnevale et al., 2016); and gingival inflammation increased in 20 people after 2 weeks of vaping instead of smoking (Wadia et al., 2016). A cross-sectional study, a design the Methods say was left out of the 15, compared nasal biopsies from 12 people who vaped, 14 who smoked and 13 who did neither: immune genes suppressed in people who smoked were also suppressed in people who vaped, with more gene changes and stronger suppression (Martin et al., 2016). In cell studies 21 of 27, and in animal studies 3 of 5, favoured e-cigarettes as less harmful than cigarettes and none found them more harmful than cigarettes. Synthesis: health effects of e-cigarettes are still not well understood but current evidence points to them being less harmful than cigarettes; all but one of the human studies showed significant short-term improvements in people who switched, though most studies were small; some studies found similar harm and none found e-cigarettes more harmful among people who switched to exclusive e-cigarette use; whether e-cigarettes reduce health risk still needs support from epidemiological studies and randomised trials. Conclusion 18-2: substantial evidence that completely switching from regular cigarette use to e-cigarettes results in reduced short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems (the committee's judgment).

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › opening section, 4th paragraph; Evidence Review: Levels of Evidence Available, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: As described in the chapter's opening, the committee writes that e-cigarettes have not been theoretically or experimentally proven to be safe, and that the evidence reviewed in the report suggests they may be less harmful than combustible cigarettes in at least some scenarios. It adds that, because the efficacy of e-cigarettes to actually reduce harm remains unclear, some researchers have raised concerns, citing McKee and Capewell (2015): continued use of a substance with its own potential health risks (including uncertainty about long-term risks), a possible increase in use of conventional tobacco products through starting and relapse, and questionable terms of engagement with the tobacco industry. The chapter states that epidemiological studies and randomised trials of the long-term health effects of exclusive e-cigarette use would give the strongest evidence of harm reduction and that, in their absence, the committee looks at biomarkers of disease and exposure levels. The chapter gives no overall figure for how much less harmful e-cigarettes are. The McKee and Capewell article itself (a BMJ Analysis) is anchored separately in this claim.

evidence.locator: Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Use E-Cigarettes Concurrently with Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes (Dual Users) › Synthesis; Conclusions 18-3 and 18-4
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies, for people who keep smoking while also using e-cigarettes (dual use) the committee found limited evidence on patterns of use and a lack of evidence on exposure and health outcomes among those who do not reduce their smoking. People with dual use did not on average smoke fewer cigarettes than people who smoked only, although e-cigarettes may help some of them maintain a reduction in smoking; the committee writes that it is very unlikely that people who do not reduce smoking after starting e-cigarettes will reduce the health risks of smoking, and that they may be exposed to additional adverse effects of e-cigarettes. Conclusion 18-3: no available evidence whether or not long-term dual use changes illness or death compared with smoking only. Conclusion 18-4: insufficient evidence that e-cigarette use changes short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems in people who continue to smoke. These are the committee's judgments.

evidence.locator: Opening section (before the first heading), 1st and 2nd paragraphs; References 1 to 3
evidence.extracted: The editorial states that in July 2013 a group of 12 experts rated the relative harm of 12 nicotine-containing products on 14 criteria for harm to self and others (reference 1, Nutt et al., 2014, not read), concluding that combustible cigarettes were the most harmful and e-cigarettes substantially less harmful, and that the result was repeated in the popular media as e-cigarettes being 95% less risky or 95% less harmful than combustible cigarettes. It adds that the authors of the 2013 work noted as a limitation the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most of the criteria (quoted from page 224 of that paper); that Public Health England and the Royal College of Physicians endorsed and publicised the assertion; that senior Public Health England staff emphasised the evidence underlying the figure despite its being lacking; and that much was written questioning the figure's validity in 2014 to 2016 (no source cited for the last two). All of this is the authors' account: none of the originals was read.

evidence.locator: Today's Electronic Cigarettes Are Different, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors argue that products today differ from those of July 2013 to the extent that the 2013 estimate, even if valid then, can no longer apply: many devices reach a power output 10 to 20 times that of most over-the-counter 2013 models and so make more aerosol, exposing the person vaping to more nicotine and other toxicants and people nearby to more of any harmful aerosol constituents, and raising the chance of malfunction; there are thousands of flavours whose lung toxicity is unknown; and liquids with protonated nicotine (nicotine salt) are widely marketed and, relative to free-base nicotine, are less aversive to inhale, which the authors say allows higher nicotine concentrations and likely more dependence. No source is cited in the text for the statements on power, flavours or dependence; reference 4 (Jackler and Ramamurthi, 2019, not read) is cited for the marketing of protonated nicotine liquids and the 'nicotine arms race'; the online Appendix A, a nonexhaustive list of evidence of harm, was not read.

evidence.locator: Second headed section (harm to cells), 1st paragraph; third headed section (harm in people), 1st paragraph; references 5 and 6
evidence.extracted: The authors state that e-cigarette aerosols contain toxicants and are harmful to living cells in vitro and in vivo (volatile aldehydes, carcinogenic furans, chloropropanols and acetal compounds are named) and that animals exposed to aerosol show adverse effects, including in cardiovascular models (no source cited). For people they cite one report of airway epithelial injury in healthy young adults who smoked cigarettes occasionally and used an e-cigarette with or without nicotine (two randomised trials, Chaumont et al., 2019); state without a citation that wheezing has been associated with use and that heart rate, blood pressure and platelet activation rise while flow-mediated dilation and heart rate variability fall; and cite a one-page item in a journal supplement (reference 6, a conference abstract by its citation), which they call a preliminary report, for a possibly higher risk of heart attack and coronary artery disease in people who vape. The section headings state harm categorically; the conclusion speaks of potential harm.

evidence.locator: Electronic Cigarettes Increase Smoking Risk, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors quote the National Academies' conclusion of substantial evidence that e-cigarette use raises the risk of ever using cigarettes among young people and young adults, and argue that, to the extent that first use of e-cigarettes causes later smoking in someone who would otherwise never have smoked, vaping could be considered as harmful as smoking for that person. The statement is conditional on causation and concerns a person who would not otherwise have smoked, not the comparison of vaping with smoking in people who already smoke.

evidence.locator: Electronic Cigarette Aerosol Is Not Harmless, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors argue that differences in toxicant content between aerosol and smoke, by themselves, cannot show lesser lethality, because toxicity depends on the extent and mode of use; that propylene glycol is toxic when injected over days and that aerosols containing it and glycerol cause inflammation in human lungs (no source cited); and that, because the toxicants sometimes differ, so might the diseases. They also state that there is little doubt that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco-specific nitrosamines or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, largely absent from the aerosol, and that what diseases they may die of, and whether use hastens death, will be part of the evidence needed for valid risk estimates. The editorial offers no estimate of the size of the difference.

evidence.locator: Conclusions; Call to Action
evidence.extracted: Conclusion: the 2013 estimate, which lacked evidence, cannot be valid today and should not be relied upon further; future estimates should rest on the evidence now available and be revised as evidence accrues. The call to action calls the 95% safer estimate a factoid, unreliable information repeated until accepted as fact, and asks readers to highlight its unreliable provenance, the changes in devices and liquids, the accumulation of evidence of potential harm, the increased prevalence of use and the growing evidence that e-cigarette use is associated with later smoking. The editorial gives no alternative figure and does not weigh the evidence on lower toxicant exposure in people who switch: it is an argument, with no data, search or appraisal of the studies it cites.

evidence.locator: Acknowledgments; Conflicts of Interests
evidence.extracted: Funding as printed: US National Institutes of Health grants and the Center for Tobacco Products of the US Food and Drug Administration; the sponsor had no role in the preparation of the work. Interests as printed: two authors are paid consultants in litigation against the tobacco industry and are named on a patent for a device that measures the puffing behaviour of people who use electronic cigarettes; one of them has also, since September 2019, been a consultant in litigation against the electronic cigarette industry; another author reports personal fees from Hydra Biosciences LLC and Sanofi SA and non-financial support from GlaxoSmithKline Pharmaceuticals, outside the submitted work. No tobacco or vape industry funding of the editorial is stated.

evidence.locator: Abstract › Data sources, Data synthesis, Registration; Methods › 1st paragraph; Top-up review; Inclusion and exclusion criteria, 1st paragraph; Risk of bias assessment; Integrated data analysis › GRADE assessment, Data synthesis; Discussion › 3rd paragraph, last sentence
evidence.extracted: The Australian review combines an umbrella review of 8 major independent reviews published 2017 to 2021 with a top-up systematic review (searched July 2020, for studies published July 2017 to July 2020), 400 publications in all; the systematic review is registered in PROSPERO and labelled prospective, but its protocol was posted on 31 August 2020, after the search; the top-up studies were appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools and the evidence graded with GRADE and the National Academies framework. It is based on work commissioned by the Australian Department of Health. It looked at the health effects of e-cigarettes in people and excluded animal, in vitro and biomarker studies as outside its scope, so, on the editors' reading, the biomarker evidence on which the UK review's conclusion on relative harm mainly rests was not counted (the Australian authors note that the UK review focused on comparing e-cigarettes with smoking and on biomarkers).

evidence.locator: Results › Health outcomes, Box 3, rows 'Cardiovascular disease (21)', 'Cancer (1)' and 'Respiratory disease (58)'; the three paragraphs after Box 3
evidence.extracted: Australian review, Box 3 (health outcome, number of studies): cardiovascular disease (21 studies): clinical outcomes such as heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death, and subclinical atherosclerosis: no available evidence; other cardiovascular outcomes in people who smoke: moderate evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes acutely increase heart rate, blood pressure and arterial stiffness, limited evidence of endothelial dysfunction and limited evidence that long-term nicotine e-cigarette use after switching from smoking reduces blood pressure; in people who do not smoke, insufficient evidence. Cancer (1 study): invasive cancer and pre-cancer outcomes: no available evidence. Respiratory disease (58 studies): asthma, bronchitis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: insufficient evidence in people who smoke and none for people who do not; reduced exacerbations or progression in people who smoke and switch: insufficient evidence. The review states that evidence is insufficient or unavailable on cardiovascular disease, cancer, respiratory conditions other than lung injury and most other conditions, and rated the certainty of evidence for clinical and subclinical outcomes low or very low.

evidence.locator: Limitations, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review states that e-cigarettes are relatively new, diverse and changing rapidly, that long-term evidence is unavailable and that the products studied do not necessarily reflect current options (limited information on newer nicotine salt products). It describes confounding between the effects of e-cigarette use and of smoking as a major problem that statistical adjustment is unlikely to fully overcome, particularly for the health conditions most affected by smoking, because older people who vape generally smoke regularly, are trying to quit or have quit, while younger people who vape often do not smoke regularly; it concludes that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to quantify the effects of e-cigarettes and that people neither smoking nor using e-cigarettes should be the main comparison group. Statements that e-cigarettes are safer than smoking, and terms such as tobacco harm reduction, may be useful when discussing the minority of people who smoke who use e-cigarettes to quit completely but are not applicable to people who do not smoke; comparisons with the effects of smoking do not permit reliable ascertainment of the direct health impact of e-cigarettes.

evidence.locator: Limitations, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review rated the certainty of evidence very low for most clinical and subclinical outcomes. It notes that the tobacco and related industries can influence research, so its risk-of-bias assessment took account of competing interests such as financial support from tobacco or pharmaceutical industries; it writes that risks of bias were noted across health outcomes, but significant concerns in other domains meant they were unlikely to have large effects on its interpretation or the overall certainty of evidence. It states that it applies the precautionary principle (exposure to an agent with uncertain effects to be avoided), which it considers appropriate when serious adverse impacts are scientifically plausible, particularly those affecting future generations. Products not reported as nicotine or non-nicotine were assumed to be largely nicotine e-cigarettes (Box 3 note).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review states that a key finding of its synthesis was the general paucity of evidence on the effects of nicotine and non-nicotine e-cigarettes on many major clinical outcomes, including cancer, cardiovascular, metabolic, mental health, developmental, reproductive and neurological outcomes (other than seizures). It describes an English review it found after its search (reference 40, the UK review of 2022) as noting the lack of direct evidence on major clinical outcomes and that most serious adverse events were infrequent, as focusing on comparing the effects of e-cigarette use with those of smoking and on biomarkers, and as generally finding more favourable results for e-cigarettes than for cigarettes. It concludes that its findings concur broadly with those of other major reviews, including that the direct impact of e-cigarettes on clinical disease outcomes is largely unknown.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph; Conclusions, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review notes that in many countries dual smoking and e-cigarette use is the most frequent pattern of e-cigarette use and that the direct health impact of dual use is unknown. It writes that e-cigarettes may be beneficial for people who smoke who use them to quit completely and promptly, but that the limited evidence, their risks, uncertainty about effects on major clinical outcomes and continued smoking by most people who use them leave their overall safety and efficacy unclear. Its conclusions: strong or conclusive evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes can be harmful to health, particularly for people who do not smoke and for children and adolescents (a statement not framed against smoking); evidence for effects on most important health outcomes uncertain; people who smoke and switch completely and promptly may benefit.

evidence.locator: Results › Smoking behaviour, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Box 4, row 'Smoking uptake (28)'; Discussion, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Meta-analyses of 25 longitudinal studies found strong evidence that young people who have never smoked and who use e-cigarettes are about three times as likely as those who do not to start smoking tobacco and to go on to smoke regularly (residual confounding cannot be excluded; the review deemed the link likely causal on Bradford-Hill criteria); limited evidence that people who had stopped smoking and use e-cigarettes are about twice as likely to resume smoking. The review names this, with poisoning, dependence (addiction) and toxicity from inhalation, among the risks that disproportionately affect people who do not smoke and young people. This concerns the harm of starting to smoke, a different comparison from vaping against smoking, and the UK review left it out of its scope.

evidence.locator: Acknowledgements, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Competing interests; Methods, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Funding and interests as printed: the review was conducted as part of an independent programme examining the health impacts of e-cigarettes, funded by the Australian Department of Health and the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC); the report on which the article is based was reviewed by members of the NHMRC Electronic Cigarettes Working Committee and staff of the Australian Department of Health and went through an independent methodological review as part of standard NHMRC processes; competing interests: no relevant disclosures. The work also provided evidence for the 2021 update of the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners smoking cessation guidelines and a 2022 statement of the NHMRC Chief Executive Officer.

evidence.locator: Quality of the evidence, 3rd paragraph, 1st and 2nd sentences; 4th paragraph, last two sentences; reference 12
evidence.extracted: The authors write that the prominently featured 95% less harmful figure in the 2015 English report was not, as might be expected, based on a detailed review of evidence supplemented by modelling, but came from a single meeting of 12 people convened to develop a multicriteria decision analysis model synthesising their opinions on the harms of different nicotine-containing products, summarised in a research paper (Nutt et al., 2014, reference 12, not read). They report that the paper itself conceded, as a limitation, the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most criteria, and that none of the links or limitations they describe is discussed in the 2015 report. This is the authors' account; the 2014 paper and the 2015 report were not read. It matches the account in the 2020 editorial anchored above, which quotes the same limitation, so the two are critics' accounts that agree, not independent checks.

evidence.locator: Quality of the evidence, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; references 13 to 17
evidence.extracted: On the meeting's funding and membership, as the authors report it: one sponsor, a company called EuroSwiss Health, is one of several companies registered at one address near Geneva with the same chief executive, who is reported to have received funding from British American Tobacco for a book on nicotine as harm reduction (the book states that its conclusions were developed independently of the company) and who endorsed that company's public health credentials in its 2013 sustainability report; a supporting organisation, Lega Italiana Anti Fumo, had as chief scientific adviser one of the 12 attendees, who declared funding from an e-cigarette manufacturer but not funding he is reported elsewhere to have received from Philip Morris International. The rationale for choosing the panel is not given; it included several known e-cigarette advocates, some declaring industry funding in the paper, and some people not known for expertise in tobacco control; Public Health England's tobacco lead attended. The authors quote the paper's statement that the sponsor had no role in any stage of the process or in the writing and was not present at the workshop. The ties are sourced to a company register entry, two Tobacco Tactics web pages, the book and a company report (none read) and are worded as reported; the article does not claim that they changed the ratings. Recorded as a reason to read the 2014 paper closely, not as evidence about harm.

evidence.locator: Quality of the evidence, 2nd paragraph (begins on p. 1); reference 11
evidence.extracted: The authors argue that where risks are uncertain the precautionary principle should apply, so that, without scientific consensus that a substance is not harmful to the public, the burden of proof lies with those taking an action; that the report's headline message, widely quoted in the media, that best estimates show e-cigarettes to be 95% less harmful to health than cigarettes seemingly left little room for uncertainty about long-term risks; and that the report did not cite a 2014 systematic review (Pisinger and Døssing, reference 11, not read) that found serious methodological problems in many of its 76 studies, a third (34%) published by authors with conflicts of interest, and concluded that no firm conclusions on safety could be drawn, while adding that e-cigarettes could hardly be considered free of harm.

evidence.locator: Defining the role of e-cigarettes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; references 8 and 9
evidence.extracted: The authors describe two sides that compare with different references: supporters focus on people who already smoke and compare e-cigarettes with smoking, while those concerned about uptake by people who would not otherwise smoke and about long-term effects argue that, although e-cigarettes lack some of the most harmful substances in cigarettes, such as tar, they contain others, such as formaldehyde (a carcinogen) and diverse flavourings, so non-smoking should also be a comparison. They add that reduced smoking, as opposed to quitting, may not lower the overall risk of death (a 16-year Copenhagen cohort of 19,732 people, reference 8, not read); that two thirds of people who use e-cigarettes also smoke (no source given), a pattern the 2015 report rarely mentions; and that in one cohort dual use among people who vaped daily apparently stayed above 80% after 12 months of follow-up (reference 9, not read).

evidence.locator: Uncertainty around harms, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Where next for policy on e-cigarettes?, 2nd paragraph (ends on p. 3); Key messages box (page headed Page 4 of 3)
evidence.extracted: The authors state that none of the research so far (in context, on youth uptake and a gateway to smoking) can be considered conclusive and longer-term studies are needed; that the report seemed to equate a lack of evidence of risk to bystanders with evidence of no effect; that it omitted the lack of evidence on the risks of long-term dual use; that perhaps its most striking feature was a consistent adoption of the most optimistic position on limited evidence; and they agree with England's chief medical officer that evidence on the long-term use of e-cigarettes is still lacking. Key messages: Public Health England's endorsement of the safety and efficacy of e-cigarettes rests on uncertain evidence, and public health strategies should follow the precautionary principle until better evidence is available. The article offers no estimate of its own of how much less harmful e-cigarettes are than cigarettes, presents no new data, does not discuss measurements of toxicant exposure or short-term health measures in people who switched from smoking, and reports no reply from the authors of the 2015 report or of the 2014 paper. The National Academies' summary of its concerns (the National Academies anchor above) matches its themes, except relapse, which the article does not mention.

evidence.locator: Author affiliations (p. 1); Competing interests; Provenance and peer review (p. 3)
evidence.extracted: Interests as printed: the authors have read and understood BMJ policy on declaration of interests and have no relevant interests to declare. Provenance: not commissioned; externally peer reviewed. No funding statement is printed. The article is a BMJ Analysis article, not an editorial; its authors are professors of European public health (London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine) and of clinical epidemiology (University of Liverpool).

evidence.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 1st to 4th paragraphs; references 28 to 31
evidence.extracted: In a 2022 commentary on the Australian review, the authors argue that the review did not address relative risk and that a meaningful assessment of the risk of vaping nicotine compares it with the far greater risk of continuing to smoke, because most people who vape frequently are current or former smokers who could not stop by other methods (no source given). They write that harm reduction from vaping rests on substantially lower exposure to toxins and carcinogens in vapour than in smoke (references 28 and 29) and is confirmed by considerably lower biomarkers in the blood, urine and saliva of people who switch (references 30 and 31, which by their titles compare exposure between groups, one of them cross-sectional), and that smoke contains over 7,000 toxic chemicals and solid particles while vaping aerosols generally have fewer than 100 detectable chemicals, most at far lower concentrations (reference 29). None of the cited studies was read. The commentary does not mention the 95% figure, the 2015 report or the 2015 critique.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full

evidence.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 11th and 12th paragraphs; references 49 and 50
evidence.extracted: The authors write that, given the reduced number and dose of carcinogens in vapour, lifetime cancer risk from vaping has been estimated at less than 0.5% of that from smoking (references 49 and 50, which by their titles estimate cancer potency or lung cancer risk from emissions and particle measurements; not read), and that the Cochrane review detected no evidence of harm in studies of up to 2 years, although the studies were few and longer ones are needed. The cancer figure is a modelled estimate from what aerosol contains, not a measured rate of cancer in people who vape.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full

evidence.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 5th to 9th paragraphs; references 32 to 45
evidence.extracted: The commentary grants several limits: the effect of inhaled flavourings is largely unknown and could carry risk, with no harm shown so far and ongoing monitoring needed; most cardiovascular effects of vaping are consistent with those of nicotine (transiently raised pulse and blood pressure, cardiac contractility, arrhythmogenesis), and nicotine may pose some risk in people with existing cardiovascular disease; and human studies on cardiovascular outcomes are limited. For benefit it cites two studies with sustained falls in blood pressure and one with better vascular function after 4 weeks in people who switched, and improved respiratory symptoms, lung function, asthma, COPD, mucociliary clearance and fewer respiratory infections after switching. Seven of the nine human studies or reviews cited (references 35, 36 and 38 to 42) share authors, by the author lists printed, and the sentence on in vitro and animal studies cites two human studies (references 39 and 40, by their titles) and no animal study.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full

evidence.locator: 5 Net public health effects of vaping, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; references 51 to 54
evidence.extracted: The authors argue that the key public health question is the net population effect, which depends on the harm difference between vaping and smoking, on effectiveness for stopping smoking and on uptake by people who do and do not smoke; they report that numerous modelling studies, with one exception, conclude that benefits considerably exceed harms (one US model, under current patterns of vaping and substitution: 1.8 million premature smoking- and vaping-attributable deaths avoided and 38.9 million life-years gained from 2013 to 2060). As they describe them, these models evaluate net effects under a wide range of assumptions about the reduction in harm compared with smoking, so they take the size of the difference as an input rather than measuring it (editors' reading). None of the models was read.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493-1498), read in full

evidence.locator: Conflict of interest
evidence.extracted: No funding statement is printed. Interests as printed: Colin Mendelsohn was a board member of the Australian Tobacco Harm Reduction Association (ATHRA), a registered health promotion charity, from October 2017 to January 2020, and Alex Wodak is a board member; ATHRA accepted unconditional seed funding from the vape retail industry to get established, which ceased in March 2019; both were directors in March 2018 when ATHRA received a donation from Knowledge Action Change Communications, a UK private sector public health agency, sourced from a surplus from the Global Forum on Nicotine conference in May 2017; that agency is legally separate from Knowledge Action Change, which has received two grants from tobacco companies (in 2012 a small development research grant from Nicoventures, then owned by British American Tobacco, to evaluate a nicotine delivery device in Scottish prisons, conducted with the Scottish Prison Service and publicly declared; in 2018 a grant for preparing The Global State of Tobacco Harm Reduction report from the Foundation for a Smoke-Free World, which is funded by an annual grant from Philip Morris International and whose bylaws and pledge agreement are stated to preclude any influence by Philip Morris International and the tobacco industry over how it spends its funds or focuses its activities). Mendelsohn is the author of the book Stop Smoking Start Vaping (Aurora Press); he and Wodak state that they have never received payments from electronic cigarette or tobacco companies; Wayne Hall and Ron Borland have no interests to declare. Recorded as a reason to read closely, not to discount.

risk_of_bias.note: The 95% figure began as an expert rating (known here only through the editorial's account); the UK review's pooled biomarker results include many tobacco-industry-funded confinement trials of up to 7 days and most of its studies had methodological concerns; the National Academies' human studies were mostly small and several tested a manufacturer's own product (the chapter does not say who funded them); the editorial, the 2015 analysis and the 2022 commentary appraise nothing (cards sc_eissenberg_2020, sc_mckee_2015 and sc_mendelsohn_2022: overall high) and the Australian review applies a precautionary principle and excluded biomarker studies. The reviews are read as summaries, not at the study level.

inconsistency.note: Counted once, under risk of bias: the sides read a largely shared body of evidence differently and answer different questions (exposure and short-term measures against clinical outcomes and starting to smoke); the exposure findings themselves point the same way.

indirectness.note: The question is lifetime harm (disease and death). What is measured is exposure biomarkers, short-term measurements (single sessions to 12 months in the UK review; to about two years in the National Academies' studies) and expert ratings; products have changed since most of the studies and newer ones are little studied.

imprecision.note: No estimate of harm is pooled, so precision is not rated.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources.

grade.reasoning: Observational, indirect evidence (exposure biomarkers, short-term measurements and expert judgement) starts low and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on the size of the difference, which is what the sources support, with the direction (lower exposure to smoke toxicants) reported beside it. The National Academies' conclusive and substantial ratings concern exposure and short-term outcomes in people who switched completely, not lifetime harm; the UK review's statement is an expert judgment on a body of evidence that reaches only 12 months, as its authors say, and the Australian review's reading rests on a different set of evidence. Overlapping reports are counted once. The 2015 analysis and the 2022 commentary, read in full (McKee & Capewell, 2015; Mendelsohn et al., 2022), add arguments about where the figure came from and which comparison matters, not measurements, and change no rating.

debate.question: How much less harmful than smoking is vaping: does the evidence support the often-quoted figure of at least 95% less harmful (smoking at least 20 times more harmful), and can anyone show the size of the difference yet?
debate.evidence_yes: The UK government-commissioned review (McNeill et al., 2022, King's College London, commissioned by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities) states that, on the evidence it reviewed, its own 2015 estimate that vaping is at least 95% less harmful than smoking remains broadly accurate over the short and medium term, and that it may now be better to say that vaping carries only a small fraction of the risks of smoking. Under that sits its systematic review of exposure biomarkers: against people who smoke, people who vape had lower levels in pooled analyses of nitrosamine breakdown products (58% to 94% lower), of acrolein, acrylonitrile and butadiene breakdown products (71%, 94% and 83% lower) and of blood carboxyhaemoglobin, with nicotine levels not different in people who vaped and smoked at least weekly; the better-run studies of short and medium term effects found no major causes of concern; immediately after use vaping raised heart rate less than smoking; in longer cross-sectional studies blood pressure was lower in people who vaped than in people who smoked; and the review expects cardiovascular risk to be much less than that of smoking from the toxicant profile (an expectation, not a measurement). The National Academies (2018, chapter 18, as the committee describes it) rated as conclusive the evidence that completely substituting e-cigarettes for cigarettes reduces exposure to numerous toxicants and carcinogens, and as substantial the evidence that completely switching reduces short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems: all but one of the human studies it reviewed, lasting from single sessions to about two years, showed short-term improvement and none found e-cigarettes more harmful among people who switched; laboratory emissions of smoke constituents were 9- to 450-fold higher than of aerosol, toxicants were 82% to more than 99% lower per puff, and 21 of 27 cell studies and 3 of 5 animal studies favoured e-cigarettes. A 2022 commentary on the Australian review (Mendelsohn et al., 2022; no funding statement; interests as printed, in full in the anchor: two of the four authors were or are board members of the Australian Tobacco Harm Reduction Association, a registered health promotion charity that accepted unconditional seed funding from the vape retail industry until March 2019, and both state they have never received payments from electronic cigarette or tobacco companies; one is the author of a book titled Stop Smoking Start Vaping; the other two declare no interests) does not mention the 95% figure but argues that a meaningful assessment compares vaping with the far greater risk of continuing to smoke, since most people who vape frequently are current or former smokers who could not stop by other methods. It cites substantially lower exposure to toxins and carcinogens from vapour than from smoke (over 7,000 toxic chemicals in smoke against fewer than 100 detectable chemicals in aerosols, as cited), lower biomarkers in people who switched (cited to two group comparisons of exposure), sustained falls in blood pressure, better vascular function and better respiratory measures in people who switched (seven of the nine human studies or reviews it cites share authors), modelled estimates that lifetime cancer risk from vaping is less than 0.5% of that from smoking, and no evidence of harm in the Cochrane review's few studies of up to 2 years; none of these studies was read. Even the critics grant part of this: the editorial says there is little doubt that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco-specific nitrosamines or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, the Australian review says people who smoke and switch completely and promptly may benefit, and the 2015 analysis grants that e-cigarettes lack some of the most harmful substances in cigarettes, such as tar.
debate.evidence_no: The earliest critique read is a BMJ analysis article published in September 2015, shortly after the English report (McKee & Capewell, 2015; not commissioned; externally peer reviewed; no relevant interests declared; no funding statement). It argues that the prominently featured figure came not from a detailed review of evidence with modelling but from a single meeting of 12 people who built a multicriteria decision analysis model of their opinions on the harms of nicotine-containing products, and that the resulting paper conceded the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most criteria (Nutt et al., 2014, not read); that the chief executive of the meeting's sponsor and the chief scientific adviser of a supporting organisation, who attended, are reported elsewhere to have received tobacco-company funding (sources: a company register, web pages, a book and a company report; the 2014 paper states that its sponsor had no role and was not present); that the panel's selection was not explained and included known e-cigarette advocates; and that the English report discussed none of this. It argues that where risks are uncertain the precautionary principle should apply, with the burden of proof on those who act; that the report did not cite a 2014 systematic review of 76 studies that found serious methodological problems and concluded that no firm conclusions on safety could be drawn; that people who do not smoke should also be a comparison, because e-cigarettes, while lacking some of the most harmful substances in cigarettes such as tar, contain others such as formaldehyde and flavourings; and that dual use matters (two thirds of people who use e-cigarettes also smoke, no source given; above 80% after 12 months among people who vaped daily in one cohort), because cutting down, unlike quitting, may not lower the risk of death. It offers no estimate of its own and presents no data. Five years later a six-author editorial in the American Journal of Public Health (Eissenberg et al., 2020; funding and interests as printed: US National Institutes of Health grants and the FDA Center for Tobacco Products; two authors are paid consultants in litigation against the tobacco industry and named on a patent for a puffing-behaviour device, one of them also a consultant in litigation against the e-cigarette industry since September 2019; one author reports fees from two pharmaceutical companies) argues that the figure came from a July 2013 rating by 12 experts of 12 products on 14 criteria whose own authors listed the lack of hard evidence for most harms of most products on most criteria as a limitation (as the editorial quotes; the 2013 paper was not read), that Public Health England and the Royal College of Physicians nonetheless endorsed it, that devices and liquids have changed (power output 10 to 20 times higher in many devices, thousands of flavours, nicotine salts), that evidence of potential harm from cell, animal and short-term human studies has accumulated, that lower toxicant content in aerosol does not by itself show lower lethality, and that the estimate cannot be valid today; it offers no alternative figure and cites a conference abstract for its heart-attack claim. The Australian review (Banks et al., 2023; funded by the Australian Department of Health and the National Health and Medical Research Council; no relevant disclosures) holds that comparisons with smoking do not permit reliable ascertainment of the direct health impact of e-cigarettes, that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to quantify effects and people who neither smoke nor vape the main comparison group, that evidence on clinical cardiovascular disease and invasive cancer is not available, and that certainty is very low for most clinical and subclinical outcomes; it rates acute rises in heart rate and blood pressure after nicotine e-cigarette use in people who smoke as moderate evidence. The National Academies state that e-cigarettes have not been proven safe, give no overall figure for how much less harmful they are, say that long-term epidemiological studies and randomised trials would be the strongest evidence and are lacking, and describe concerns raised by McKee and Capewell (2015) about continued use of a product with its own risks, more use of conventional tobacco products and engagement with the tobacco industry (their summary matches the themes of that article, described above, except relapse, which it does not mention). The UK review itself says that, against people who use no nicotine, exposure to harmful substances is similar or higher; that the degree of any residual risk remains unclear; that acute vaping might impair blood-vessel function as much as acute smoking; that its findings reach at most 12 months of follow-up; and that vaping is not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked. The 2022 commentary on the other side grants that human studies on cardiovascular outcomes are limited, that nicotine may pose some risk in people with existing cardiovascular disease and that the effects of inhaled flavourings are largely unknown.
debate.neither_can_show: No source read reports how often any disease, or death, occurs in people who only vape compared with people who smoke or who use no nicotine: the UK review could summarise follow-up of no more than 12 months and says the size of any residual risk is unclear; it and the Australian review each report no available evidence on clinical cardiovascular outcomes such as heart attack and stroke, and no evidence on cancer risk relative to smoking or non-use (UK, quoting the National Academies) or on invasive cancer (Australian). The 95% figure was an expert rating across several criteria, not a ratio of disease rates (as the 2020 editorial and the 2015 analysis describe it, two critics' accounts that quote the same limitation; the 2014 paper and the 2015 report were not read, the UK pages read give no basis for the 2015 figure, and no source read reports a reply from the figure's authors to this account), and the UK review's reaffirmation is its own judgment from biomarker evidence, not a measured ratio. A level of a chemical in the body is not a risk: a 90% lower level of a carcinogen breakdown product does not by itself give a 90% lower risk of cancer. Most people who vape smoked for many years before, and past smoking changes many biomarkers; no study read compares people who smoked for many years and quit, whether or not they now vape, or follows people who vape and have never smoked for years, so neither the comparison with smoking nor the comparison with using no nicotine can be made cleanly. The two reviews do not weigh the same evidence: the UK review rests mainly on exposure and potential-harm biomarkers, which the Australian review excluded, while the Australian review asks about clinical outcomes (and about starting to smoke, which the UK review left to a Cochrane review) and takes people who use no nicotine as its main comparison. The 2022 commentary on the Australian review states the same divide from the other side: the comparison that matters is with continuing to smoke, argued from exposure, short-term and modelled evidence, while the 2015 analysis asks for both comparisons; none of these sources brings a measured rate of disease. Both are government-commissioned and both rest on judgment: the UK authors assess an estimate stated in their own earlier series of reports (three of the eight 2022 authors are among the six named for the 2015 report in the editorial's reference list) and say a great deal of expert judgement is involved in their evidence statements; many of their pooled results come from tobacco-industry-funded trials in confinement of up to 7 days, with independent work still called for; the Australian review applies a precautionary principle and assumed products not reported as nicotine or non-nicotine were nicotine e-cigarettes; the editorial argues one side with no data, and its authors' interests are as printed above. In many countries the most frequent pattern is to vape while still smoking (the Australian review), and the National Academies found no evidence on the long-term health of people who do so; products have changed since most of these studies and newer ones are little studied.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). From the sources read so far (the Australian review, the editorial, the 2015 analysis and the 2022 commentary read in full; a National Academies chapter and the UK review's summary pages as they describe the studies), two things are reported consistently: against people who smoke, people who vape have much lower levels of many smoke-related toxicants in the body and, in people who switched completely, better short-term measures of breathing and circulation, although some short-term effects, such as blood-vessel function after a single session, were similar to smoking; and nobody has measured how much the rates of disease and death differ. Against people who use no nicotine, exposure to harmful substances is similar or higher. Neither the lower exposure nor the lack of long-term data is disputed in the sources read; the editorial disputes only that lower toxicant content by itself shows lower lethality. What is disputed is whether the old at least 20-fold figure, which began as an expert rating, can still stand as a size: the UK review says it broadly does for the short and medium term, as its own judgment; the 2015 analysis, the editorial and the Australian review say it cannot be relied on. The strongest argument for the figure is the consistency and size of the exposure reductions across independent pooled analyses and the finding that no study showed more harm in people who switched completely; the strongest against is that none of this is a rate of disease, the longest follow-up summarised was a year, and the pooled evidence rests on measurements of chemicals in the body, some from industry-funded trials. The 2015 analysis and the 2022 commentary, now read in full, do not change this: the first questions where the figure came from and how the meeting behind it was chosen and funded, the second argues for the comparison with smoking from exposure and modelled evidence, and neither brings a measured rate. The editors offer no number: any figure would claim more than the sources show, and both halves belong together: much lower exposure to smoke toxicants than smoking, and not risk-free.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Cohorts that follow people for decades with biologically verified use and count disease and death separately for people who only vape, people who smoke, people who smoked and have quit with and without vaping, people who both smoke and vape, and people who have never used nicotine, reported as absolute risks so that the difference can be read directly; independent biomarker studies outside confinement, with follow-up beyond 12 months and agreed biomarkers and definitions (the UK review's own list); a transparent, repeatable estimate that sets out the outcomes, their weights and the evidence for each, updated for current devices and liquids and pre-registered (as the editorial calls for), produced by a panel chosen by stated rules with declared interests (the 2015 analysis's objection); and trials or natural experiments comparing people who switch completely with people who keep smoking on clinical outcomes. None of the sources read reports any of these: the longest follow-up the UK review could summarise was 12 months and the longest in the National Academies chapter was about two years.

statement: In adults who smoke and had not smoked for at least 2 hours, who were not using nicotine replacement or in a stop-smoking programme and were mostly not trying to quit, in 19 randomized trials pooled from their raw data (a systematic review searched to May 2011; 15 trials with 797 observations for strength of desire to smoke and 17 with 837 for desire to smoke; Haasova et al., 2013), a short bout of exercise, mostly moderate walking or cycling, compared with sitting quietly or a similar passive activity is associated with less desire to smoke rated right afterwards: about 2 points less on a 1-to-7 scale (strength of desire −1.91, 95% CI −2.59 to −1.22; desire to smoke −2.03, −2.60 to −1.46). The abstract calls these standardized mean differences, but the methods compute differences in scale points. Every trial pointed the same way, but the size ranged from a fraction of a point to more than 4 points (I² 92% to 94%), and the three trials that included isometric (muscle-tensing) exercise showed among the smallest effects. Craving was rated only once, immediately or 5 minutes after exercising, so how long the reduction lasts, and whether it helps people stop or stay stopped, were not studied. Participants knew whether they had exercised, the review did not assess the trials' risk of bias, and 17 of the 19 trials list at least one of the review's authors. The review was paid for from internal institutional funds, and its authors report no connection with the tobacco or pharmaceutical industries. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In 19 small studies, people who had not smoked for a few hours rated their urge to smoke lower straight after a short walk or bike ride than after sitting still, by about 2 points on a 7-point scale. Every study found the same direction, but the size varied a lot, and tensing muscles while sitting helped least. The urge was measured only minutes later, people knew whether they had exercised, and no study here checked whether exercise helps people stop smoking.
population: Adults who smoke, abstaining for at least 2 hours in laboratory studies, not using nicotine replacement or in a cessation programme, mostly not trying to quit
exposure: A single short bout of physical activity, mostly moderate walking or cycling (study conditions in the study card)
comparator: Sitting quietly or another passive condition (listening, a video, a cognitive task, body scanning)
outcome: Self-rated strength of desire to smoke and desire to smoke (single 7-point items) immediately or 5 minutes after the bout, adjusted for the rating before
magnitude: Two-stage random-effects IPD meta-analysis: strength of desire −1.91 points (95% CI −2.59 to −1.22), 15 trials, 797 observations, I² 94.2%; desire to smoke −2.03 (−2.60 to −1.46), 17 trials, 837 observations, I² 92.0%. One-stage model: −1.89 and −2.03, with 95% of trials' true effects expected between −3.56 and −0.22 and between −3.45 and −0.62. Single trials −0.22 to −4.54.

evidence.locator: Methods › Search strategy; Inclusion/exclusion criteria
evidence.extracted: Searches ended on 31 May 2011 and were limited to English-language papers from 2004 onwards; eligible trials were randomized crossover or parallel trials with at least 2 hours of abstinence before baseline; people in cessation programmes or using NRT were excluded.

evidence.extracted: 19 randomized trials (7 parallel, 12 crossover; 14 published, the rest theses) with 10 to 84 participants each; bouts of 5 to 40 minutes, mostly moderate walking or cycling, against passive controls; craving rated immediately before and after the bout, or 5 minutes after it in three studies.

evidence.extracted: Every study favoured exercise, from −0.22 to −4.54 points for strength of desire; the three studies that included isometric exercise had among the smallest effects, with intervals including zero in two of them for strength of desire (−0.55 and −0.22), and the largest effect came from the study with the highest baseline craving.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 26); Methods › Data analyses, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 28); Results › One-stage individual participant data meta-analysis (p. 32)
evidence.extracted: The abstract reports the pooled results as standardized mean differences, but the methods derive each effect as the difference between groups in post-intervention ratings adjusted for baseline, and the one-stage model reports a mean difference.

evidence.locator: Results › Literature search (p. 28); Study characteristics and quality assessment, 4th paragraph (p. 30); Declarations of interest (p. 35); References 27-29 and 39-67 (pp. 36-37)
evidence.extracted: Titles were screened by the first author alone; quality was reported only as randomization (one study allocated by recruitment order); the review was paid for from internal institutional funds, and the authors report no connection with the tobacco or pharmaceutical industries; editors' count from the reference list and the text: 17 of the 19 included trials list at least one of the review's authors.

risk_of_bias.note: Participants could not be blinded to exercising and the outcome is a self-rating taken minutes later; the trials' risk of bias was not assessed; most trials are by the review's authors.

inconsistency.note: All trials favour exercise, but the size ranges from about 0.2 to 4.5 points (I² 92% to 94%), only partly explained by the kind of exercise.

indirectness.note: Worded for the population and timing studied (temporary abstinence, craving minutes after exercise); quitting is not claimed.

imprecision.note: Narrow pooled intervals.

publication_bias.note: Unpublished theses were included and gave similar results; no small-study test; not downgraded.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high. Risk of bias −1 (unblinded self-rated outcome, no appraisal of the trials, trials mostly by the review's authors) and inconsistency −1 (a tenfold range in size) give low. Worded as an association because the size, and how much of it is exercise rather than expectation, are uncertain, although the design is randomized. Status replicated: 19 trials from several research groups point the same way; agreement with an earlier aggregate meta-analysis (Roberts et al., 2012) is not counted as independent because the trials overlap.

statement: In adults who smoked, mostly moderately to heavily, and stopped (12 placebo-controlled trials published from 1984 to 2000, with 15 to 240 people each; a systematic review without pooling, funded by SmithKline Beecham; West & Shiffman, 2001), using nicotine gum (8 trials), a nicotine inhaler (3) or a sublingual nicotine tablet (1) compared with a placebo product is associated with fewer withdrawal symptoms in the first week after stopping: irritability was lower in all 9 trials that reported it, total withdrawal discomfort in 6 of 7, anxiety in 3 of 4 and low mood in the only trial that reported it, while results were mixed for restlessness (2 of 5), poor concentration (5 of 9), sleep disturbance (1 of 2) and hunger (2 of 5). Craving was lower in 7 of 11 trials: in all 4 trials of the inhaler or tablet but in only 3 of the 7 gum trials. The review counted significant results and gives no sizes; where a trial did not report a symptom the table is blank, so non-significant results may be missing. Five trials kept people who had smoked again in their analyses, more people dropped out of the placebo groups in three, and one trial used low-nicotine gum as its comparator. No trial of the lozenge was found, nothing is known beyond the first week, and patches and nasal spray were not included. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In 12 older studies, people who had just stopped smoking were less irritable in the first week if they used nicotine gum, an inhaler or a tablet than if they used a dummy product without nicotine. Most studies also found less overall discomfort and anxiety. Cravings were lower in all the inhaler and tablet studies but in fewer than half of the gum studies. The review only counted which studies found a difference, not how big it was, and a medicine company (SmithKline Beecham) paid for it.
population: Adults who smoked (mostly moderate to heavy smoking), without psychiatric or acute physical illness, who stopped in placebo-controlled trials published 1984 to 2000
exposure: Oral nicotine products: nicotine gum, inhaler or sublingual tablet (study conditions in the study card)
comparator: A placebo product of the same kind (low-nicotine gum in one trial)
outcome: Withdrawal symptoms and craving in the first week of abstinence, counted as significant or not in each trial
magnitude: No effect sizes. Fractions of trials with a significant reduction: irritability 9/9, depression 1/1, anxiety 3/4, total withdrawal 6/7, craving 7/11 (gum 3/7; inhaler 3/3; tablet 1/1), poor concentration 5/9, restlessness 2/5, hunger 2/5, sleep disturbance 1/2.

evidence.extracted: Of 27 studies reporting effects of oral nicotine on at least one withdrawal symptom, 12 met the criteria (published placebo-controlled randomized trials, product started within 24 hours of stopping, symptoms assessed over at least 24 hours in the usual environment, biochemical verification): 8 gum, 3 inhaler, 1 sublingual tablet and no lozenge; good data existed only for the first week.

evidence.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 117); Table 3, craving column (p. 121)

statement: In adults who have used classic psychedelics, evidence is insufficient to say whether anything people do during a difficult experience makes it shorter or easier: no study read here tested a way of coping, and what is known is what people say helped, looking back. Two independent surveys agree only that a calming or accepting response (trying to calm the mind; letting go or accepting the experience) was the one most often named as helpful; their lists and questions differed, so their percentages cannot be compared. In a self-selected online survey of 529 people recalling a challenging experience with a classic psychedelic or an analogue (psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, DMT or mescaline; use combined with non-classic drugs such as MDMA or ketamine was allowed) (Wood et al., 2024), the responses, of 26 listed, most often tried and judged helpful were letting go, accepting or surrendering (84.5%), observing the mind without fighting it (77.3%) and closing the eyes or lying or sitting down (73.9%); the least often were directing anger at the experience (9.4%), trying to sleep (9.7%), telling it to stop (10.6%) and taking another drug or alcohol (12.1%). People who judged more of the 11 responses that the authors grouped as acceptance and reappraisal helpful rated their emotional breakthrough higher (r = 0.50), but that group also includes breathing, closing the eyes, questioning the experience, telling it to stop and directing anger at it; both were rated at one sitting, sometimes years later, and judging a response helpful may itself reflect how the experience ended. Sixteen people who had attended psilocybin retreats, chosen because their difficult ceremonies had been followed by personal change, wrote of breathing on purpose, opening their eyes and moving, engaging with the surroundings, asking for help, and facilitators' touch, listening, reassurance and reminders to breathe, among other responses. In a US online panel, 613 adults who had used a classic psychedelic, including 362 who said they had never had a challenging experience, ticked what had helped during their most challenging one: trying to calm the mind 257 (41.9%), changing location 168 (27.4%), asking a friend for help 124 (20.2%), changing the people around 124 (20.2%), smoking cannabis 113 (18.4%) and changing the music 99 (16.2%); fewer ticked drinking alcohol (54, 8.8%) or taking another drug (22, 3.6%) (Simonsson et al., 2023). No study tested any of these responses, including taking cannabis, alcohol or another drug, which in the other survey was among the responses least often judged helpful (12.1%). As summarized second-hand in a mini review (Piercey et al., 2024), 91% of respondents to an earlier survey of difficult experiences with psilocybin mushrooms used at least one such strategy and rated them only modestly effective, and 65.9% of surveyed callers to a psychedelic peer-support phone line (the drugs they had taken are not stated) said it helped ease their distress. None of these studies compared people who did something with people who did not. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Looking back, people most often said that letting go, watching their thoughts without fighting them, calming the mind, or closing their eyes and lying down helped during a difficult trip; moving somewhere else or asking a friend also came up. None of the studies tested whether any of these actually helps: no study compared people who did them with people who did not.
population: Adults who have used classic psychedelics and recalled a challenging experience: a self-selected online sample (529), retreat attendees chosen for personal change after difficult ceremonies (16) and a US online panel (613, including 362 who said they had never had a challenging experience)
exposure: Responses during a challenging experience (accepting, observing, lying down, calming the mind, changing place, people or music, asking for help, taking another drug), as respondents recalled them and judged their helpfulness
comparator: None: no comparison of people who used a response with people who did not
outcome: Self-judged helpfulness during the experience; emotional breakthrough rated afterwards (Emotional Breakthrough Inventory)
magnitude: No effect estimates. Tried and judged helpful (Wood et al., 2024; n = 529): letting go 84.5%, observing the mind 77.3%, closing the eyes or lying down 73.9%; least often anger 9.4%, trying to sleep 9.7%, telling it to stop 10.6%, another drug or alcohol 12.1%. Count of the 11 responses grouped as acceptance and reappraisal judged helpful, against emotional breakthrough rated at the same sitting: r = 0.50. Ticked as helpful (Simonsson et al., 2023; n = 613, including 362 who said they had never had a challenging experience): calming the mind 41.9%, changing location 27.4%, asking a friend 20.2%, changing the people around 20.2%, cannabis 18.4%, changing the music 16.2%, alcohol 8.8%, another drug 3.6%. The two surveys' percentages are not comparable (different lists, questions and denominators). Second-hand (Piercey et al., 2024): 91% used strategies, rated modestly effective; 65.9% of helpline callers found it helpful.

statement: In people who use classic psychedelics outside research or therapy, evidence is insufficient to say whether harm reduction habits lower the chance of a difficult experience. The one survey read here that measured both (Palmer and Maynard, 2022; pre-registered) asked 163 self-selected, mostly male, experienced people (median 11.5 lifetime uses), reached through university societies and online psychedelic communities, to recall their first experience (a median of 42 months earlier) and their most recent one (a median of 2 months earlier): which listed practices they had used before, during and after, how challenging it had been (Challenging Experience Questionnaire) and how much emotional breakthrough it brought (Emotional Breakthrough Inventory). A score adding up the practices each person used, each weighted by how important the sample rated it for safety, correlated weakly with lower challenge for the first experience (r = −0.21, 95% CI −0.35 to −0.06) and not significantly for the most recent (r = −0.15, −0.30 to 0.00), and with more breakthrough on both occasions (r = 0.24, 0.09 to 0.38), 2 to 6% of the variation (editors' intervals and calculation). The score counted practices after the experience, which cannot have shaped it, was weighted by the respondents' own judgments, was recalled at the same sitting as the outcomes and was not adjusted for anything, and people who stopped after a difficult first experience could not take part. Scores were higher for the most recent experience (48.7 against 40.1), for practices before and after use but not during it, while challenge scores were about the same (17.1 and 17.3% of the maximum). Most were with trusted friends, a practice the sample rated important; few had a sober sitter, which it rated low; and few tested their drugs, although testing was rated important. In a US online panel, 182 of 613 people (29.7%) linked their most challenging experience to having had no preparation; that link went with slightly higher challenge ratings for the same experience, rated at the same sitting (standardized beta 0.09), but not with later thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others (adjusted odds ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.56 to 2.45) (Simonsson et al., 2023). A mini review that relies heavily on the first survey for its outcome evidence summarizes it as more strategies going with fewer challenging experiences, which overstates it (the score was weighted, and the link with challenge held for the first experience only); the review adds a catalogue of strategies named in the literature and finds outcome research scarce: besides that survey, one preparedness-scale study of psychedelic use (drug class not stated), one ketamine study (design not stated) and, for MDMA, a rapid scoping review whose reference is a preprint, all second-hand (Piercey et al., 2024). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small survey, people who recalled using more safety habits had slightly easier first trips, but not clearly easier recent ones, and the habits counted included things done after the trip. People remembered everything at once, often years later, and those who stopped after a difficult first trip could not take part. A review found almost no other studies of whether these habits work.

outcome: Challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire), emotional breakthrough (Emotional Breakthrough Inventory), thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others

(2023): no preparation linked to the most challenging experience by 182 of 613; challenge standardized beta 0.09; thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others adjusted OR 1.17 (0.56 to 2.45).
